# Runwick documentation

> Runwick is a background-job library for .NET 10. An app writes a job to a store (PostgreSQL, SQLite or Redis) and a worker, in the same process or another, runs its handler. Delivery is at-least-once; schedules, retries, rate limits, uniqueness, a transactional outbox, a management API, a dashboard and a CLI are included.

---

# Introduction

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/introduction

> Runwick is a background-job library for .NET 10 that stores jobs in PostgreSQL, SQLite or Redis and runs them on workers you control.

Runwick is a background-job library for .NET 10. Your app writes a job to a store (PostgreSQL, SQLite or Redis), and a worker picks it up and runs your handler. The worker can run inside your app or in a separate process.

It is a library, not a service. There is no Runwick server to deploy. The store is the single source of truth, and workers never talk to each other: they talk to the store.

![Runwick dashboard: a job's details, status history and the resources each attempt used](/images/dashboard-job.png)

## How it works

<Steps>
  <Step title="You describe a job and a handler">

A job is a plain record with a stable name. A handler is a class that knows what to do with it.

```csharp
[JobName("email.welcome")]   // the stored name; CLR type names are never stored
public sealed record SendWelcomeEmail(Guid UserId) : IQueueJob;

public sealed class SendWelcomeEmailHandler : IJobHandler<SendWelcomeEmail>
{
    public Task HandleAsync(SendWelcomeEmail job, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        // Do the work. This code may run more than once.
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}
```

  </Step>
  <Step title="Your app dispatches it">

```csharp
await dispatcher.DispatchAsync(new SendWelcomeEmail(userId));   // IJobDispatcher from DI
```

`DispatchAsync` returns only after the store has confirmed the write.

  </Step>
  <Step title="A worker runs it">

A worker reserves the job from the store, holds a lease on it while it runs, and records the result. If the handler fails and there are attempts left, the job waits for a retry delay and runs again. If it runs out of attempts, it ends up `failed`, where an operator can retry it.

  </Step>
</Steps>

Producer, worker, scheduler and management are roles, not separate programs. One process can take any combination of them. See [Choosing a store](/docs/choosing-a-store) for the common shapes.

## What you get

- **Three stores, one API.** PostgreSQL is the reference store, for many hosts. SQLite suits a single machine. Redis needs one durable primary. Your jobs and handlers do not change between them.
- **Retries and timeouts.** Each job has an execution budget (3 by default) and an exponential, partly random retry delay. Timeouts are off unless you set one.
- **Queues and priorities.** Worker pools read named queues with high, medium and low lanes. Queues can be paused.
- **Uniqueness, rate limits and concurrency caps.** All off until you declare them.
- **Schedules.** Cron and one-time schedules that create at most one job per occurrence.
- **Same-transaction work.** On PostgreSQL and SQLite, you can create a job, or complete one, in the same transaction as your own data.
- **Transactional outbox.** Commit a message with your business data, then deliver it to any store.
- **Operations.** A management HTTP API, a web dashboard and the `runwick` command line. All three share the same permissions and audit trail.
- **Observability.** OpenTelemetry traces and metrics, structured logs and health checks.

## What it promises, and what it does not

Runwick's guarantees are deliberately narrow, and the docs say so plainly.

- **At-least-once delivery.** A handler can run more than once: after a crash, a lost lease or a lost reply. Write handlers that are safe to repeat, and pass an idempotency key to outside systems.
- **One exactly-once case.** If your handler's effect is a change in the same PostgreSQL or SQLite database as Runwick's tables, the change and the job's completion can commit together. Nothing else is exactly-once: not emails, not HTTP calls, not Redis.
- **Cooperative cancellation.** Cancelling a job signals its `CancellationToken`. Runwick cannot stop code that ignores the token.
- **A lease running out does not prove the old handler stopped.** Two copies of a handler can briefly overlap.
- **Durable settings are checked, not assumed.** Runwick refuses store settings that could lose jobs, such as SQLite without `synchronous=FULL` or Redis without `appendfsync always`.

<Callout type="warning" title="Pre-1.0">
The API and storage formats can still change before 1.0. The work to certify the stores for 1.0 (Windows and macOS checks, a reference benchmark and a 24-hour soak test) is not finished, so no store is labelled "certified" yet.
</Callout>

[Delivery guarantees](/docs/delivery-guarantees) has the full list.

## Requirements

- .NET 10. Every package targets `net10.0` only.
- One store: PostgreSQL 16, 17 or 18; a local SQLite file (the engine is bundled); or Redis 8.2 or newer.
- No Node or npm. The dashboard's web files are inside its package.

# Installation

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/installation

> Install Runwick and one store package, add the optional packages you need, install the CLI and create the store's schema.

Runwick is split into small packages. Every app needs `Runwick` and exactly one store package. Everything else is optional.

## Packages

| Package | Install when |
|---|---|
| `Runwick` | always, in any process that dispatches or runs jobs |
| `Runwick.Postgres` | your store is PostgreSQL |
| `Runwick.Sqlite` | your store is a SQLite file on one machine |
| `Runwick.Redis` | your store is a single Redis primary |
| `Runwick.Contracts` | you want to share job types with a project that has no database code. It holds `IQueueJob`, `IJobHandler<T>`, the attributes and `IJobDispatcher` |
| `Runwick.AspNetCore` | you want the [management HTTP API](/docs/management-api) or the [health checks](/docs/health-checks) |
| `Runwick.Dashboard` | you want the [web dashboard](/docs/dashboard). It brings in `Runwick.AspNetCore` |
| `Runwick.OpenTelemetry` | you want [metrics and traces](/docs/observability) |
| `Runwick.Outbox` | you want the [transactional outbox](/docs/outbox), plus `Runwick.Outbox.Postgres` or `Runwick.Outbox.Sqlite` for the source database |
| `Runwick.Testing` | reserved for test helpers. It has no public types in this release; see [Testing](/docs/testing) for the patterns to use today |
| `Runwick.Cli` | a .NET tool, installed with `dotnet tool install`. The command is `runwick` |

Use the same version for every Runwick package.

## Add the packages

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="PostgreSQL">

```bash
dotnet add package Runwick
dotnet add package Runwick.Postgres
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="SQLite">

```bash
dotnet add package Runwick
dotnet add package Runwick.Sqlite
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Redis">

```bash
dotnet add package Runwick
dotnet add package Runwick.Redis
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

Add the optional packages the same way, for example:

```bash
dotnet add package Runwick.Dashboard        # dashboard (includes the management API package)
dotnet add package Runwick.OpenTelemetry    # metrics and traces
```

## The command line tool

The `runwick` command migrates stores, raises one-time capabilities, and talks to the management API for jobs, queues and workers.

```bash
dotnet tool install --global Runwick.Cli
runwick version
```

See [CLI](/docs/cli) for the full command list.

## Requirements

- **.NET 10.** Every package targets `net10.0` only. There are no .NET 8, .NET 9, .NET Framework or .NET Standard builds.
- **No Node or npm.** The dashboard's web files ship inside its package.
- **One store:**
  - **PostgreSQL** 16, 17 or 18 (18 is the reference version). Connect to the primary directly.
  - **SQLite** 3.38 or newer. The engine is bundled with `Microsoft.Data.Sqlite`, so there is nothing to install. The file must be on a local disk.
  - **Redis** 8.2 or newer, one standalone primary with durable settings (see below).

The tested operating systems are Linux x64 and Windows x64. Runwick makes no claim for Native AOT or trimming.

## Create the schema

Workers never change the schema when they start. You create it once, as a deployment step, before the first app starts. Running the migration again on a store that is already up to date does nothing.

Each store has a `MigrateAsync` method, and the CLI runs the same code.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="PostgreSQL">

```csharp
using Runwick.Postgres.Migrations;

var result = await RunwickPostgresMigrations.MigrateAsync(connectionString);
Console.WriteLine($"schema revision {result.SchemaRevision}");
```

```bash
export MY_CONN="Host=localhost;Database=app;Username=migrator;Password=..."
runwick migrate --provider postgres --connection-env MY_CONN
```

Run the migration with a role that may create schemas. Everything goes into one schema, `runwick`, and that name cannot be changed. Your running app can then use a role with data access only.

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="SQLite">

```csharp
using Runwick;

await RunwickSqliteMigrations.MigrateAsync("Data Source=/var/lib/my-app/runwick.db");
```

```bash
export MY_CONN="Data Source=/var/lib/my-app/runwick.db"
runwick migrate --provider sqlite --connection-env MY_CONN
```

Use a file on a local disk. A file on a network share, or an in-memory database, is refused when the app starts.

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Redis">

```csharp
using Runwick;

await RunwickRedisMigrations.MigrateAsync("localhost:6379");
```

```bash
export MY_CONN="localhost:6379"
runwick migrate --provider redis --connection-env MY_CONN
```

The server must run with these settings, or Runwick refuses to start:

```bash
redis-server --appendonly yes --appendfsync always --no-appendfsync-on-rewrite no \
  --maxmemory-policy noeviction --aof-load-truncated no
```

Replicas, Redis Cluster and Sentinel are refused.

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

<Callout type="info" title="Connection strings stay out of your shell history">
The CLI never takes a connection string as an argument. Pass the name of an environment variable with `--connection-env`, or pipe the string in with `--connection-stdin`.
</Callout>

# Quick start

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/quick-start

> Go from an empty project to a background job that a worker picks up and runs.

This page builds one small console app that is both a producer and a worker. It dispatches a job, and its own worker runs it. The same job and handler work unchanged when you later split them into a web app and a separate worker service.

You need the .NET 10 SDK and one store. Docker is the quickest way to get PostgreSQL or Redis; SQLite needs nothing.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Create a project and start a store">

```bash
dotnet new worker -n QuickStart
cd QuickStart
dotnet add package Runwick
```

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="PostgreSQL">

```bash
dotnet add package Runwick.Postgres
docker run -d --name runwick-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pg -p 5432:5432 postgres:18
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="SQLite">

```bash
dotnet add package Runwick.Sqlite
# no server: the store is a file on local disk
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Redis">

```bash
dotnet add package Runwick.Redis
docker run -d --name runwick-redis -p 6379:6379 redis:8.2 \
  redis-server --appendonly yes --appendfsync always --no-appendfsync-on-rewrite no \
  --maxmemory-policy noeviction --aof-load-truncated no
```

Runwick refuses a Redis server without these durability settings.

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

  </Step>
  <Step title="Define a job and its handler">

Create `Jobs.cs`. A job is a record that implements `IQueueJob` and has a `[JobName]`. The name is what gets stored, so you can rename or move the C# type later without breaking jobs already in the store.

```csharp
using Runwick;

namespace QuickStart;

[JobName("email.welcome")]
public sealed record SendWelcomeEmail(Guid UserId) : IQueueJob;

public sealed class SendWelcomeEmailHandler(ILogger<SendWelcomeEmailHandler> logger, IJobContext context)
    : IJobHandler<SendWelcomeEmail>
{
    public Task HandleAsync(SendWelcomeEmail job, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        // Stop promptly when cancellationToken is cancelled. This code may run more than once.
        logger.LogInformation("Welcome email for {UserId}, execution {Execution}", job.UserId, context.ExecutionNumber);
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}
```

The handler is created from dependency injection, in a fresh scope for each run, so constructor injection works as usual. `IJobContext` tells it which job and which execution it is on.

  </Step>
  <Step title="Create the schema">

Workers never create the schema themselves. Run the migration once, before the app starts. In a real deployment this is a separate step with its own credentials; here it runs at the top of `Program.cs` to keep things short.

Delete the template's `Worker.cs` and replace `Program.cs` with:

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="PostgreSQL">

```csharp
using QuickStart;
using Runwick;
using Runwick.Postgres.Migrations;

var conn = "Host=localhost;Username=postgres;Password=pg;Database=postgres";
await RunwickPostgresMigrations.MigrateAsync(conn);
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="SQLite">

```csharp
using QuickStart;
using Runwick;

var conn = "Data Source=runwick.db";
await RunwickSqliteMigrations.MigrateAsync(conn);
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Redis">

```csharp
using QuickStart;
using Runwick;

var conn = "localhost:6379";
await RunwickRedisMigrations.MigrateAsync(conn);
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

You can run the same migration from the command line instead: `runwick migrate --provider postgres --connection-env MY_CONN`. See [Installation](/docs/installation#create-the-schema).

  </Step>
  <Step title="Register Runwick and a worker">

Continue `Program.cs` below the migration. Only the `Use...` line depends on the store.

```csharp
var builder = Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddRunwick(runwick =>
{
    runwick.Application("quickstart")
        .UsePostgres(conn)                       // or .UseSqlite(conn) or .UseRedis(conn)
        .AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining<SendWelcomeEmail>();
    runwick.AddHandler<SendWelcomeEmail, SendWelcomeEmailHandler>();
    runwick.AddWorker(w => w.Pool("main", p => p.Queues("default").FixedConcurrency(4)));
});

using var host = builder.Build();
await host.StartAsync();
```

- `Application("quickstart")` names your app inside the store, so several apps can share one database.
- `AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining` registers every `[JobName]` type in that assembly.
- `AddWorker` makes this process a worker. Pool `main` reads queue `default` and runs at most 4 jobs at once. Jobs with no `[Queue]` go to `default`.

Leave out `AddWorker` in an app that only dispatches.

  </Step>
  <Step title="Dispatch a job and watch it run">

Add this after `StartAsync`:

```csharp
var dispatcher = host.Services.GetRequiredService<IJobDispatcher>();
var receipt = await dispatcher.DispatchAsync(new SendWelcomeEmail(Guid.NewGuid()));
Console.WriteLine($"Dispatched job {receipt.JobId.Value}");

await host.WaitForShutdownAsync();
```

Run it:

```bash
dotnet run
```

You should see the `Dispatched job` line, then the handler's log line a moment later. Press <Kbd>Ctrl</Kbd>+<Kbd>C</Kbd> to stop. The worker stops taking new jobs and gives running ones time to finish.

In a web app, inject `IJobDispatcher` into an endpoint or a service instead of resolving it by hand:

```csharp
app.MapPost("/users/{id:guid}/welcome", async (Guid id, IJobDispatcher dispatcher) =>
{
    await dispatcher.DispatchAsync(new SendWelcomeEmail(id));
    return Results.Accepted();
});
```

  </Step>
</Steps>

## What just happened

`DispatchAsync` returned only after the store confirmed the job was written. The worker found the job, took a lease on it, ran your handler in its own dependency-injection scope, and recorded the result as `succeeded`.

If the handler had thrown, the job would have waited a few seconds and run again. By default a job runs at most 3 times, so 2 automatic retries, before it ends up `failed`.

<Callout type="warning" title="If dispatch reports an unknown outcome">
A network failure can leave `DispatchAsync` unable to tell whether the write happened. The job may or may not exist. [Dispatching](/docs/dispatching) and [Delivery guarantees](/docs/delivery-guarantees) explain how to handle it safely.
</Callout>

## Check it with the sample host

The repository ships a sample host for PostgreSQL that migrates, dispatches a batch of jobs, runs them on an in-process worker, and prints how many succeeded:

```bash
dotnet run --project samples/Runwick.Samples.Host -- \
  --conn "Host=localhost;Username=postgres;Password=pg;Database=postgres" --migrate --dispatch 10
```

It prints `10 succeeded` and exits with code 0 when every job ran.

## Add the dashboard (optional)

The dashboard runs inside an ASP.NET Core app and needs your own sign-in, such as cookie authentication registered with `AddAuthentication().AddCookie()` and `app.UseAuthentication()`. There is no anonymous mode.

```bash
dotnet add package Runwick.Dashboard
```

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRunwickManagement(m => m
    .AuthenticationSchemes("Cookies")                     // you bring the sign-in
    .MapGrants(principal => ManagementRoles.Operator));   // using Runwick.Management;
builder.Services.AddRunwickDashboard("default", d => { });

app.MapRunwickManagement("/runwick/api");
app.MapRunwickDashboard("/runwick");
```

This example gives every signed-in user the Operator role; map roles from your own claims in a real app. Sign in, open `/runwick`, and you can see the job, its attempts and its status history. [Dashboard](/docs/dashboard) covers permissions and setup in full.

# Choosing a store

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/choosing-a-store

> Compare PostgreSQL, SQLite and Redis as Runwick stores, see where each one stops, and pick a deployment shape.

All three stores give the same job behaviour: the same states, retries, receipts, uniqueness and rate rules. Your jobs and handlers do not change between them. The stores differ in where they can run, what they survive, and whether a job can share a transaction with your own data.

## At a glance

| | PostgreSQL | SQLite | Redis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | `Runwick.Postgres` | `Runwick.Sqlite` | `Runwick.Redis` |
| Server | PostgreSQL 16, 17 or 18 (18 is the reference) | a local file, SQLite 3.38 or newer (bundled) | Redis 8.2 or newer, one standalone primary |
| Hosts | many, connected to the primary | one machine only | many, all reaching one primary |
| Job or completion in the same transaction as your data | yes, same database | yes, same file | no, use the [outbox](/docs/outbox) |
| How workers notice new jobs | LISTEN/NOTIFY wake-up, with polling as the fallback | polling | polling |
| Refused at startup | nothing listed; replicas and proxies are simply not certified | a network share, an in-memory database, sync weaker than `FULL` | a replica, Cluster, Sentinel, wrong persistence settings |
| High availability | not certified | none | none |

Runwick checks each store's durability settings when it starts and again while it runs. It refuses settings that could lose jobs rather than run on them.

## Which one to pick

<Accordion>
  <AccordionItem title="PostgreSQL: the default choice">

Pick PostgreSQL if you already run it, if your workers run on more than one host, or if you want to commit a job in the same transaction as your business data. It is the reference store: the one the rest of Runwick is measured against.

```csharp
runwick.Application("my-app").UsePostgres("Host=db;Database=app;Username=app;Password=...");
```

  </AccordionItem>
  <AccordionItem title="SQLite: one machine, no server">

Pick SQLite for a single-machine app, a desktop or edge service, or a small internal tool where running a database server is not worth it. Every process that uses the file must be on the same machine.

```csharp
runwick.Application("my-app").UseSqlite("Data Source=/var/lib/my-app/runwick.db");
```

  </AccordionItem>
  <AccordionItem title="Redis: when Redis is what you run">

Pick Redis if you already operate a durable Redis primary and do not need jobs to share a transaction with your business database. If you need that, put the [outbox](/docs/outbox) in your PostgreSQL or SQLite database and let it deliver to Redis.

```csharp
runwick.Application("my-app").UseRedis("redis:6379");
```

  </AccordionItem>
</Accordion>

## Limits to plan around

### PostgreSQL

- Connect to the primary directly. Decisions about who owns a job never read from a replica.
- High-availability setups and connection poolers (proxies) are not certified. If you use one, you are outside what has been tested.
- The schema is always named `runwick`. You cannot change it.

### SQLite

- One file on one machine. There is no multi-host support and no high availability.
- Writes use WAL with `synchronous=FULL`. A weaker setting is refused.
- Only one write happens at a time across all processes. Nothing here claims SQLite matches PostgreSQL's throughput.
- Durability is whatever your disk and its fsync give you. Restoring the file from a backup is a break in history: receipts and uniqueness windows from before the restore do not carry over as one continuous record.
- A test that kills a process is not a power-loss test, and Runwick does not claim it is.

### Redis

- One primary, no high availability. Failover, Sentinel promotion and Cluster are not supported. A promoted replica may have lost jobs that were already acknowledged.
- The server must run with `appendonly yes`, `appendfsync always`, `no-appendfsync-on-rewrite no`, `maxmemory-policy noeviction` and `aof-load-truncated no`. Redis without `appendfsync always` is not a supported configuration.
- One application lives in one hash slot. Its throughput is bounded by one server thread, and one very large command can delay everything else for that application.
- Redis cannot join your business transaction. There is no same-transaction completion.
- Nothing here says Redis is faster than PostgreSQL. No speed comparison is claimed.

<Callout type="info" title="Switching stores later">
Your jobs and handlers stay the same, so code written for one store runs on another by changing the `Use...` line. Jobs already in the old store stay there.
</Callout>

## Roles are configuration, not programs

A Runwick process can take any combination of four roles:

| Role | How you turn it on |
|---|---|
| Producer | any code that calls `IJobDispatcher.DispatchAsync`. Every app with `AddRunwick` can dispatch |
| Worker | `runwick.AddWorker(...)` |
| Scheduler | `runwick.AddScheduler()` |
| Management | `app.MapRunwickManagement(...)`, and optionally the dashboard |

There is nothing else to deploy. The store is the only shared piece, and processes never talk to each other directly.

### Deployment shapes

| Shape | What runs where |
|---|---|
| One app, embedded worker | your web app dispatches and works in one process |
| One app, external worker | the web app only dispatches; a separate worker service runs the jobs |
| Many replicas, embedded workers | every replica both dispatches and works |
| Replicas plus a worker tier | the web tier only dispatches; a worker tier only works |
| Mixed | some replicas embed workers, and extra external workers run too |

PostgreSQL and Redis support all five shapes across hosts. SQLite supports all five as long as every process is on the same machine.

A web app that only dispatches registers the store and the jobs, and leaves out `AddWorker`:

```csharp
// Web app: producer only
builder.Services.AddRunwick(runwick =>
{
    runwick.Application("shop")
        .UsePostgres(connectionString)
        .AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining<SendWelcomeEmail>();
});
```

The worker service registers the same jobs, plus handlers and a worker:

```csharp
// Worker service
builder.Services.AddRunwick(runwick =>
{
    runwick.Application("shop")
        .UsePostgres(connectionString)
        .AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining<SendWelcomeEmail>();
    runwick.AddHandlersFromAssemblyContaining<SendWelcomeEmailHandler>();
    runwick.AddWorker(w => w.Pool("main", p => p.Queues("default").FixedConcurrency(8)));
});
```

Put the job records in a shared project that references only `Runwick.Contracts`, so the web app does not need your handler code.

### Worth knowing before you deploy

- **Automatic concurrency.** `AutoConcurrency(min, max)` adjusts a pool inside one process. It does not coordinate across the cluster.
- **Schedules.** Pausing a schedule stops new jobs from being created. It does not pause jobs the schedule already created.
- **The scheduler capability.** Before any process can register a schedule, an operator raises the `scheduler` capability once per application with `runwick store activate-capability --name scheduler`. Until then, startup fails with `scheduler_not_active`. See [Schedules](/docs/schedules).

# Jobs and handlers

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/jobs-and-handlers

> Define a job contract with a stable name, write the handler that runs it, and register both.

A **job** is a small data record that describes work to do. A **handler** is the class that does the work. Runwick stores the job, and a worker later decodes it and calls the handler.

```csharp
[JobName("email.welcome")]
public sealed record SendWelcomeEmail(Guid UserId, string Locale) : IQueueJob;

public sealed class SendWelcomeEmailHandler(IEmailSender emails) : IJobHandler<SendWelcomeEmail>
{
    public Task HandleAsync(SendWelcomeEmail job, CancellationToken cancellationToken) =>
        emails.SendWelcomeAsync(job.UserId, job.Locale, cancellationToken);
}
```

## The job contract

A job contract is a concrete class or record that implements `IQueueJob`. `IQueueJob` is an empty marker interface. Payloads are data only: they carry no behaviour, and attributes on them cannot resolve services or do I/O.

Every contract needs a **stable name**. The name is what Runwick stores, so you can rename, move or re-namespace the class without breaking queued jobs. The CLR type name is never stored.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="Attributes">

```csharp
[JobName("email.welcome")]
[Queue("emails")]
[Priority("medium")]
[MaxExecutions(3)]
public sealed record SendWelcomeEmail(Guid UserId, string Locale) : IQueueJob;
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Fluent">

```csharp
// The contract has no attributes; the host names and configures it.
public sealed record BuildReport(string ReportId, int Rows) : IQueueJob;

runwick.AddJob<BuildReport>()
    .Named("reports.build")
    .ToQueue("reports")
    .WithPriority("low")
    .WithMaxExecutions(5);
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

You can use both. Identity settings (`[JobName]` and `Named`, `[PayloadVersion]` and `AtVersion`) must agree if both are present, or startup fails with `identity_conflict`. For queue, priority and `MaxExecutions` the fluent value wins over the attribute. The full order is in [Configuration](/docs/configuration).

| Attribute | Fluent twin | What it sets |
|---|---|---|
| `[JobName("x")]` | `.Named("x")` | The stored name. Required. |
| `[PayloadVersion(n)]` | `.AtVersion(n)` | The payload version. Default 1. |
| `[Queue("q")]` | `.ToQueue("q")` | Default queue. Default `default`. |
| `[Priority("p")]` | `.WithPriority("p")` | `low`, `medium` or `high`. Default `medium`. |
| `[MaxExecutions(n)]` | `.WithMaxExecutions(n)` | Run budget, 1 to 100. Default 3. |
| `[UseJobMiddleware("alias")]` | `.UseMiddleware("alias")` | Middleware by alias. |

Attributes are not inherited. A derived class never picks up its base class's name.

<Callout type="tip" title="Hangfire in the same file">

Hangfire also has a `QueueAttribute`. If a file imports both, alias Runwick's: `using JobQueue = Runwick.QueueAttribute;` and write `[JobQueue("emails")]`.

</Callout>

### Naming rules

| Name | Rule |
|---|---|
| Job name | 1 to 200 characters of `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -`, starting with a letter or digit |
| Application, queue, pool, middleware alias | Same characters, 1 to 128 |

Names are case-sensitive and never trimmed. A dotted style such as `email.welcome` or `billing.invoice.send` reads well in the dashboard. Two contracts with the same name fail startup with `duplicate_job_name`.

## The handler

A handler implements `IJobHandler<TJob>` with one method, `HandleAsync(TJob job, CancellationToken cancellationToken)`.

- Returning normally means success.
- Throwing an exception means a retryable failure, unless it is a `PermanentJobFailureException`. See [Retries and timeouts](/docs/retries-and-timeouts).
- The token is cancelled on a user cancel, a timeout, a lost lease or shutdown. Pass it to every awaited call. See [Cancellation](/docs/cancellation).

Handlers are registered as **scoped** services. Runwick creates a fresh DI scope for every attempt, so a scoped `DbContext` belongs to that one attempt and is disposed afterwards. Inject anything you need into the constructor, including `IJobContext` (see [Job context](/docs/job-context)).

<Callout type="warning" title="Handlers can run more than once">

Runwick is at-least-once. A crash after the work but before the result is saved runs the handler again. Make the effects safe to repeat. See [Delivery guarantees](/docs/delivery-guarantees).

</Callout>

There is one handler per job name per worker. Binding two handlers to one job fails with `duplicate_handler`.

## Registration

Registration happens inside `AddRunwick`. Nothing is scanned automatically.

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRunwick(runwick =>
{
    runwick.Application("my-app")
        .UsePostgres(connectionString)
        .AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining<SendWelcomeEmail>();      // contracts with [JobName]
    runwick.AddHandlersFromAssemblyContaining<SendWelcomeEmailHandler>();
    runwick.AddWorker(w => w.Pool("main", p => p.Queues("default", "emails").FixedConcurrency(4)));
});
```

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining<T>()` | Registers every non-abstract class in that assembly that implements `IQueueJob` and has `[JobName]`. Classes without `[JobName]` are skipped. |
| `AddHandlersFromAssemblyContaining<T>()` | Registers every class in that assembly that implements one or more `IJobHandler<TJob>`, and registers each `TJob`. |
| `AddHandler<TJob, THandler>()` | Binds one handler and registers its job. |
| `AddJob<TJob>()` | Registers a contract and returns a builder to configure it. |
| `ConfigureJob<TJob>()` | Configures a contract registered elsewhere. On its own it registers nothing (`job_not_registered`). |

Each scan only looks at the one assembly you point it at, and runs in a fixed order.

Configuration is checked once, at startup. Runwick collects every error and throws one `RunwickConfigurationException` that lists them all, so a typo in a queue name stops the app before it does any work.

## Payload serialization

Payloads are stored as UTF-8 JSON using Runwick's own fixed profile, `runwick.json` version 1. It does not use your ASP.NET JSON settings, so changing those can never change what is in the queue.

The profile is strict:

- Property names are camelCase. Unknown properties and duplicate properties are rejected when reading.
- Numbers must be real JSON numbers. Enums are written as their member names.
- `DateTime` values must be UTC. Prefer `DateTimeOffset` for instants.
- Members typed `object`, `[Flags]` enums, `[JsonConverter]` and attributes that loosen the rules are rejected at startup. Use `JsonElement` for free-form data.
- Polymorphism works only for closed hierarchies declared with `[JsonPolymorphic]` and `[JsonDerivedType]`.

You can supply source-generated metadata with `runwick.AddJsonTypeInfoResolver(MyJsonContext.Default)`.

### Payload limits

These limits are fixed. Dispatch fails before anything is written if a payload breaks them.

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Serialized payload | 1 MiB |
| Nesting depth | 32 levels |
| One string value | 256 KiB |
| Properties per object | 256 |
| Elements per array | 16,384 |

Keep payloads small. Store a file or a large document elsewhere and put its ID in the job.

### Changing a payload's shape

The worker decodes the stored bytes fresh on every run. If you change the record, raise the version and register an upgrade from the old shape:

```csharp
[JobName("email.welcome")]
[PayloadVersion(2)]
public sealed record SendWelcomeEmail(Guid UserId, string Locale) : IQueueJob;

// The old shape: a plain decoding type, no [JobName], no IQueueJob needed.
public sealed record SendWelcomeEmailV1(Guid UserId);

runwick.ConfigureJob<SendWelcomeEmail>()
    .Upgrade<SendWelcomeEmailV1, SendWelcomeEmail>(1, 2, v1 => new SendWelcomeEmail(v1.UserId, "en"));
```

Each step goes up by exactly one version. Upgrades run on the worker, after the run is authorized, and must be pure functions. A worker only picks up jobs whose version it can decode, so during a rolling deploy old workers leave version 2 jobs alone. More in [Upgrades](/docs/upgrades).

## Runwick.Contracts for shared job types

`Runwick.Contracts` holds `IQueueJob`, the handler interface, the attributes and the dispatch types. It has no dependencies.

Put your job records in a class library that references only `Runwick.Contracts`. Producers and workers both reference that library, and the library never pulls in database drivers or handler code.

```bash
dotnet add src/MyApp.Jobs package Runwick.Contracts
```

The app that actually dispatches still needs `Runwick` and a store package, because `IJobDispatcher` is implemented there. A producer-only app simply leaves out `AddWorker` and does not need the handlers.

## Next

- [Dispatching](/docs/dispatching): create jobs.
- [Queues and priorities](/docs/queues-and-priorities): route them.
- [Retries and timeouts](/docs/retries-and-timeouts): what happens when they fail.

# Dispatching

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/dispatching

> Create jobs with IJobDispatcher, set queue, priority, start time and metadata, dispatch in batches, and handle an unknown outcome.

Dispatching writes a job to the store. Inject `IJobDispatcher` (a singleton) anywhere in your app:

```csharp
app.MapPost("/users", async (CreateUser request, IJobDispatcher dispatcher, CancellationToken ct) =>
{
    var userId = Guid.NewGuid();
    // ... save the user ...
    var receipt = await dispatcher.DispatchAsync(new SendWelcomeEmail(userId, "en"), cancellationToken: ct);
    return Results.Accepted(value: new { jobId = receipt.JobId.ToString() });
});
```

`DispatchAsync` returns only after the store has confirmed the write. There is no "fire and forget" mode.

The job's type must be registered (see [Jobs and handlers](/docs/jobs-and-handlers)). Runwick looks it up by the object's runtime type.

## The receipt

`DispatchAsync` returns a `DispatchReceipt`:

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `JobId` | The job's permanent ID. It stays the same across retries. |
| `OperationId` | The ID of this dispatch command. |
| `Disposition` | `Created` for a new job, or `Reused` when a [uniqueness](/docs/uniqueness) key matched an existing job. |
| `DuplicateMatch` | Which key matched: `None`, `Active`, `Window` or `ActiveAndWindow`. |
| `PolicyDrift` | `true` when a reused job was created under a different retry or timeout policy than the current one. |
| `ConfirmedAcknowledgementProfile` | The durability rule the store confirmed, for example `postgres.synchronous-commit`. |

A receipt tells you which job it is. It is not a status snapshot: a reused job may already have finished.

## Dispatch options

Pass a `DispatchOptions` to change one dispatch. Every property is optional.

```csharp
await dispatcher.DispatchAsync(
    new BuildReport("2026-11", Rows: 50_000),
    new DispatchOptions
    {
        Queue = "reports",
        Priority = "high",
        NotBefore = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.AddMinutes(30),
        Metadata = new Dictionary<string, string> { ["tenant"] = "acme" },
    },
    ct);
```

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Queue` | Sends the job to another registered queue. An unknown queue fails with `unknown_queue`. |
| `Priority` | `low`, `medium` or `high`. Raises or lowers the job's declared priority. |
| `NotBefore` | The earliest time the job may start. |
| `Uniqueness` | Active and window keys. See [Uniqueness](/docs/uniqueness). |
| `Metadata` | Business metadata such as a tenant. The handler reads it from `IJobContext.Metadata`. |

### Delayed jobs

`NotBefore` is a lower bound, not an exact start time. The job waits in `pending` until that instant and then becomes eligible like any other job. It starts when a worker has a free slot. A time in the past means "eligible now". The value is rounded up to the next millisecond.

There is no separate "schedule" call for one-off delays. For repeating work, use [Schedules](/docs/schedules).

### Metadata rules

- Keys use the name grammar (`A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -`, up to 128 characters). Values must be valid text without control characters.
- At most 32 entries and 16 KiB in total.
- Metadata is part of what a [window key](/docs/uniqueness) compares, so the same key with different metadata is a conflict.

Runwick also captures the current trace context (`traceparent`, `tracestate`) at dispatch, so the run is linked to the request that created it.

## Batch dispatch

`DispatchManyAsync` dispatches up to 100 jobs in **one** store transaction:

```csharp
var items = invoices
    .Select(i => new BatchDispatchItem(new SendInvoice(i.Id), new DispatchOptions { Priority = "low" }))
    .ToList();

var batch = await dispatcher.DispatchManyAsync(items, cancellationToken: ct);

foreach (var item in batch.Items)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{item.Ordinal}: {item.Receipt?.JobId}");
}
```

- Every item is created (or reused) or none is.
- `Items` has one result per input, in input order (`Ordinal` is the 0-based index).
- The limits are 100 items and 2 MiB for the whole batch. Split larger inputs yourself.
- If any item is invalid, the whole batch is rejected before anything is written. The `DispatchValidationException` lists every bad ordinal in `ItemFailures`.
- Duplicates inside one batch resolve as if dispatched one after another: a later item that matches an earlier one is `Reused`.

By default a [uniqueness conflict](/docs/uniqueness) in any item fails the whole batch with `UniquenessConflictException`. Set `ContinueOnConflict` to commit the other items and report the conflicts per item:

```csharp
var batch = await dispatcher.DispatchManyAsync(items, new BatchDispatchOptions { ContinueOnConflict = true }, ct);

foreach (var failed in batch.Items.Where(i => i.Failure is not null))
{
    logger.LogWarning("Item {Ordinal} conflicted: {Code}", failed.Ordinal, failed.Failure!.Code);
}
```

## Errors

Every Runwick exception has a stable `Code` and a `Disposition`. The disposition answers "did anything get written?":

| Disposition | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `KnownNotApplied` | Nothing was written. It is safe to fix the input and try again. |
| `OutcomeUnknown` | The write may or may not have happened. |

Common cases:

| Exception | Code | Disposition |
|---|---|---|
| `DispatchValidationException` | for example `payload_too_large`, `invalid_key` | known not applied |
| `UniquenessConflictException` | `uniqueness_conflict`, `uniqueness_composition_conflict` | known not applied |
| `LocalCapacityExceededException` | `local_capacity_exceeded` | known not applied, never sent |
| `StoreUnavailableException` | `store_unavailable` | known not applied |
| `DispatchOutcomeUnknownException` | `outcome_unknown` | **unknown** |
| `DispatchCanceledAfterSendException` | `cancelled_after_send` | **unknown** |

### When the outcome is unknown

A network failure after the command was sent leaves Runwick unable to say whether the store committed it. It does not guess. It throws an exception with `Disposition == ErrorDisposition.OutcomeUnknown` that carries the `OperationId` and, when available, the prepared request.

You have three honest options:

<Steps>
  <Step title="Re-send the same prepared request">

The exception's `Prepared` property holds the exact request. Sending it again through `IPreparedJobDispatcher` is safe: the store recognises the operation ID and returns the original receipt instead of creating a second job.

```csharp
catch (DispatchOutcomeUnknownException ex) when (ex.Prepared is not null)
{
    var receipt = await preparedDispatcher.DispatchAsync(ex.Prepared, ct);
}
```

  </Step>
  <Step title="Or ask the store">

`IPreparedJobDispatcher.ResolveAsync(operationId)` returns `Confirmed` (with the receipt), `NotObserved`, `Recovering` or `ExpiredUnknown`. `NotObserved` is **not** proof the write failed: the original command may still be running.

  </Step>
  <Step title="Or rely on a window key">

If the dispatch had a [window key](/docs/uniqueness), dispatching again with the same key and payload returns the same job.

  </Step>
</Steps>

<Callout type="warning" title="Do not just call DispatchAsync again">

A plain second `DispatchAsync` is a new operation. Without a uniqueness key it can create a second job.

</Callout>

A prepared request is valid for 5 minutes by default (`ProducerOptions.CommandLifetime`). After that the store guarantees it will never apply it, and re-sending it gives a definite answer (`command_expired`) for 24 hours more.

### Cancellation

The `CancellationToken` only stops **waiting**. It never cancels a job the store has accepted. Cancelled before the command was sent, you get a plain `OperationCanceledException` (nothing written). Cancelled after, you get `DispatchCanceledAfterSendException`, which means the outcome is unknown.

## Prepared dispatch

`IPreparedJobDispatcher` splits dispatch into two steps. `Prepare` validates and serializes the job and fixes its operation ID and deadline without touching the store. `DispatchAsync(prepared)` sends it, as many times as you need.

```csharp
var prepared = preparedDispatcher.Prepare(new ChargeCard(orderId, amount));
await SaveOperationIdAsync(orderId, prepared.OperationId);   // survive a crash
var receipt = await preparedDispatcher.DispatchAsync(prepared, ct);
```

`Export()` turns a prepared request into bytes you can store and `ImportPrepared(bytes)` reads them back. The bytes contain the payload unencrypted, so keep them out of logs.

## Producer limits

Each process limits how many dispatch calls it sends at once, so a burst cannot exhaust the database connection pool. Configure them with `runwick.Producer(...)`:

```csharp
runwick.Producer(p =>
{
    p.MaxConcurrentCalls = 8;                       // calls in flight at once
    p.MaxWaitingOperations = 64;                    // callers allowed to wait for a slot
    p.AdmissionWait = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1);      // longest wait for a slot
    p.CommandLifetime = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5);    // prepared request deadline; 5 min is also the maximum
});
```

The values above are the defaults. When all slots are busy and the wait runs out, or too many callers are already waiting, the call fails at once with `LocalCapacityExceededException`. Nothing was sent, so it is safe to retry later. A batch counts as one call.

Dispatch works while a queue is paused. Pausing only stops workers from picking jobs up.

## Next

- [Uniqueness](/docs/uniqueness): stop duplicate jobs.
- [Transactions](/docs/transactions): create a job in the same transaction as your own data.
- [Outbox](/docs/outbox): dispatch reliably to a different store.

# Queues and priorities

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/queues-and-priorities

> Route jobs to queues, use the high, medium and low priority lanes, tune weights and aging, and pause a queue.

A **queue** is a named stream of jobs, such as `emails` or `reports`. Workers subscribe to queues. Inside each queue there are three **priority lanes**: `high`, `medium` and `low`. A lane is one queue and priority pair.

Every job has exactly one queue and one priority. The defaults are queue `default` and priority `medium`.

## Putting a job in a queue

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="Attributes">

```csharp
[JobName("email.welcome")]
[Queue("emails")]
[Priority("high")]
public sealed record SendWelcomeEmail(Guid UserId) : IQueueJob;
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Fluent">

```csharp
runwick.ConfigureJob<SendWelcomeEmail>()
    .ToQueue("emails")
    .WithPriority("high");
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Application default">

```csharp
// Applies to every job that does not set its own queue or priority.
runwick.JobDefaults(d => d.ToQueue("work").WithPriority("low"));
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

A single dispatch can override both:

```csharp
await dispatcher.DispatchAsync(job, new DispatchOptions { Queue = "emails-bulk", Priority = "low" });
```

## Registering queues

A queue exists once something registers it. A job whose effective queue is `emails` registers `emails`. You can also declare a queue directly, which is also where you give it a [concurrency cap](/docs/rate-limits-and-concurrency):

```csharp
runwick.Queue("emails-bulk");
runwick.Queue("pdf", q => q.MaxConcurrent(5));   // at most 5 running at once, across all workers
```

Dispatching to an unregistered queue fails with `unknown_queue`. Queue names follow the name grammar: 1 to 128 characters of `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -`, case-sensitive.

## Subscribing workers

A worker has one or more **pools**. Each pool subscribes to queues and has its own number of slots:

```csharp
runwick.AddWorker(w => w
    .Pool("mail", p => p.Queues("emails", "emails-bulk").FixedConcurrency(8))
    .Pool("heavy", p => p.Queue("reports", weight: 1).Queue("pdf", weight: 3).FixedConcurrency(2)));
```

`Queues(...)` gives each queue weight 1. `Queue(name, weight)` sets a weight from 1 to 1,000. When several queues in a pool have work, weights decide how often each gets the next free slot. With `reports` at 1 and `pdf` at 3, about three in four claims go to `pdf`.

Subscriptions are explicit. Registering a handler never subscribes a pool to anything. A job in a queue no pool subscribes to simply waits. See [Workers](/docs/workers) for pool sizing.

## Priority lanes

Priority is not a sort order. Each pool picks a lane using **weighted round robin**, with default weights `high` 6, `medium` 3, `low` 1. When all three lanes in a queue have work, roughly 60% of claims come from `high`, 30% from `medium` and 10% from `low`. Low-priority work keeps moving; it just moves more slowly.

You can change the weights per pool. Each must be from 1 to 1,000:

```csharp
w.Pool("main", p => p
    .Queues("default")
    .LaneWeights(high: 10, medium: 3, low: 1));
```

Weights share out **chances to claim** a job. They do not reserve CPU, they do not interrupt a running job, and a long job holds its slot as long as it runs.

### Aging

In the default mode a lower lane that has waited a long time gets an extra turn. After 8 claims from a queue, if the oldest eligible job in a lower lane has waited at least 60 seconds, the next claim goes to that lane. These two numbers are fixed.

Aging changes the ratios on purpose so that `low` jobs do not wait forever behind a steady stream of `high` jobs. It is not a start-time guarantee, and it never changes a job's stored priority.

### Lane selection modes

```csharp
p.LaneSelection(LaneSelectionMode.StrictWithAging);
```

| Mode | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `Weighted` (default) | Weighted round robin, with aging. |
| `StrictWithAging` | Always the highest lane that has work, with aging as the escape valve. |
| `Strict` | Always the highest lane that has work. No aging. |

<Callout type="warning" title="Strict mode can starve low lanes">

In `Strict` mode a steady supply of `high` jobs means `low` jobs never run. Use it only when that is what you want.

</Callout>

Between queues, the choice is always weighted, whatever the lane mode.

## Pausing a queue

Pausing a queue stops workers from **claiming** new jobs from it. That is all it does:

- Jobs already running keep running and finish normally.
- Dispatching into a paused queue still works. Jobs pile up as `pending`.
- Nothing is cancelled or released.

Resume the queue and workers pick the backlog up again.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="CLI">

```bash
runwick queues list
runwick queues pause emails
runwick queues resume emails
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="C#">

```csharp
using Runwick.Management;

// IQueueControl comes from DI. The revision is the one you last read for this queue.
var result = await queueControl.PauseAsync("emails", expectedRevision, new ManagementActor("ops-bot", "Ops bot", "service"), reason: "provider outage");
if (!result.Succeeded)
{
    Console.WriteLine(result.Code);   // for example a revision conflict
}
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

Every change carries the queue revision you last saw. If someone else changed the queue in between, you get a conflict instead of a surprise. Pauses and resumes are written to the audit trail. The dashboard has the same buttons; see [Dashboard](/docs/dashboard) and [Management API](/docs/management-api).

<Callout type="info" title="In-process control has no permission check">

`IQueueControl` trusts the actor you pass. The HTTP API, dashboard and CLI check permissions first.

</Callout>

## Next

- [Rate limits and concurrency](/docs/rate-limits-and-concurrency): cap how much runs at once.
- [Workers](/docs/workers): pools, fixed and automatic concurrency.

# Retries and timeouts

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/retries-and-timeouts

> How many times a job runs, how long Runwick waits between tries, how execution timeouts work, and how failures are recorded.

When a handler fails, Runwick waits a little and runs it again, up to a budget. When the budget is spent, the job ends in `failed` and stays there until someone retries it.

| Setting | Default | Where |
|---|---|---|
| `MaxExecutions` | 3 (the first run plus up to two retries) | attribute, fluent, `JobDefaults` |
| Retry delay | 5 s first, doubling, never more than 60 s, half-random | fluent, `JobDefaults` |
| `ExecutionTimeout` | none | fluent, `JobDefaults` |

These values are copied onto the job when it is dispatched. Changing the configuration later does not change jobs already in the queue.

## MaxExecutions

`MaxExecutions` counts **runs that actually started**: each time a worker is authorized to call your handler. It includes the first run, so `MaxExecutions(3)` means at most two automatic retries. The allowed range is 1 to 100.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="Attribute">

```csharp
[JobName("payments.capture")]
[MaxExecutions(5)]
public sealed record CapturePayment(Guid OrderId) : IQueueJob;
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Fluent">

```csharp
runwick.ConfigureJob<CapturePayment>().WithMaxExecutions(5);
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Application default">

```csharp
runwick.JobDefaults(d => d.WithMaxExecutions(5));
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

Precedence, later wins: library default, then `JobDefaults`, then the attribute, then fluent job configuration.

### Crashes before the handler starts

A worker can claim a job and die before calling the handler, for example during a deploy. No user code ran, so Runwick does not charge `MaxExecutions` for it. It counts these on a separate guard instead: after 5 consecutive claims that never started, the job fails with `reservation_abandonment_exhausted`. The delay between these re-queues starts at 1 second and grows to 30 seconds.

```csharp
runwick.ConfigureJob<CapturePayment>()
    .WithMaxUnstartedAbandonments(5)                                         // 1 to 100; cannot be turned off
    .WithUnstartedRecoveryDelay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));
```

A crash in the tiny window right after a run is authorized but before your method is called still costs one execution.

## Retry delay

After a failed run, the next try waits an exponential delay with "equal jitter": the nominal delay is `initial × 2^(n−1)`, capped at the maximum, and the actual delay is a random value between half the nominal and the full nominal. The randomness spreads out jobs that failed together.

With the defaults (5 s initial, 60 s maximum):

| After run | Waits between |
|---|---|
| 1 | 2.5 s and 5 s |
| 2 | 5 s and 10 s |
| 3 | 10 s and 20 s |
| 5 and later | 30 s and 60 s |

```csharp
runwick.ConfigureJob<CapturePayment>()
    .WithRetryDelay(initialDelay: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30), maxDelay: TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10));
```

Both values must be whole milliseconds, from 1 ms to 24 hours, and the initial delay must not exceed the maximum. There is no attribute for the retry delay.

The chosen delay is stored with the outcome. If the store's reply is lost and the write is repeated, the same delay is reused.

## What counts as a failure

| What the handler does | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Returns normally | Succeeded |
| Throws any exception | Retryable failure |
| Throws `PermanentJobFailureException` | Permanent failure: no more retries |
| Runs past `ExecutionTimeout` | Timed out (retryable) |
| Stops because of a user cancel | Cancelled |
| Stops because the worker is shutting down | Interrupted (retryable) |
| Payload cannot be decoded or upgraded | Permanent failure |

A retryable outcome is retried only while the budget lasts. After that the job is `failed`.

### Failing permanently

Throw `PermanentJobFailureException` when retrying cannot help, such as invalid input:

```csharp
public async Task HandleAsync(CapturePayment job, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var order = await orders.FindAsync(job.OrderId, ct)
        ?? throw new PermanentJobFailureException("order_not_found", $"Order {job.OrderId} does not exist.");

    await gateway.CaptureAsync(order, idempotencyKey: job.OrderId.ToString(), ct);
}
```

The code follows the name grammar (`A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -`, up to 128 characters).

### Deciding in middleware

[Middleware](/docs/job-context#middleware) can turn exceptions into explicit results:

```csharp
public sealed class HttpRetryMiddleware : IJobMiddleware
{
    public async Task<JobExecutionResult> InvokeAsync(IJobContext context, JobExecutionDelegate next, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        try
        {
            return await next();
        }
        catch (HttpRequestException ex) when (ex.StatusCode == HttpStatusCode.TooManyRequests)
        {
            return JobExecutionResult.Retry("rate_limited", TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2));
        }
        catch (HttpRequestException ex) when (ex.StatusCode == HttpStatusCode.BadRequest)
        {
            return JobExecutionResult.Failed("bad_request", "The provider rejected the request.");
        }
    }
}

runwick.UseMiddleware<HttpRetryMiddleware>();   // every job
```

`Retry(reason, delay)` still uses up one execution. The delay is used as given (no jitter), capped at the job's maximum retry delay. A `null` delay uses the normal policy. A negative delay is a contract fault and fails the job permanently.

## Execution timeout

There is no timeout by default. Set one per job or for the whole application:

```csharp
runwick.ConfigureJob<BuildReport>().WithExecutionTimeout(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2));
runwick.JobDefaults(d => d.WithExecutionTimeout(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10)));

// Turn an inherited default off for one job:
runwick.ConfigureJob<ReindexEverything>().WithoutExecutionTimeout();
```

The timeout must be a whole number of milliseconds, at most 30 days. There is no attribute for it.

When the time is up, Runwick:

1. records the cause `Timeout` and cancels the handler's `CancellationToken`;
2. waits up to the cancellation grace (10 seconds) for the handler to return;
3. records the run as **timed out**, even if the handler then returned normally.

A timed-out run is retryable and costs one execution.

The clock measures the local pipeline: from the moment the worker starts the run, including decoding, DI and middleware, until the handler's task completes. It does not measure what happened in the outside world. A payment that went through just before the timeout fired still went through.

<Callout type="warning" title="Timeouts need cooperative handlers">

.NET cannot safely stop running code. If the handler ignores the token, it keeps running after the grace period. The worker then stops renewing the lease and writes no result; the job is recovered after the lease expires and may run again elsewhere. See [Cancellation](/docs/cancellation).

</Callout>

## How failures are recorded

Every run is an **attempt**, and every attempt is kept (until [retention](/docs/retention) removes it) with:

- its outcome (succeeded, retryable failure, permanent failure, timed out, interrupted, cancelled, abandoned);
- an error code, the exception type and message;
- the full exception text, capped at 16 KiB with a truncation marker.

A `Failed(code, message)` message longer than 1,024 bytes is truncated.

Exception text can contain sensitive data. The dashboard, API and CLI show it only with a separate permission, and each reveal is audited:

```bash
runwick jobs get 0193a7c2-5b1e-7c3d-9f00-1a2b3c4d5e6f
runwick jobs reveal-error <attempt-id>
```

## Retrying a failed job by hand

A `failed` or `cancelled` job can be retried from the dashboard, the API or the CLI. This starts a new **generation** of the same job ID with a fresh execution budget. The old attempts stay in the history.

```bash
runwick jobs retry 0193a7c2-5b1e-7c3d-9f00-1a2b3c4d5e6f
```

In C#, use `IJobControl.RetryAsync` from `Runwick.Management`. See [Management API](/docs/management-api).

## Next

- [Cancellation](/docs/cancellation): how the token works.
- [Delivery guarantees](/docs/delivery-guarantees): why a run can repeat.

---

# Uniqueness

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/uniqueness

> Stop duplicate jobs from being created with active keys and window keys, and know what uniqueness does not prevent.

Uniqueness stops the **same job from being created twice**. A user double-clicks "Sign up", or a client retries a request whose response was lost: you want one job, not two.

Runwick has two kinds of key, for two different questions:

| Key | Question | Held for |
|---|---|---|
| **Active key** | "Is one of these already queued or running?" | As long as the job is `pending`, `reserved`, `running` or `retrying` |
| **Window key** | "Did I already ask for exactly this?" | A fixed time after the first dispatch, even after the job finished |

Keys are scoped to the application and the job name. The same key on two different job types does not collide.

## Active keys

While a job with a given active key is waiting or running, another dispatch with the same key creates nothing. It returns the existing job with `Disposition = Reused` and `DuplicateMatch = Active`. When the job finishes (succeeded, failed or cancelled) the key is free again.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="Per job type (fluent)">

```csharp
runwick.ConfigureJob<RecalculateStats>()
    .UniqueWhileActive(job => $"tenant:{job.TenantId}");
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Per dispatch">

```csharp
await dispatcher.DispatchAsync(
    new RecalculateStats(tenantId),
    new DispatchOptions { Uniqueness = new DispatchUniqueness(ActiveKey: $"tenant:{tenantId}", WindowKey: null, Window: null) });
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

Use it for work where a second copy in the queue is pointless, such as "recalculate statistics for tenant X".

<Callout type="info" title="First writer wins">

The second dispatch's payload is discarded. Check `receipt.Disposition` if you need to know that your payload was not the one stored.

</Callout>

## Window keys

A window key makes a dispatch **idempotent** for a fixed time. For the length of the window after the *first* dispatch, any dispatch with the same key and the same request returns the same job, even if that job finished hours ago.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="Per job type (fluent)">

```csharp
runwick.ConfigureJob<PlaceOrder>()
    .UniqueWithinWindow(job => job.RequestId, TimeSpan.FromHours(24));
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Per dispatch">

```csharp
app.MapPost("/orders", async (PlaceOrderRequest body, [FromHeader(Name = "Idempotency-Key")] string requestId, IJobDispatcher dispatcher) =>
{
    var receipt = await dispatcher.DispatchAsync(
        new PlaceOrder(body.CartId),
        new DispatchOptions { Uniqueness = new DispatchUniqueness(ActiveKey: null, WindowKey: requestId, Window: TimeSpan.FromHours(24)) });
    return Results.Accepted(value: new { jobId = receipt.JobId.ToString() });
});
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

The window does not slide. It is measured from the first dispatch, so retrying with the same key cannot keep it alive forever. After the window the key is forgotten and a new dispatch creates a new job. There is no default window; you always choose it. It must be positive, in whole milliseconds, and at most 3,650 days.

### Same key, different request

Runwick stores a fingerprint of what you asked for: the payload, job name, queue, priority, start time, keys, resource keys and business metadata. If you reuse a window key with a **different** request, that is not a retry. It is a bug or a key collision, and dispatch fails with `UniquenessConflictException` (`uniqueness_conflict`) instead of quietly handing back an unrelated job. The exception's `ConflictingJobId` names the existing job.

A difference only in retry or timeout settings (for example after you changed a default) is not a conflict. The dispatch returns the existing job with `PolicyDrift = true`, and the existing job keeps its original settings.

## Using both

A dispatch can carry both keys:

```csharp
new DispatchUniqueness(ActiveKey: $"welcome:{userId}", WindowKey: requestId, Window: TimeSpan.FromHours(1))
```

The window key makes retries of *this* request safe. The active key makes *any* request for that user collapse onto one queued job. If a new window key meets an existing active job, the window key is linked to that job, so later retries find it even after it finishes. If the two keys point at two different jobs, dispatch fails with `uniqueness_composition_conflict`.

## Declared keys are required

When a job type declares `UniqueWhileActive` or `UniqueWithinWindow`, that key is **required** for every dispatch of it. There is no option to skip it.

- If the dispatch also passes an explicit key for the same dimension, the two must be equal (and the windows equal), or it fails with `uniqueness_key_mismatch`.
- A selector that returns `null` fails with `uniqueness_required`. A selector that throws fails with `key_selector_failed`.
- Selectors run once, when the dispatch is prepared. Keep them pure and fast.

Job types without declared keys can pass keys per dispatch, or not.

## Key rules

- 1 to 512 bytes as UTF-8.
- Valid Unicode with no control characters.
- Case-sensitive and compared exactly: no trimming, no case folding, no Unicode normalization.

A key that breaks these rules fails with `invalid_key` before anything is written.

## In batches

In `DispatchManyAsync`, items behave as if dispatched one after another in input order. A later item that matches an earlier one is `Reused`. Conflicts fail the whole batch unless you set `ContinueOnConflict`. See [Dispatching](/docs/dispatching#batch-dispatch).

## What uniqueness does not do

Uniqueness is about **inserting** jobs. It is not an execution lock and it never promises a handler runs once.

| You want to avoid… | Use |
|---|---|
| Two copies queued at once | Active key |
| A client retry creating a second job | Window key |
| Two jobs touching the same thing at the same moment | A [resource scope](/docs/rate-limits-and-concurrency) with capacity 1 |
| A repeated run having a visible effect twice | Idempotent handlers: pass an idempotency key to the other side (see [Delivery guarantees](/docs/delivery-guarantees)) |

Things to keep in mind:

- An active key is about being queued. Retries and crash recovery can still run the job more than once.
- A window key lives in the store. Restoring the database from a backup can bring back or lose keys.
- Window keys are not tied to job retention. A key can outlive the job's history, and the reused job may already be cleaned up.

## Next

- [Rate limits and concurrency](/docs/rate-limits-and-concurrency)
- [Delivery guarantees](/docs/delivery-guarantees)

# Rate limits and concurrency

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/rate-limits-and-concurrency

> Cap how many jobs run at once and how many start per time window, per process or across every worker.

There are two different limits, and they answer different questions:

| | Concurrency limit | Rate limit |
|---|---|---|
| Question | How many run **at the same time**? | How many **start** per window of time? |
| Example | "At most 5 PDF renders at once" | "At most 100 calls to the email API per minute" |
| Checked when | a worker claims the job | the run is authorized, just before the handler |

A 1 ms job barely touches a concurrency limit but counts fully against a rate limit. A 10-minute job holds a concurrency slot the whole time but counts once against a rate limit.

## Per process or across all workers

Some limits live in one process's memory. Others live in the store and hold across every worker.

| Setting | Scope |
|---|---|
| `FixedConcurrency(n)` / `AutoConcurrency(min, max)` on a pool | This process, this pool |
| `MaxOutstandingAttempts(n)` on a worker (default 16) | This process, all pools |
| `runwick.Queue("q", q => q.MaxConcurrent(n))` | All workers |
| `MaxConcurrent(n)` on a job | All workers |
| `PerResource(selector, n)` on a job | All workers, per key |
| `RollingWindow(...)`, `RollingWindowPerResource(...)` | All workers |

Four processes with `FixedConcurrency(8)` run up to 32 jobs. If you need "5 at most, anywhere", use a store-backed limit. Pool sizing is covered in [Workers](/docs/workers).

## Concurrency caps

A store-backed concurrency limit is called a **scope**. Each scope has a capacity. A job that needs a scope must get a free slot in it when it is claimed; a crashed worker's slot frees itself when its lease runs out.

```csharp
// Queue scope: at most 20 jobs from "emails" running anywhere.
runwick.Queue("emails", q => q.MaxConcurrent(20));

// Job-type scope: at most 5 renders running anywhere.
runwick.ConfigureJob<RenderPdf>().MaxConcurrent(5);

// Resource scope: at most 1 job per invoice at a time.
runwick.ConfigureJob<RecalculateInvoice>().PerResource(job => $"invoice:{job.InvoiceId}", 1);
```

| Kind | Key | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `queue` | the queue name | `emails`, capacity 20 |
| `job-type` | the job name | `pdf.render`, capacity 5 |
| `resource` | what your selector returns | `invoice:123`, capacity 1 |

A job can need several scopes at once, for example its queue, its type and two resources. It must get a slot in **all** of them or it waits. The limit is 8 scopes per job (`too_many_scopes`). All capacities must be at least 1.

A resource scope with capacity 1 is a distributed lock on one thing. Use it for "never recalculate the same account twice at the same time". [Uniqueness](/docs/uniqueness) cannot do this: it controls creating jobs, not running them.

### The resource selector

The selector runs once, when the job is dispatched. Its result is stored with the job. Keep it a pure function of the payload. The key follows the same rules as uniqueness keys: 1 to 512 UTF-8 bytes, no control characters, case-sensitive. A throwing selector fails the dispatch with `key_selector_failed`.

### Changing a capacity

Queue and job-type scopes are created at startup if they do not exist. Resource scopes are created by the first dispatch that needs them. **An existing scope is never overwritten from code.** If you change `MaxConcurrent(5)` to `MaxConcurrent(10)` and redeploy, the stored capacity stays 5 and the difference is reported as drift.

Change a live capacity with the CLI, the dashboard or `ICapacityControl`:

```bash
runwick capacity list --kind job-type
runwick capacity set job-type pdf.render 10
```

```csharp
using Runwick.Management;

var result = await capacity.SetScopeCapacityAsync("job-type", "pdf.render", 10, expectedPolicyRevision,
    new ManagementActor("ops-bot", "Ops bot", "service"));
```

Lowering a capacity revokes nothing. Jobs already running keep their slots; new claims wait until the count drops below the new limit.

### Fencing tokens

A worker can lose its lease and keep running, for example after a long pause. With a capacity-1 resource scope, another worker can then take the slot while the first one is still writing. Runwick cannot stop the first worker's code, but each new holder of a capacity-1 resource scope gets a **fencing token**: a number that only goes up.

```csharp
public sealed class SyncInvoiceHandler(IJobContext context, InvoiceApi api) : IJobHandler<SyncInvoice>
{
    public Task HandleAsync(SyncInvoice job, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // One capacity-1 resource scope (PerResource(..., 1)), so one fence.
        var fence = context.Fences.Single();
        return api.UpdateAsync(job.InvoiceId, job.Data, fencingToken: fence.Value, ct);
    }
}
```

The token only protects you if the other system remembers the highest value it has seen and rejects lower ones.

## Rate limits

A rate limit allows at most N **run authorizations** in any rolling window of time:

```csharp
// At most 100 runs of this job type per minute, across all workers.
runwick.ConfigureJob<SendSms>().RollingWindow(maxExecutions: 100, window: TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1));

// At most 10 runs per customer per second.
runwick.ConfigureJob<CallPartnerApi>()
    .RollingWindowPerResource(job => $"customer:{job.CustomerId}", maxExecutions: 10, window: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1));
```

| Bound | Value |
|---|---|
| Limit | 1 to 100,000 per window |
| Window | whole milliseconds, 1 second to 24 hours |
| Rate scopes per job | at most 8, and at most one `RollingWindow` for the job type |

"Rolling" means the window always ends now. It is never "this calendar minute", so 200 cannot slip through across a minute boundary.

### What happens at the limit

When a scope is full, the job is **deferred**: it goes back to waiting with a new earliest start time, roughly when the oldest run in the window drops out (at least 250 ms later, plus up to 100 ms of jitter). A deferral costs nothing: no execution, no retry budget. The worker's slot is freed at once. The deferral time is a hint, not a reservation; another worker may take the capacity first.

If a job needs several rate scopes, it needs room in all of them, or none is charged. A run that fails after it was authorized keeps its charge, and its retry needs a new one.

### What a rate limit counts

The limit counts authorizations, the moment Runwick says "run now". It does not count your handler's later HTTP calls. A handler that waits five minutes before calling the API, or calls it three times, is not tracked. If your provider is strict, add a limiter around the HTTP client too.

### Turn on rate_admission first

Rate limits need the store capability `rate_admission`, raised once per application. Until then, dispatching a job that has a rate limit is refused with `rate_admission_not_active` and nothing is written.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Start the application once">

This registers the application in the store.

  </Step>
  <Step title="Activate the capability">

```bash
runwick store activate-capability --name rate_admission --application my-app --provider postgres --connection-env MY_CONN
```

Use `--provider sqlite` or `--provider redis` for the other stores. From code: `RunwickPostgresMigrations.ActivateCapabilityAsync(connectionString, "my-app", "rate_admission", "deploy")` (the SQLite and Redis migration classes have the same method).

  </Step>
  <Step title="Restart">

The step is done once per application.

  </Step>
</Steps>

<Callout type="warning" title="This cannot be undone">

A capability is never lowered. After activation, older Runwick binaries that do not know `rate_admission` can no longer create jobs for that application. Upgrade every process first. See [Upgrades](/docs/upgrades).

</Callout>

Rate scopes, like concurrency scopes, are created by the first dispatch that needs them and are not overwritten from code later.

## Next

- [Workers](/docs/workers): pool sizes and automatic concurrency.
- [Queues and priorities](/docs/queues-and-priorities)
