# Schedules

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/schedules

> Create jobs on a cron timetable or at one fixed time, handle missed runs and daylight saving, and pause or trigger a schedule.

A **schedule** turns "every night at 02:00" into ordinary jobs. The scheduler only creates jobs; workers run them like any other job, with the same retries, limits and guarantees.

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRunwick(runwick =>
{
    runwick.Application("my-app")
        .UsePostgres(connectionString)
        .AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining<NightlyCleanup>();

    runwick.AddScheduler();                                       // run the scheduler role in this process

    runwick.AddSchedule("nightly-cleanup", new NightlyCleanup(RetentionDays: 30))
        .Cron("0 2 * * *", timeZone: "Europe/Berlin");
});
```

## Turn on the scheduler capability first

Schedules need the store capability `scheduler`, raised once per application. Until then, startup fails with `scheduler_not_active`, and the error message names the command to run.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Start the application once">

This registers the application in the store. The first start fails at the scheduler; that is expected.

  </Step>
  <Step title="Activate the capability">

```bash
runwick store activate-capability --name scheduler --application my-app --provider postgres --connection-env MY_CONN
```

Use `--provider sqlite` or `--provider redis` for the other stores. From code: `RunwickPostgresMigrations.ActivateCapabilityAsync(connectionString, "my-app", "scheduler", "deploy")`, or the same method on `RunwickSqliteMigrations` and `RunwickRedisMigrations`.

  </Step>
  <Step title="Restart">

This is done once per application and cannot be undone. Older Runwick binaries that do not know the capability can no longer create jobs for that application afterwards.

  </Step>
</Steps>

## Where the scheduler runs

`AddScheduler()` runs the scheduler role in this process. You can run it in as many processes as you like. There is no leader election: each occurrence has a unique key in the store, so only one process can create its job.

`AddSchedule` without `AddScheduler` in the same process is allowed. The schedule is then registered the first time a process that runs the scheduler and declares it starts.

```csharp
runwick.AddScheduler(s =>
{
    s.PollInterval = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1);       // while work is due
    s.IdlePollInterval = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5);   // backs off to this when idle
    s.JobsPerSecond = 100;                          // per scheduler process
    s.Burst = 32;
});
```

The values above are the defaults. `AddScheduler` may be called once.

## Defining a schedule

`AddSchedule(key, job)` takes a key and the job instance to create on each occurrence. The payload is frozen when the schedule is registered. The job type must be registered. Each key may be declared once.

Every schedule has exactly one of `Cron` or `Once` (`schedule_definition_missing` otherwise).

### Cron

```csharp
runwick.AddSchedule("hourly-sync", new SyncCatalog())
    .Cron("15 * * * *");                                         // 15 past every hour, UTC

runwick.AddSchedule("weekday-report", new BuildReport("daily", 0))
    .Cron("0 9 * * MON-FRI", timeZone: "America/New_York");

runwick.AddSchedule("heartbeat", new Heartbeat())
    .Cron("*/30 * * * * *", ScheduleCronFormat.SixField);        // every 30 seconds
```

| Format | Fields |
|---|---|
| `FiveField` (default) | minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week |
| `SixField` | second, minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week |

Each field takes `*`, a value, a range `a-b`, a step `*/n` or `a-b/n`, or a comma list of those. Months accept `JAN`–`DEC` and days of week `SUN`–`SAT`; Sunday is 0 or 7.

Not supported: macros such as `@daily`, `?`, `L`, `W`, `#`, `H`, year fields and `TZ=` prefixes. An expression is at most 256 characters.

When both day of month and day of week are restricted, a date matches if **either** matches. `0 9 1 * MON` runs at 09:00 on the 1st of every month and on every Monday.

### Time zones

Without a zone, schedules run in UTC. A zone must be an IANA ID such as `Europe/Berlin`. Windows IDs and `Local` are refused. Runwick ships a pinned copy of the time-zone database, so a server's OS update cannot silently move a schedule.

Daylight saving needs two decisions:

```csharp
runwick.AddSchedule("berlin-0230", new Tick())
    .Cron("30 2 * * *", timeZone: "Europe/Berlin")
    .OnGap(ScheduleGap.Shift)       // 02:30 does not exist in spring: run at the next valid time
    .OnFold(ScheduleFold.Earlier);  // 02:30 happens twice in autumn: run the first one
```

| Option | Values |
|---|---|
| `OnGap` | `Skip` (default), `Shift` |
| `OnFold` | `Earlier` (default), `Later`, `Both` |

### Once

```csharp
runwick.AddSchedule("launch-mail", new SendLaunchMail())
    .Once(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 12, 1, 9, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
```

After its one occurrence the schedule is finished. For a single delayed job you usually want `DispatchOptions.NotBefore` instead; see [Dispatching](/docs/dispatching).

## At most one job per occurrence

Each occurrence, such as "02:00 on 5 March", creates **at most one job**. The job it creates is at-least-once like every job, so its handler can still run more than once. Make it safe to repeat.

When a schedule is first registered, the first occurrence is the first one after that moment. There is no backfill of earlier times.

The handler can read which occurrence it belongs to from `IJobContext.Schedule`. See [Job context](/docs/job-context).

## Missed occurrences

If no scheduler was running when an occurrence was due, and it is now more than the grace period late (default 60 seconds), the misfire policy decides:

```csharp
runwick.AddSchedule("nightly-cleanup", new NightlyCleanup(30))
    .Cron("0 2 * * *")
    .OnMisfire(MisfirePolicy.CatchUp, grace: TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5))
    .CatchUpLimits(maxJobsPerEpisode: 100, maxAge: TimeSpan.FromDays(2));
```

| Policy | What happens |
|---|---|
| `RunOnce` (default) | One job now, recorded as covering the whole missed range. |
| `Skip` | No job. The skipped range is recorded. |
| `CatchUp` | One job per missed occurrence, oldest first, in small paced batches. |

Grace can be 0 to 24 hours. Catch-up stops at 1,000 jobs per episode by default (1 to 10,000) and refuses occurrences older than 7 days by default (1 minute to 31 days). When it hits either limit it creates no more jobs and flags the schedule as needing review, rather than silently dropping occurrences.

## Overlap

By default a new occurrence's job can run while the previous one is still running.

```csharp
runwick.AddSchedule("import", new ImportFeed()).Cron("*/5 * * * *").Overlap(ScheduleOverlap.Serialize);
```

`Serialize` adds a capacity-1 [concurrency scope](/docs/rate-limits-and-concurrency) shared by the schedule's jobs, so only one runs at a time. It does not stop jobs being created: if each run takes longer than the interval, jobs queue up.

## Options for the created jobs

`WithOptions` sets the queue, priority, metadata and active uniqueness of every job the schedule creates:

```csharp
runwick.AddSchedule("import", new ImportFeed())
    .Cron("*/5 * * * *")
    .WithOptions(new DispatchOptions { Queue = "imports", Priority = "low" });
```

- `NotBefore` is refused (`schedule_delay_unsupported`).
- Window uniqueness is refused (`schedule_window_unsupported`).
- An active key makes every occurrence share one key, so it requires `.AllowOccurrenceReuse()` (`schedule_occurrence_reuse_required`). An occurrence that finds the key held is linked to the existing job instead of creating a new one.

## Changing a schedule in code

Registration never overwrites. If you change a schedule's cron, zone, payload or options in code and redeploy, the scheduler logs a warning that the stored definition differs, and the **stored definition stays in effect**. Pause and enabled state are never reset by a restart either.

There is no public operation to edit a stored schedule in this release. To change timing, declare the new definition under a new key and pause the old one.

## Pausing, resuming and triggering

Pausing a schedule stops it creating jobs. Jobs it already created are not paused or cancelled.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="CLI">

```bash
runwick schedules list
runwick schedules pause nightly-cleanup
runwick schedules resume nightly-cleanup --policy skipPaused
runwick schedules trigger nightly-cleanup
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="C#">

```csharp
using Runwick.Management;

var actor = new ManagementActor("ops-bot", "Ops bot", "service");
await schedules.PauseAsync("nightly-cleanup", expectedControlRevision, actor, reason: "maintenance");
await schedules.ResumeAsync("nightly-cleanup", expectedControlRevision + 1, ResumePolicy.SkipPaused, actor);
await schedules.TriggerAsync("nightly-cleanup", expectedDefinitionRevision, triggerId: Guid.CreateVersion7(), actor);
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

On resume you choose what happens to occurrences missed while paused: `SkipPaused`, `RunOnce` or `CatchUp`.

**Trigger** creates one extra job now, even while the schedule is paused. It never moves the timetable. The trigger ID is an idempotency key: the same ID returns the same job.

A schedule flagged as needing review can be cleared with `runwick schedules revalidate <key>` once you have fixed the cause. Every one of these actions is audited. `IScheduleControl` trusts the actor you pass; the HTTP API, dashboard and CLI check permissions.

## Next

- [Job context](/docs/job-context): read the occurrence in a handler.
- [Rate limits and concurrency](/docs/rate-limits-and-concurrency)

# Cancellation

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/cancellation

> Cancelling a job is a request, not a kill. How the token works, how long Runwick waits, and how to write handlers that stop cleanly.

Cancellation in Runwick is a **request**, not a kill. .NET has no safe way to stop code that is already running, and Runwick does not try. It cancels the `CancellationToken` your handler received and waits for your code to notice.

## What happens when you cancel a job

| The job is… | What happens |
|---|---|
| Waiting (`pending` or `retrying`) | It moves to `cancelled` and never runs. |
| Running | The store records "cancel requested". The worker cancels the handler's token. Your code must stop. |
| Already finished | Nothing changes. The answer says the job had already finished; it is not reported as a successful cancel. |

If the handler stops by throwing `OperationCanceledException`, the run ends as **cancelled** and is not retried. If the handler finishes successfully before the cancel reaches it, success wins; the history shows both the request and the success.

### Cancelling from the CLI, dashboard or API

```bash
runwick jobs cancel 0193a7c2-5b1e-7c3d-9f00-1a2b3c4d5e6f
```

`runwick jobs cancel-many --file jobs.jsonl` cancels up to 100 jobs at once. In C#, use `IJobControl` from `Runwick.Management`:

```csharp
using Runwick.Management;

var result = await jobControl.CancelAsync(
    new JobTarget(jobId, ExpectedGeneration: 1, ExpectedRevision: revision),
    new ManagementActor("ops-bot", "Ops bot", "service"),
    reason: "customer asked to stop");

Console.WriteLine($"{result.Succeeded} {result.Code} {result.State}");
```

The target carries the generation and revision you last saw. If the job changed in between, you get a conflict rather than cancelling something you did not look at. A rejection comes back as a result with a `Code`, not as an exception.

The dashboard, CLI and API show **"cancel requested"** until the worker reports how the run ended. They never claim a cancel "stopped the handler".

## One token, four causes

The same token is cancelled for four different reasons:

| Cause | When |
|---|---|
| `UserRequested` | Someone cancelled the job. |
| `Timeout` | The job's `ExecutionTimeout` ran out. See [Retries and timeouts](/docs/retries-and-timeouts). |
| `Shutdown` | The worker is stopping. |
| `LeaseLost` | The worker could not renew its lease in time and no longer owns the job. |

`IJobContext.CancellationCauses` is a flags value that tells you which ones Runwick has seen. More than one can be set.

```csharp
public sealed class ExportHandler(IJobContext context, ILogger<ExportHandler> logger) : IJobHandler<ExportOrders>
{
    public async Task HandleAsync(ExportOrders job, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        try
        {
            await ExportAsync(job, ct);
        }
        catch (OperationCanceledException) when (ct.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            logger.LogInformation("Export {JobId} stopped: {Causes}", context.JobId, context.CancellationCauses);
            throw;   // let Runwick classify it
        }
    }
}
```

Rethrow rather than swallow. Runwick classifies the run from the causes:

| Cause | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Timeout | Timed out. Retryable. |
| User request | Cancelled. Not retried. |
| Shutdown | Interrupted. Retryable, and picked up again after restart. |
| Lease lost | The worker writes no result. The store's recovery decides once the lease expires. |

An `OperationCanceledException` that is not caused by any of these, for example your own `HttpClient` timeout, is an ordinary retryable failure.

## Write handlers that cooperate

<Steps>
  <Step title="Pass the token everywhere">

Give `ct` to every database call, HTTP call and `Task.Delay`. Most .NET APIs stop promptly when it is cancelled.

  </Step>
  <Step title="Check it in loops">

```csharp
foreach (var chunk in chunks)
{
    ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
    await ProcessAsync(chunk, ct);
}
```

  </Step>
  <Step title="Keep uninterruptible steps short">

If a step cannot be interrupted, keep it well under the grace period.

  </Step>
  <Step title="Make each step safe to repeat">

A cancelled or interrupted run may have done part of its work. A retried run starts from the top. See [Delivery guarantees](/docs/delivery-guarantees).

  </Step>
</Steps>

## Grace period

After the first user, timeout or shutdown cancellation, Runwick waits up to `CancellationGrace` (default 10 seconds) for the handler to return. Repeated signals do not restart the clock.

- **Handler returns within grace:** the worker cleans up the DI scope and records the outcome normally.
- **Handler ignores the token:** after the grace period the worker stops renewing the lease and writes no result. The code keeps running in the process, holding its pool slot and DI scope until it actually returns. When the lease expires, the store's recovery closes the attempt: cancelled if a cancel was requested, otherwise retried or failed by the usual budget. Another worker may then run the job while the old code is still going.

```csharp
runwick.AddWorker(w => w
    .Pool("main", p => p.Queues("default"))
    .Configure(o => o.CancellationGrace = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(20)));
```

Worker timings are checked against each other at startup; see [Configuration](/docs/configuration).

<Callout type="warning" title="A handler that ignores the token can run twice at once">

Concurrency limits count valid leases, not code that is still physically running. If overlap would be harmful, honour the token and use [fencing tokens](/docs/rate-limits-and-concurrency#fencing-tokens).

</Callout>

## Shutdown

When the host stops, the worker stops claiming new jobs and lets running handlers finish. After the drain phase (15 seconds by default) it cancels the remaining handlers with cause `Shutdown`, gives them a few seconds, then records what it knows. The whole shutdown budget is 25 seconds by default, inside .NET's usual 30-second host shutdown timeout. Keep the host's timeout above Runwick's. See [Workers](/docs/workers) and [Deployment](/docs/deployment).

## Cancelling a dispatch call

The token you pass to `DispatchAsync` is different. It only stops **waiting** for the store; it never cancels a job the store has accepted. See [Dispatching](/docs/dispatching#cancellation).

## Next

- [Job context](/docs/job-context)
- [Retries and timeouts](/docs/retries-and-timeouts)

---

# Job context

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/job-context

> Read facts about the current run with IJobContext, log with them, and wrap runs in middleware.

`IJobContext` gives a handler read-only facts about the run it is in: the job ID, which run this is, the queue, metadata, schedule and more. Inject it into the handler's constructor. It is not a `HandleAsync` argument, so handlers that do not need it simply leave it out.

```csharp
public sealed class SendInvoiceHandler(IJobContext context, ILogger<SendInvoiceHandler> logger, IMailer mailer)
    : IJobHandler<SendInvoice>
{
    public async Task HandleAsync(SendInvoice job, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        logger.LogInformation("Sending invoice {InvoiceId}, job {JobId}, run {Run} of {Max}",
            job.InvoiceId, context.JobId, context.ExecutionNumber, context.MaxExecutions);

        // The job ID is the same on every retry: a good idempotency key.
        await mailer.SendAsync(job.InvoiceId, idempotencyKey: context.JobId.ToString(), ct);
    }
}
```

There is one context per run. It can only be resolved inside the run's DI scope; resolving it anywhere else throws `InvalidOperationException`.

## What it exposes

### Identity

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Application` | The application name. |
| `JobId` | The job's permanent ID. Stable across retries and manual retries. |
| `AttemptId` | The ID of this one attempt. New on every try. |
| `JobName` | The stored job name, for example `email.welcome`. |
| `CreatedAt` | When the store created the job. |

### Runs and budget

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ExecutionNumber` | Which run this is within the current generation, from 1. |
| `MaxExecutions` | The run budget for this generation. |
| `Generation` | 1 for the original dispatch. A manual retry or rerun starts generation 2, 3 and so on, each with a fresh budget. |

`ExecutionNumber == MaxExecutions` means this is the last automatic try. You might log louder, or send a different alert, on that run.

### Routing and payload

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Queue`, `Priority` | Where the job was routed. |
| `OriginalPayloadVersion` | The version of the stored bytes. |
| `CurrentPayloadVersion` | The version handed to the handler after upgrades. |
| `SerializerProfileId`, `SerializerProfileVersion` | `runwick.json`, 1. |
| `GetPayload<TJob>()` | The same upgraded payload the handler received. Useful in middleware. `TJob` must be the registered current type. |

### Metadata, tracing and fences

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Metadata` | Business metadata passed at dispatch, such as a tenant. |
| `Trace` | The W3C `traceparent` and `tracestate` captured at dispatch. |
| `Fences` | One fencing token per capacity-1 resource scope this run holds. See [Rate limits and concurrency](/docs/rate-limits-and-concurrency#fencing-tokens). |
| `Schedule` | The schedule occurrence that created this job, or `null`. |
| `CancellationCauses` | Which cancellation causes Runwick has seen. See [Cancellation](/docs/cancellation). |
| `Items` | A per-run dictionary for passing data between middleware and the handler. Never saved. |

Everything except `Items` and `CancellationCauses` stays the same for the whole run.

### Scheduled jobs

For a job created by a [schedule](/docs/schedules), `Schedule` holds:

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ScheduleName` | The schedule key. |
| `ScheduledAt` | The occurrence this job belongs to. |
| `CoveredFrom`, `CoveredUntil` | The time range the job covers. After a missed run with the `RunOnce` policy, one job can cover several occurrences. |

```csharp
if (context.Schedule is { } s)
{
    logger.LogInformation("Cleanup for {From:u} to {Until:u}", s.CoveredFrom, s.CoveredUntil);
}
```

## What it does not expose

The context is read-only by design. It has no database connection, no lease, no way to extend the lease or the timeout, and **no progress reporting**. Lease renewal is done by the worker, not the handler, so a handler cannot keep a job alive forever.

If you need to report progress, write it to your own table or cache keyed by `JobId`.

## Logging

Runwick does not add a logging scope for you. Inject `ILogger<T>` as usual and include the IDs you need:

```csharp
using (logger.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object>
{
    ["JobId"] = context.JobId.ToString(),
    ["AttemptId"] = context.AttemptId.ToString(),
}))
{
    await DoWorkAsync(job, ct);
}
```

When tracing is on, each run gets a `process {queue}` span, and the handler runs inside a `runwick.execute` child span. Spans your own code starts become its children, and the run is linked to the dispatch that created it. See [Observability](/docs/observability).

## Middleware

Middleware wraps every run, like ASP.NET Core middleware wraps a request. It receives the same context and token as the handler:

```csharp
public sealed class TenantMiddleware(ITenantAccessor tenants) : IJobMiddleware
{
    public async Task<JobExecutionResult> InvokeAsync(IJobContext context, JobExecutionDelegate next, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        if (!context.Metadata.TryGetValue("tenant", out var tenant))
        {
            return JobExecutionResult.Failed("tenant_missing", "Every job needs a tenant.");
        }

        tenants.Current = tenant;
        context.Items["tenant"] = tenant;
        return await next();   // call exactly once
    }
}
```

A middleware either calls `next()` exactly once and returns its result, or returns a result without calling it. Calling `next()` twice, or returning while it is still running, is a contract fault and fails the job permanently.

| Result | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `JobExecutionResult.Succeeded()` | Success. Return it explicitly if you skip the handler on purpose. |
| `JobExecutionResult.Retry(reason, delay)` | Retryable failure. Costs one run. |
| `JobExecutionResult.Failed(code, message)` | Permanent failure. |
| `JobExecutionResult.Cancelled(reason)` | Ends the job as cancelled. |

Register middleware globally, per job, or by alias so that a contracts assembly can name middleware without referencing its code:

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="Global">

```csharp
runwick.UseMiddleware<TenantMiddleware>();
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Per job">

```csharp
runwick.ConfigureJob<SendInvoice>().UseMiddleware<AuditMiddleware>();
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="By alias">

```csharp
// In the contracts assembly:
[JobName("billing.invoice.send")]
[UseJobMiddleware("audit", Order = 10)]
public sealed record SendInvoice(Guid InvoiceId) : IQueueJob;

// On the worker:
runwick.AddMiddleware<AuditMiddleware>("audit");
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

The order, outer to inner, is: global middleware in registration order, then attribute aliases by `Order` (ties by alias name), then fluent per-job middleware, then the handler. Middleware is scoped and resolved fresh for every run. A worker that sees an alias nobody registered refuses to start (`unknown_middleware_alias`); a producer-only app does not check aliases.

Middleware cannot extend leases, reset budgets or finish a job itself. Those are the worker's job.

## Next

- [Retries and timeouts](/docs/retries-and-timeouts)
- [Testing](/docs/testing): run handlers without a database.

# PostgreSQL

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/postgresql

> Run Runwick on PostgreSQL 16, 17 or 18, create its schema with a migration role, and stage jobs in your own transactions.

PostgreSQL is Runwick's reference store. The rest of Runwick is measured against it. Producers and workers can run on many hosts, as long as they all connect to the same primary. It is also the store where a job can share a transaction with your own data.

## Requirements

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Server | PostgreSQL 16, 17 or 18 (18 is the reference) |
| Database | `UTF8` encoding, `standard_conforming_strings = on` (the default) |
| Extensions | None |
| Topology | Connect directly to the primary |
| Package | `Runwick.Postgres` (uses Npgsql) |

The migration checks the server version and encoding before it writes anything, and stops with a clear error if they do not match.

## Install

```bash
dotnet add package Runwick
dotnet add package Runwick.Postgres
```

## Create the schema

Runwick never changes the schema when your application starts. You run the migration as a separate deployment step, from code or from the command line:

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="C#">

```csharp
using Runwick.Postgres.Migrations;

var result = await RunwickPostgresMigrations.MigrateAsync(migrationConnectionString);
Console.WriteLine($"schema revision {result.SchemaRevision}, phases: {string.Join(", ", result.AppliedPhases)}");
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="CLI">

```bash
export RUNWICK_MIGRATE_CONN="Host=db;Database=app;Username=runwick_owner;Password=..."
runwick migrate --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_MIGRATE_CONN
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

The migration is safe to run again: a fully applied migration is a no-op. Two runners at once do not collide, because the runner holds a PostgreSQL advisory lock for the whole run. It waits up to 60 seconds for that lock. If it fails, it throws `PostgresMigrationException`, whose `Code` says what went wrong (for example `server_version_unsupported` or `migration_lock_unavailable`).

The CLI never takes a connection string as an argument, because command lines are visible to other users of the machine. Pass the name of an environment variable (`--connection-env`) or pipe it in (`--connection-stdin`). Use the CLI version that matches your Runwick packages: it installs the migrations compiled into it.

## Roles: migration role and runtime role

Use two database roles:

- **Migration role.** Creates and owns the `runwick` schema. It runs `MigrateAsync`, and the store administration commands (`runwick store status`, `store admission`, `store activate-capability`, `store reidentify`).
- **Runtime role.** Used by your application. It needs data access to the tables in the `runwick` schema, and no DDL rights.

Runwick does not create database roles or grant privileges for you. Grant the runtime role access with your usual tooling after the migration has run.

<Callout type="info" title="Capabilities are a one-time step">

Schedules and rate limits need a capability raised once per application, with the migration role: `runwick store activate-capability --name scheduler --application my-app --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_MIGRATE_CONN`. Use `--name rate_admission` for rate limits. See [Schedules](/docs/schedules) and [Upgrades](/docs/upgrades).

</Callout>

## Register the store

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRunwick(runwick =>
{
    runwick.Application("billing")
        .UsePostgres(builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Runwick")!)
        .AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining<SendInvoice>();
    runwick.AddHandler<SendInvoice, SendInvoiceHandler>();
    runwick.AddWorker(w => w.Pool("main", p => p.Queues("default").FixedConcurrency(4)));
});
```

`UsePostgres` takes the connection string and an optional `Action<PostgresOptions>`. Runwick creates and owns its own Npgsql data sources, and never logs the connection string.

| Option | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `PostgresOptions.Schema` | `runwick` | Only `runwick` is supported in this release. Any other value is refused at startup. |

An empty connection string fails at startup with `missing_store`.

### Connections

Runwick keeps separate connection pools for lease work (claim, renew, finish) and for everything else, so a burst of dispatches cannot starve lease renewals. With default settings, plan for about 23 connections per worker process: 8 for lease work, 14 for other work and 1 for the listener described below. A process that only dispatches opens no lease-work pool. Raising `ProducerOptions.MaxConcurrentCalls` adds the same number of connections. Add your own business connections on top when you size `max_connections`.

### How workers notice new jobs

Workers poll for due work. On PostgreSQL, a committed dispatch also sends a `NOTIFY` on a dedicated listener connection, so idle workers wake up sooner. The notification is only a hint. If it is lost, polling still finds the job.

## Primary only

Ownership decisions (who holds a job's lease) are never read from a replica. Point every Runwick process at the primary.

<Callout type="warning" title="Poolers and high availability are not certified">

Connection poolers such as PgBouncer, proxies, and failover setups have not been tested with Runwick. If you use one, you are outside what has been tested. In particular, do not route Runwick through anything that could send a query to a replica.

</Callout>

## Create a job in your own transaction

When your business tables and Runwick's tables are in the same database, you can create a job in the same transaction as your own rows. Inject `IPostgresJobDispatcher` and call `StageAsync` with your open `NpgsqlTransaction`:

```csharp
using Runwick.Postgres;

public sealed class SignupService(NpgsqlDataSource db, IPostgresJobDispatcher jobs)
{
    public async Task SignUpAsync(string email, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await using var connection = await db.OpenConnectionAsync(ct);
        await using var tx = await connection.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);

        var userId = Guid.NewGuid();
        await using (var insert = new NpgsqlCommand("INSERT INTO users (id, email) VALUES ($1, $2)", connection, tx))
        {
            insert.Parameters.AddWithValue(userId);
            insert.Parameters.AddWithValue(email);
            await insert.ExecuteNonQueryAsync(ct);
        }

        StagedDispatch staged = await jobs.StageAsync(new SendWelcomeEmail(userId), tx, cancellationToken: ct);

        await tx.CommitAsync(ct);   // the user row and the job commit together, or neither does
    }
}
```

`StageAsync` returns a `StagedDispatch`, not a `DispatchReceipt`. Nothing is durable until you commit. Runwick never commits, rolls back or retries your transaction. If the transaction fails with a serialization error or a deadlock, retrying the whole transaction is your job. `StageManyAsync` stages a batch of up to 100 jobs the same way.

The other direction works too: a handler can mark its job as succeeded inside your transaction. [Transactions](/docs/transactions) covers both, with their rules and limits.

## What PostgreSQL does not promise

- No high availability. A failover or a restored backup is a break in history: receipts, uniqueness windows and fences from before it are not guaranteed to carry over.
- Delivery is still at-least-once. A handler can run more than once. See [Delivery guarantees](/docs/delivery-guarantees).
- Durability is what your server's settings give you. A confirmed dispatch means PostgreSQL committed it. Runwick does not check `synchronous_commit`; keep it `on` (the default), or a crash can lose writes that were already confirmed.

## Next steps

<Cards>
  <Card title="Transactions" icon="blocks" href="/docs/transactions">
    Stage jobs and complete them inside your own transaction.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Upgrades" icon="rocket" href="/docs/upgrades">
    Migrate, drain and roll back safely.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Deployment" icon="server" href="/docs/deployment">
    Process shapes, shutdown timing and connection budgets.
  </Card>
</Cards>

# SQLite

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/sqlite

> Run Runwick on one SQLite file for apps whose workers all live on one machine, with WAL and synchronous=FULL enforced.

The SQLite store keeps all of Runwick's data in one database file. It behaves like the PostgreSQL store: the same job states, retries, receipts, uniqueness and rate rules. It suits an app that runs on a single machine, in one process or several, and that does not want a database server.

## Requirements

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Engine | SQLite 3.38 or newer. The bundled native library already is. |
| Topology | One file on a local disk. Every process that uses it runs on the same machine. |
| Durability | WAL journal mode and `synchronous=FULL`, on every connection |
| Package | `Runwick.Sqlite` (uses Microsoft.Data.Sqlite) |

## Install and create the file

```bash
dotnet add package Runwick
dotnet add package Runwick.Sqlite
```

Run the migration once before the app starts. It creates the file if needed, creates the tables and switches the file to WAL mode:

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="C#">

```csharp
using Runwick;

await RunwickSqliteMigrations.MigrateAsync("Data Source=/var/lib/my-app/runwick.db");
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="CLI">

```bash
export RUNWICK_SQLITE="Data Source=/var/lib/my-app/runwick.db"
runwick migrate --provider sqlite --connection-env RUNWICK_SQLITE
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

Running it again does nothing if the schema is already current.

## Register the store

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRunwick(runwick =>
{
    runwick.Application("my-app")
        .UseSqlite("Data Source=/var/lib/my-app/runwick.db", o =>
        {
            o.WriterBusyTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2);
            o.ReaderThreads = 2;
        })
        .AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining<ResizeImage>();
    runwick.AddHandler<ResizeImage, ResizeImageHandler>();
    runwick.AddWorker(w => w.Pool("main", p => p.Queues("default").FixedConcurrency(4)));
});
```

The connection string must name a file with `Data Source=<path>`. Runwick opens its own connections from it and never logs it.

| Option | Default | Allowed | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `WriterBusyTimeout` | 2 s | 100 ms to 30 s | How long a write waits for another process to release the file's write lock. |
| `ReaderThreads` | 2 | 1 to 8 | Threads for read-only calls, each with its own connection. |

A value outside its range fails at startup with `invalid_policy`.

### How the store uses threads

The .NET SQLite library runs its "async" methods synchronously. So Runwick runs its database work on a few dedicated threads: one writer and `ReaderThreads` readers. The worker's lease and scheduling loops never wait inside a SQLite call.

## Durability: WAL and synchronous=FULL

Every connection Runwick opens sets `synchronous = FULL` and `foreign_keys = ON`, then reads the settings back. The file must be in WAL mode, which the migration sets once and SQLite remembers. A reply from the store means the commit is on disk, as far as your disk's fsync goes.

If any of these settings does not stick, the store refuses to start with `store_profile_mismatch`. There is no "faster but less safe" mode.

## Setups that are refused

| Setup | What happens |
|---|---|
| In-memory database (`:memory:`, `Mode=Memory`), empty `Data Source` | Refused at startup with `invalid_policy` |
| `Mode=ReadOnly`, `Cache=Shared`, `Foreign Keys=False` | Refused at startup with `invalid_policy` |
| A file on a network share (a UNC path or network drive on Windows; NFS, SMB/CIFS, 9p, sshfs, Ceph, GlusterFS and similar on Linux) | Refused at startup. The message names the filesystem type. |
| A file not in WAL mode (for example, never migrated) | Refused with `store_profile_mismatch` |
| SQLite older than 3.38 | Refused with `engine_version_unsupported` |

On Linux the check reads the mount table. A filesystem Runwick does not recognise as either local or network is accepted, but reported as unverified rather than verified.

<Callout type="warning" title="One machine, really">

SQLite's locking only works between processes on the same machine. A file shared over the network can corrupt silently, which is why Runwick refuses it. A container volume is fine if every container that opens the file runs on the same host and the volume is a local disk.

</Callout>

## One writer at a time

SQLite lets one transaction write to a file at once, across all processes. Every Runwick write takes that lock up front. Workers send routine work in batches (claim and start up to 32 jobs, renew up to 64 leases, finish up to 32 jobs in one transaction), so they wait for the lock and sync to disk once per batch rather than once per job.

This has two practical effects:

- Nothing here says SQLite matches PostgreSQL's throughput. Measure your own load.
- While any write transaction is open on the file, every Runwick write waits, lease renewals included. A long transaction of your own on the same file can make leases expire. Keep them short.

## Polling

There are no wake-up notifications between processes. Workers find new jobs by polling, which is enough for correctness. Within one process, a commit wakes that process's own workers, scheduler and outbox relay straight away. A job dispatched by another process is picked up on the next poll.

## Your transaction, the same file

If your business tables live in the same SQLite file, you can create a job, or complete one, in your own transaction with `ISqliteJobDispatcher` and `ISqliteJobCompletion`. Your connection must use the same file and have `foreign_keys = 1` and `synchronous = FULL`. Begin the transaction with `BeginTransaction(deferred: false)` so it takes the write lock at the start:

```csharp
using Microsoft.Data.Sqlite;
using Runwick.Sqlite;

await using var connection = new SqliteConnection("Data Source=/var/lib/my-app/runwick.db");
await connection.OpenAsync(ct);
await using (var pragma = connection.CreateCommand())
{
    pragma.CommandText = "PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; PRAGMA synchronous = FULL;";
    await pragma.ExecuteNonQueryAsync(ct);
}

using var tx = connection.BeginTransaction(deferred: false);
// ... insert your own rows on tx ...
await jobs.StageAsync(new ResizeImage(imageId), tx, cancellationToken: ct);   // jobs: ISqliteJobDispatcher
tx.Commit();
```

A `SQLITE_BUSY` error from your transaction reaches you unchanged; retrying the whole transaction is up to you. See [Transactions](/docs/transactions) for the full rules.

## What SQLite does not promise

- No multi-host support and no high availability.
- No durability beyond your disk and its fsync behaviour. Restoring the file from a backup is a break in history.
- A killed process is not a power-loss test. Runwick's tests claim crash consistency, not protection from a disk that lies about fsync.

## Next steps

<Cards>
  <Card title="Choosing a store" icon="server" href="/docs/choosing-a-store">
    When SQLite fits, and when to move to PostgreSQL.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Transactions" icon="blocks" href="/docs/transactions">
    Commit jobs with your own rows in the same file.
  </Card>
</Cards>

# Redis

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/redis

> Run Runwick on one durable Redis primary with append-only fsync on every write, and know the limits that come with it.

The Redis store keeps Runwick's data on one Redis primary that writes every change to its append-only file and syncs it to disk before it replies. Producers and workers can run on many hosts. Job behaviour is the same as on PostgreSQL: the same states, retries, receipts, uniqueness and rate rules.

Redis is only safe for jobs with the right server settings, so Runwick checks them before it starts and keeps checking while it runs.

## Requirements

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Server | Redis 8.2 or newer |
| Topology | One standalone primary. No Cluster, no Sentinel. |
| Persistence | AOF with `appendfsync always` (see below) |
| Package | `Runwick.Redis` (uses StackExchange.Redis) |

## Server configuration

Start Redis with these settings. Runwick refuses to run with anything else:

```conf
# redis.conf
appendonly yes
appendfsync always
no-appendfsync-on-rewrite no
maxmemory-policy noeviction
aof-load-truncated no
```

| Setting | Why |
|---|---|
| `appendonly yes`, `appendfsync always` | Every write is on disk before Redis replies, so a confirmed job survives a crash. |
| `no-appendfsync-on-rewrite no` | Keeps fsync on while the AOF is being rewritten. |
| `maxmemory-policy noeviction` | Redis must never drop keys to free memory. A full server returns errors instead. |
| `aof-load-truncated no` | A damaged AOF stops Redis at startup instead of quietly loading less data. |

Size `maxmemory` with room to spare. With `noeviction`, a full server refuses writes, and dispatches fail until you free space.

<Callout type="warning" title="Keep CONFIG GET readable">

Runwick reads the settings with `CONFIG GET` and `MODULE LIST`. If an ACL blocks either, the value counts as unverifiable and the store refuses to run. Restrict `CONFIG SET` with ACLs if you need to, but leave `CONFIG GET` and `MODULE LIST` allowed for Runwick's user. Do not remove `CONFIG` with `rename-command`. Managed Redis services that hide `CONFIG` are not supported.

</Callout>

## Install and migrate

```bash
dotnet add package Runwick
dotnet add package Runwick.Redis
```

Write the store's identity once before the first start:

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="C#">

```csharp
using Runwick;

await RunwickRedisMigrations.MigrateAsync("redis-primary:6379,password=...");
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="CLI">

```bash
export RUNWICK_REDIS="redis-primary:6379,password=..."
runwick migrate --provider redis --connection-env RUNWICK_REDIS
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

Running it again does nothing if the store is already installed. Without it, the app refuses to start because the store is not installed.

## Register the store

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRunwick(runwick =>
{
    runwick.Application("notifications")
        .UseRedis(builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Redis")!, o =>
        {
            o.ProfileRecheckInterval = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);
        })
        .AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining<SendPush>();
    runwick.AddHandler<SendPush, SendPushHandler>();
    runwick.AddWorker(w => w.Pool("main", p => p.Queues("default").FixedConcurrency(4)));
});
```

The configuration string is a StackExchange.Redis string. Runwick uses only the endpoint, credentials, TLS settings, `defaultDatabase` and `connectTimeout` from it, and never logs it. Several endpoints, or a Sentinel service name, are refused at startup with `topology_unsupported`.

| Option | Default | Allowed | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ProfileRecheckInterval` | 30 s | 5 s to 5 min | How often the settings and topology check runs while the app runs. |

## What Runwick checks

At startup, on every reconnect and every `ProfileRecheckInterval`, Runwick checks on a separate connection:

- the five settings above, through `CONFIG GET`;
- through `INFO`: `role:master`, `redis_mode:standalone`, `cluster_enabled:0`, AOF enabled, the last AOF write succeeded, and the version is at least 8.2;
- through `MODULE LIST`: the loaded modules, which are reported but allowed.

| When | A failed check means |
|---|---|
| At startup | The app does not start. The error names the setting and the value it saw, for example `appendfsync=everysec`. |
| While running | Runwick stops sending new work: no new claims, dispatches or schedule runs. Health reports the store as unhealthy (`store_profile_mismatch`) until a later check passes. Calls already sent finish as usual. |

Replicas attached to the primary are allowed and reported. But a replica promoted to primary is a different history, and Runwick does not follow a failover.

### History checks

Each process remembers the store's identity and the highest revision it has seen for the application. If Redis comes back empty (for example after `FLUSHALL`), with another store's identity, or with a lower revision, Runwick stops admitting work and treats every lease it held as lost. It does not resume until you restart the process against an intact store. This check catches a history that went backwards. It cannot prove that no write was lost.

## One application, one hash slot

Every key of an application starts with `rw:{<application>}:`, so all of them live in one hash slot. That is what lets one Lua script change a job's records together. Several applications can share one Redis database.

The cost: one application's throughput is bounded by one Redis server thread, and one very large command (for example a big batch) delays every other command of that application while it runs. If one application needs more, split the work into separate applications.

## No transactions with your data

Redis cannot join your business database's transaction. There is no `StageAsync` and no transactional completion on Redis. To create a job only when your business data commits, write it to an [outbox](/docs/outbox) in your business database; the relay delivers it to the Redis store.

## Polling

There are no wake-up notifications between processes. Workers find new jobs by polling. Within one process, a commit wakes that process's own workers.

## What Redis does not promise

- No high availability. Failover, Sentinel promotion and Cluster are not supported. A promoted replica may have lost acknowledged jobs.
- Durability is the primary's disk and `appendfsync always`. Restoring an AOF or RDB file is a break in history.
- Running Redis without `appendfsync always` is not a supported configuration, even for benchmarks.
- Results on Redis say nothing about speed compared with PostgreSQL.

## Next steps

<Cards>
  <Card title="Outbox" icon="blocks" href="/docs/outbox">
    Commit a job with your business data, then deliver it to Redis.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Health checks" icon="gauge" href="/docs/health-checks">
    See the store's status in your health endpoint.
  </Card>
</Cards>

---

# Transactions

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/transactions

> Create a job, or mark one as succeeded, inside your own PostgreSQL or SQLite transaction so it commits with your data or not at all.

When your business tables and Runwick's tables live in the same PostgreSQL database or the same SQLite file, one transaction can hold both. Runwick uses that in two places:

- **Staging a job.** Create a job in the same transaction as your own rows. Either both are saved, or neither is.
- **Completing a job.** A handler marks its job as succeeded in the same transaction as the changes it made. This is Runwick's one exactly-once case.

Redis cannot join a business transaction. With Redis, or with a business database that is not the job store, use the [outbox](/docs/outbox).

| | PostgreSQL | SQLite |
|---|---|---|
| Stage a job | `IPostgresJobDispatcher.StageAsync` | `ISqliteJobDispatcher.StageAsync` |
| Stage a batch | `StageManyAsync` (up to 100 jobs) | `StageManyAsync` (up to 100 jobs) |
| Complete the current job | `IPostgresJobCompletion.CompleteInTransactionAsync` | `ISqliteJobCompletion.CompleteInTransactionAsync` |
| Transaction type | `NpgsqlTransaction` | `SqliteTransaction` |
| Namespace | `Runwick.Postgres` | `Runwick.Sqlite` |

All of these are registered by `UsePostgres` or `UseSqlite`. You do not add anything else.

## Staging a job

```csharp
await using var connection = await db.OpenConnectionAsync(ct);
await using var tx = await connection.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);

await orders.InsertAsync(order, connection, tx, ct);
var staged = await jobs.StageAsync(new ShipOrder(order.Id), tx, cancellationToken: ct);   // IPostgresJobDispatcher

await tx.CommitAsync(ct);   // the order row and the job commit together
```

`StageAsync` takes the same `DispatchOptions` as `DispatchAsync` (queue, priority, `NotBefore`, uniqueness, metadata). It returns a `StagedDispatch` with the job ID and whether the job was `Created` or `Reused` by a uniqueness key. It is not a `DispatchReceipt`, because nothing is durable until you commit.

Rules:

- Runwick never commits, rolls back, disposes or retries your transaction.
- A serialization failure or deadlock (PostgreSQL), or `SQLITE_BUSY` (SQLite), reaches you unchanged. Retry the whole transaction. To reuse the same operation on a retry, prepare once with `IPreparedJobDispatcher.Prepare` and pass the `PreparedDispatch` to `StageAsync` each time.
- On PostgreSQL, a committed staged job wakes idle workers through the same notification as a normal dispatch. A rolled-back one never does.

### Checks on your transaction

Before writing anything, Runwick checks the transaction. A failure throws `TransactionValidationException` and leaves your transaction as it was.

| Code | Cause |
|---|---|
| `transaction_invalid` | The transaction is completed, has no connection, or is read-only. |
| `transaction_store_mismatch` | The connection points at a different database or file from the configured store. |
| `transaction_profile_mismatch` | SQLite only: the connection does not have `foreign_keys = 1` and `synchronous = FULL`. |

## Completing a job in your transaction

Inject `IPostgresJobCompletion` (or `ISqliteJobCompletion`) into the handler. It only works inside a running attempt.

```csharp
using Npgsql;
using Runwick.Postgres;

public sealed class ApplyPaymentHandler(NpgsqlDataSource db, IPostgresJobCompletion completion)
    : IJobHandler<ApplyPayment>
{
    public async Task HandleAsync(ApplyPayment job, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await using var connection = await db.OpenConnectionAsync(ct);
        await using var tx = await connection.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);

        await using (var credit = new NpgsqlCommand(
            "UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + $1 WHERE id = $2", connection, tx))
        {
            credit.Parameters.AddWithValue(job.Amount);
            credit.Parameters.AddWithValue(job.AccountId);
            await credit.ExecuteNonQueryAsync(ct);
        }

        await completion.CompleteInTransactionAsync(tx, ct);   // marks this job succeeded, inside tx
        await tx.CommitAsync(ct);                               // credit and completion commit together
    }
}
```

If the process crashes before the commit, the credit and the "succeeded" mark both vanish, and the job runs again. If it crashes after the commit, both are saved and the job never runs again. Either way, the credit is applied exactly once.

### Rules for completion

<Steps>
  <Step title="Call it once, inside the attempt">

A second call in the same attempt throws `JobCompletionException` with `completion_already_staged`. A call outside an attempt, or after the handler has returned, throws `no_active_attempt`.

  </Step>
  <Step title="Roll back when ownership is lost">

If the worker no longer owns the job (its lease expired and another worker may have it), `CompleteInTransactionAsync` throws `JobOwnershipLostException`. Roll back your transaction. Your changes must not commit without the completion.

  </Step>
  <Step title="Commit before the handler returns">

When the handler returns, Runwick looks for the staged completion. If your transaction is still open, or was rolled back while the handler returned normally, the job fails permanently with `staged_completion_not_committed`. If you rolled back on purpose and want a retry, throw an exception instead of returning.

  </Step>
  <Step title="Keep the transaction short">

While your transaction holds the staged completion, it also holds a lock on the job's row, so lease renewal for that job pauses. A transaction that stays open too long can outlive the lease (60 seconds by default). On SQLite, every Runwick write on the file waits while your write transaction is open.

  </Step>
</Steps>

If the commit succeeds and something throws afterwards, the job still counts as succeeded; the exception is kept for diagnostics only. If the reply to your `COMMIT` is lost but the commit went through, Runwick finds the stored outcome and never runs the handler again.

## What this does not cover

<Callout type="warning" title="Exactly-once stops at the database boundary">

Transactional completion covers changes in that one database or file. It does not cover emails, HTTP calls, message brokers, other databases or Redis. A handler that sends an email and then completes in a transaction can still send the email twice. For those, use idempotency keys; see [Delivery guarantees](/docs/delivery-guarantees).

</Callout>

- It does not make the handler run once. A handler can still start more than once; only the committed effects are applied once.
- Staging is not available on Redis.
- A restored database is a break in history. Completions and receipts from before the restore are not guaranteed to behave as one continuous record.

For effects outside the database, a common pattern combines both tools: record "already done" in your own table in the same transaction as the completion, and pass an idempotency key to the outside service.

```csharp
// context: the IJobContext injected into the handler; sentLog: your own table of calls already made
var alreadySent = await sentLog.ExistsAsync(context.JobId, "receipt-email", connection, tx, ct);
if (!alreadySent)
{
    await email.SendAsync(job.CustomerId, idempotencyKey: $"{context.JobId}:receipt", ct);
    await sentLog.InsertAsync(context.JobId, "receipt-email", connection, tx, ct);
}
await completion.CompleteInTransactionAsync(tx, ct);
await tx.CommitAsync(ct);
```

If the process crashes between sending and committing, the next run sends again with the same key, and a provider that honours idempotency keys ignores the duplicate.

---

# Outbox

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/outbox

> Commit a job with your business data in a database that is not the job store, then let a relay deliver it at least once.

[Staging](/docs/transactions) only works when your business tables and Runwick's tables share one database. When they do not (your data is in one PostgreSQL database and the jobs in another, or the job store is Redis), no single transaction can span both. The outbox closes that gap:

1. Your transaction writes your rows and an outbox message to your own database. They commit together.
2. A relay reads committed messages and delivers each one to the Runwick store.
3. The store remembers each delivery, so a message the relay sends twice still creates one job, within a time window.

## Packages

| Package | What it adds |
|---|---|
| `Runwick.Outbox` | The relay and the shared types (`OutboxStageOptions`, `OutboxRelayOptions`, `StagedOutboxMessage`) |
| `Runwick.Outbox.Postgres` | A PostgreSQL source: `IPostgresOutbox`, `PostgresOutboxSchema`, `AddRunwickPostgresOutbox` |
| `Runwick.Outbox.Sqlite` | A same-machine SQLite source: `ISqliteOutbox`, `SqliteOutboxSchema`, `AddRunwickSqliteOutbox` |

The **source** is your business database. The **destination** is the Runwick store the host is configured with: PostgreSQL, SQLite or Redis. Redis can be a destination but not a source.

```bash
dotnet add package Runwick.Outbox.Postgres   # brings Runwick.Outbox
```

## Set it up

<Steps>
  <Step title="Install the source schema">

Run this once per source database, with a role that may create schemas. It creates a `runwick_outbox` schema (PostgreSQL) or `runwick_outbox_*` tables (SQLite) and returns the source's ID. It is safe to run again.

```csharp
using Runwick.Outbox.Postgres;

await PostgresOutboxSchema.InstallAsync(businessDbAdminConnectionString);
```

For SQLite: `await SqliteOutboxSchema.InstallAsync("Data Source=/var/lib/my-app/app.db");` (namespace `Runwick.Outbox.Sqlite`).

  </Step>
  <Step title="Register Runwick and the outbox">

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRunwick(runwick =>
{
    runwick.Application("billing")
        .UseRedis(redisConfiguration)                    // the destination store
        .AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining<SendInvoice>();
});

builder.Services.AddRunwickPostgresOutbox(
    businessDbConnectionString,                          // the source
    relay: o => o.MaxInFlight = 4);                      // optional
```

`AddRunwickPostgresOutbox` registers `IPostgresOutbox` and the relay, which runs as a hosted service. `AddRunwickSqliteOutbox` does the same for SQLite. Only one source adapter can be registered per host; a second registration throws.

  </Step>
  <Step title="Stage messages in your transaction">

```csharp
using Runwick.Outbox;
using Runwick.Outbox.Postgres;

public sealed class InvoiceService(NpgsqlDataSource businessDb, IPostgresOutbox outbox)
{
    public async Task IssueAsync(Invoice invoice, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await using var connection = await businessDb.OpenConnectionAsync(ct);
        await using var tx = await connection.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);

        await invoices.InsertAsync(invoice, connection, tx, ct);
        await outbox.StageAsync(new SendInvoice(invoice.Id), tx, new OutboxStageOptions
        {
            MessageId = invoice.MessageId,               // optional: a stable ID you keep
            Dispatch = new DispatchOptions { Priority = "high" },
        }, ct);

        await tx.CommitAsync(ct);                        // the invoice and the message commit together
    }
}
```

  </Step>
</Steps>

`StageAsync` writes inside a savepoint on your transaction. It never contacts the destination, and never commits, rolls back or retries your transaction. If it rejects the message, your transaction is left as it was. It returns a `StagedOutboxMessage` with the message ID, the proposed job ID and `AcceptUntil`, the end of the de-duplication window. Nothing is delivered until you commit.

### Staging options

| `OutboxStageOptions` | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `MessageId` | a new UUIDv7 | A stable ID of your own. Staging the same ID with the same content again returns the stored message with `Existing = true`. The same ID with different content throws `OutboxMessageConflictException`. Never reuse an ID for something else. |
| `Dispatch` | none | Ordinary `DispatchOptions`, frozen at staging time. |
| `AcceptanceHorizon` | 7 days | How long the destination accepts and de-duplicates this message. Up to 30 days, whole milliseconds. |

### Processes that only stage

A process that stages but should not deliver can turn the relay off: `relay: o => o.Enabled = false`. It still needs `AddRunwick` with the destination store, because staging checks the destination. Before the runtime has connected to the store once, staging fails with `outbox_destination_unknown`. To stage before that, set the destination store's ID: `destination: new OutboxDestination { StoreId = storeId }` (the ID that the migration returned).

## Relay options

| `OutboxRelayOptions` | Default | Allowed |
|---|---|---|
| `Enabled` | `true` | |
| `MaxInFlight` | 4 | 1 to 64 messages |
| `LeaseDuration` | 60 s | at least 5 s, and at least 3 × `RenewalInterval` |
| `RenewalInterval` | 15 s | positive |
| `ProviderCallTimeout` | 5 s | positive, shorter than `RenewalInterval` |
| `IdlePoll` | 1 s | positive. With a PostgreSQL source, the relay listens for new messages and polls every 5 s while the listener is healthy. |
| `RetryInitial` / `RetryMax` | 1 s / 60 s | exponential, `RetryMax` at least `RetryInitial` |
| `TransportLifetime` | 30 s | at most 30 s |

Bad values throw when you register the outbox. The relay opens at most two connections to the source. Several relays can serve one source: each message is leased to one relay at a time. The relay also deletes delivered rows from the source in small batches.

The relay needs a destination store that accepts outbox deliveries; all three Runwick stores do. If the store does not, the relay fails when it starts.

## The de-duplication window

Each message carries `AcceptUntil`: the time it was staged plus its acceptance horizon (7 days by default). Up to that moment, a message the relay delivers twice, after a lost reply or a crash, maps to the same job. The destination keeps that mapping until at least 24 hours after `AcceptUntil`.

After `AcceptUntil`, the destination accepts nothing new for that message. If it was delivered in time, the relay finds the mapping and marks it delivered. If not, the message is **blocked** with `horizon_passed_undelivered`, so a person can decide. Restaging the same ID returns the original cutoff, never a longer one. To try again, stage a new message ID and accept that the work could happen twice.

## Blocked messages

The relay blocks a message, rather than retrying it forever, when it cannot be delivered as written. Examples: the job type is no longer registered (`contract_not_registered`), the message was bound to another store or application (`destination_binding_mismatch`), the window passed (`horizon_passed_undelivered`), or the store rejected it.

Blocked messages are never rewritten or retried automatically. They stay in the source table with state `blocked` and a `blocked_reason` (in PostgreSQL, `runwick_outbox.outbox_messages`). Fix the cause and reset the row to pending, or accept the loss. A destination that is simply down is not a reason to block: the relay retries with backoff.

<Callout type="warning" title="What the outbox does not promise">

- **Not exactly-once.** Delivery is at-least-once with de-duplication inside the window. A delivered message means the store accepted it; the job itself is still at-least-once like any other.
- **No ordering.** Messages are not delivered in the order they were staged, even from one source.
- **No de-duplication after the window**, after the destination's mappings are cleaned up, or after the destination is restored from a backup without them.
- **No safe source restore** beyond the destination's retained window.
- **SQLite sources are same-machine only.** Every process that uses the SQLite file must run on one machine.

</Callout>

## Errors when staging

| Code | Cause |
|---|---|
| `outbox_message_conflict` | The same message ID was staged with different content or destination. |
| `outbox_destination_unknown` | No `OutboxDestination.StoreId`, and the runtime has not connected to the store yet. |
| `outbox_horizon_invalid` | The horizon is not positive, exceeds 30 days, or is not whole milliseconds. |
| `outbox_not_installed` | The source schema is missing. Run `InstallAsync`. |
| `outbox_schema_incompatible` | The source schema has another version than this package. |
| `transaction_invalid` | The transaction is completed, has no connection, or is read-only. |

None of these writes anything. A database error such as a deadlock or `SQLITE_BUSY` reaches you unchanged; retry the whole transaction.

---

# Workers

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/workers

> Run jobs with AddWorker - pools, queues, concurrency, leases, shutdown and recovery after a crash.

A worker is any process that calls `AddWorker`. It claims jobs from the store, runs your handlers and writes the results back. The same process can also dispatch, run the scheduler or serve the dashboard. A process without `AddWorker` only produces jobs and never runs a handler.

## Adding a worker

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRunwick(runwick =>
{
    runwick.Application("my-app")
        .UsePostgres(connectionString)
        .AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining<SendWelcomeEmail>();
    runwick.AddHandlersFromAssemblyContaining<SendWelcomeEmail>();

    runwick.AddWorker(w => w
        .Pool("main", p => p.Queues("default", "emails").FixedConcurrency(8))
        .Pool("reports", p => p.Queues("reports").FixedConcurrency(2)));
});
```

`AddWorker` may be called once per application. A worker needs at least one pool, and pool names must be unique. Startup fails with a clear configuration error if any of these rules is broken.

## Pools

A pool is a group of slots (tickets) that share a set of queues. A job needs a free ticket before the worker claims it, and the ticket comes back only when the job has finished *and* its result is stored. That is what keeps memory bounded when the store is slow or away.

Use more than one pool when some work must not starve other work. In the example above, a flood of reports can never take the slots that emails need.

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Queues("a", "b")` | Subscribes to queues, each with weight 1 |
| `Queue("a", weight)` | Subscribes to one queue with a weight from 1 to 1,000. Higher weight means a larger share of claims |
| `FixedConcurrency(n)` | A fixed number of tickets. This is the default, with 4 |
| `AutoConcurrency(min, max)` | Lets the pool grow and shrink between `min` and `max` |
| `LaneSelection(mode)` | `Weighted` (default), `StrictWithAging` or `Strict` |
| `LaneWeights(high, medium, low)` | Shares of the priority lanes. Default 6 : 3 : 1 |

Rules checked at startup:

- Every queue a pool names must be used by a registered job or declared with `runwick.Queue("name")`.
- A pool subscribes to at least one queue, and to each queue only once.
- A pool is either fixed or automatic, never both.
- The sum of every pool's maximum must not exceed `MaxOutstandingAttempts`, which is 16 by default.

```csharp
runwick.Queue("imports");   // a queue no job type names by default

runwick.AddWorker(w => w
    .MaxOutstandingAttempts(32)
    .Pool("main", p => p.Queue("default", 3).Queue("imports", 1).FixedConcurrency(24))
    .Pool("slow", p => p.Queues("reports").FixedConcurrency(8)));
```

How priorities and lanes interact is explained in [Queues and priorities](/docs/queues-and-priorities).

### Automatic concurrency

`AutoConcurrency(min, max)` adjusts the pool's ticket count from how busy the tickets are and from the pool's share of waiting work. It moves carefully: it needs several samples in a row before it grows or shrinks, waits between changes, and never changes by more than a quarter at a time. It stops growing when the store looks unhealthy. Shrinking never cancels running work; it only stops refilling slots.

<Callout type="info" title="One process, not the cluster">

The automatic controller scales the slots of this process only. It does not start containers or coordinate with other replicas. To scale out, export the metrics (see [Observability](/docs/observability)) and let your platform add instances.

</Callout>

## Leases

When a worker claims a job it gets a **lease**: ownership with an expiry time decided by the store's clock. The worker renews the lease in the background while the handler runs. Every write the worker makes carries a token from the claim, so a worker that lost its lease cannot overwrite the result of whoever took over.

| `WorkerOptions` | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LeaseDuration` | 60 s | Length of each lease |
| `LeaseSafetyMargin` | 10 s | The worker stops trusting a lease this long before the store would expire it |
| `RenewalInterval` / `RenewalJitter` | 15 s / 3 s | Renewal runs every 12 to 18 s |
| `MinimumInvocationMargin` | 15 s | A handler does not start unless at least this much lease time is left |
| `ControlRequestTimeout` | 5 s | Longest wait for one store call on the ownership path |
| `CancellationGrace` | 10 s | Time a cancelled handler gets to return |
| `CleanupBudget` | 10 s | Time allowed for disposing the job's DI scope |

Change them with `Configure`:

```csharp
runwick.AddWorker(w => w
    .Pool("main", p => p.Queues("default"))
    .Configure(o =>
    {
        o.LeaseDuration = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(90);
        o.RenewalInterval = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(20);
    }));
```

The timings depend on each other. Runwick checks the rules at startup and refuses a configuration that breaks them; it never quietly adjusts a value. The full list is in [Configuration](/docs/configuration).

If a renewal is not confirmed in time, the worker treats the lease as lost for good. It cancels the handler's `CancellationToken`, stops renewing, and never writes a result for that attempt, even if a late reply arrives.

<Callout type="warning" title="A lost lease does not stop your code">

.NET has no safe way to kill a running method. A handler that ignores its token keeps running while another worker may already run the same job. Handlers must be safe to run more than once. See [Delivery guarantees](/docs/delivery-guarantees).

</Callout>

## Shutdown

When the host stops, the worker shuts down in steps, measured from the moment the stop began:

<Steps>
<Step title="Stop claiming">

No new jobs are claimed. This happens at once.

</Step>
<Step title="Drain (up to 15 s)">

Running handlers keep going. Their leases are still renewed and their results are still written.

</Step>
<Step title="Cancel (15 s to 20 s)">

Every handler still running has its `CancellationToken` cancelled and gets a few seconds to return.

</Step>
<Step title="Finish (20 s to 25 s)">

Known results are written. At 25 s the worker stops talking to the store. Anything still open is left to lease expiry and recovery by another worker.

</Step>
</Steps>

| `WorkerOptions` | Default |
|---|---|
| `ShutdownDrain` | 15 s |
| `ShutdownCancellation` | 5 s |
| `ShutdownFinalization` | 5 s |
| `ShutdownBudget` | 25 s (the three slices must fit inside it) |

The .NET host gives hosted services 30 seconds to stop by default. Keep it above Runwick's 25 seconds, and keep your container platform's grace period above the host's:

```csharp
builder.Services.Configure<HostOptions>(o => o.ShutdownTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(35));
```

If the host kills the process early, nothing is corrupted, but jobs still running wait for their leases to expire before another worker picks them up.

## When a worker crashes

Every worker runs a recovery loop, by default every 5 seconds (give or take 1 second, `RecoveryScanInterval` and `RecoveryScanJitter`). It finds jobs whose lease has expired and puts them back:

- **The handler had started.** The attempt is closed as abandoned. The job retries if it has executions left, and otherwise fails. If someone asked to cancel it meanwhile, it ends as cancelled.
- **The handler had not started yet.** The worker claimed the job but died before running it. This does not use up one of the job's executions. It is counted separately (5 times in a row by default, with short delays from 1 s to 30 s), so a job that crashes every worker before it starts still stops eventually.

There is one small gap: the store records "this execution started" just before calling your handler. A crash in that instant still costs an execution.

## Resource usage per attempt

`WorkerOptions.RecordResourceUsage` is on by default. The worker records CPU time, allocated bytes and working set for each attempt and stores them with it, so the [dashboard](/docs/dashboard) can show them. The measured cost is a few microseconds per attempt. Set it to `false` to turn it off.

## Other work a worker does

- It publishes a heartbeat ("worker X is alive, listening to these queues"), which the dashboard and `runwick workers list` show.
- It runs the cleanup loop for old records. See [Retention](/docs/retention).
- It reports a `worker` readiness check. See [Health checks](/docs/health-checks).

---

# Management API

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/management-api

> The authenticated HTTP API behind the dashboard and the CLI - sign-in, permissions, antiforgery, limits and audit.

`Runwick.AspNetCore` adds an HTTP API for reading and controlling jobs, queues, schedules, capacity and retention. The [dashboard](/docs/dashboard) and the [CLI](/docs/cli) both go through the same checks, so they share one set of permissions and one audit trail.

```bash
dotnet add package Runwick.AspNetCore
```

## Setting it up

```csharp
builder.Services.AddAuthentication(CookieAuthenticationDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddCookie();

builder.Services.AddRunwickManagement(m => m
    .AuthenticationSchemes(CookieAuthenticationDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)   // required
    .MapGrants(principal => ManagementRoles.Operator));                         // required

var app = builder.Build();
app.MapRunwickManagement("/runwick/api");   // routes under /runwick/api/v1/...
```

Both `AuthenticationSchemes` and `MapGrants` are required. `MapRunwickManagement` throws at startup when either is missing, or when a named scheme is not registered. There is no anonymous mode and no "localhost only" mode.

You bring the sign-in: cookies, OpenID Connect, JWT bearer or anything else ASP.NET Core supports. Runwick does not change your default scheme. It tries the listed schemes in order and never sends a redirect challenge.

## Permissions

`MapGrants` turns the signed-in user into a list of `ManagementGrant` values. It runs on every request. Grants never come from the request body or headers.

| Permission | Allows |
|---|---|
| `Jobs.Read` | Listing and reading jobs (no payloads) |
| `Jobs.ReadPayload` | Revealing a job's payload (audited) |
| `Jobs.ReadError` | Revealing an attempt's error detail (audited) |
| `Jobs.Cancel`, `Jobs.Retry`, `Jobs.Rerun` | Job controls |
| `Jobs.Dispatch` | Creating a job from the API or CLI (audited) |
| `Queues.Read`, `Queues.Control` | Listing queues, pausing and resuming them |
| `Schedules.Read`, `Schedules.Trigger`, `Schedules.Control`, `Schedules.Edit` | Reading, triggering, pausing and resuming, revalidating schedules |
| `Capacity.Read`, `Capacity.Edit` | Workers and concurrency scopes |
| `Settings.Read` | The host's settings page |
| `Retention.Manage` | Editing the retention policy |
| `Audit.Read` | Reading the audit trail |

The names are constants on `ManagementPermissions`. Three presets cover the usual cases:

| Preset | Contains |
|---|---|
| `ManagementRoles.Viewer` | `Jobs.Read`, `Queues.Read`, `Schedules.Read`, `Capacity.Read`, `Settings.Read` |
| `ManagementRoles.Operator` | Viewer, plus cancel, retry, rerun, queue control, schedule trigger and control |
| `ManagementRoles.Administrator` | Operator, plus `Schedules.Edit`, `Capacity.Edit`, `Retention.Manage` |

Payload, error and audit reads and `Jobs.Dispatch` are in no preset. Add them on purpose:

```csharp
IReadOnlyList<ManagementGrant> GrantsFor(ClaimsPrincipal user) =>
    user.IsInRole("ops-admin")
        ? [.. ManagementRoles.Administrator,
           new(ManagementPermissions.JobsReadPayload),
           new(ManagementPermissions.JobsReadError),
           new(ManagementPermissions.AuditRead)]
    : user.IsInRole("ops") ? ManagementRoles.Operator
    : user.IsInRole("support") ? ManagementRoles.Viewer
    : [];

builder.Services.AddRunwickManagement(m => m
    .AuthenticationSchemes("Cookies")
    .MapGrants(GrantsFor));
```

### Scoping to queues

`Jobs.*` and `Queues.*` grants can be limited to some queues:

```csharp
new ManagementGrant(ManagementPermissions.JobsRead, new HashSet<string> { "billing" })
```

Jobs outside the caller's queues answer `404`, exactly like jobs that do not exist, so hidden IDs are never confirmed. Lists are filtered before paging. Schedule, capacity, settings, retention and audit permissions are application-wide; giving them a queue list throws when the grant is built, so a mistake never widens access.

## Antiforgery

Every `POST` from a browser or a Basic client needs an antiforgery token. Fetch it with `GET {prefix}/v1/antiforgery`, then send it in the `X-Runwick-Antiforgery` header:

```bash
curl -c jar -b jar https://ops.example.com/runwick/api/v1/antiforgery
# {"token":"CfDJ8...","headerName":"X-Runwick-Antiforgery"}
```

The CLI does this for you.

## Machine clients

A service that calls the API with a bearer token has no cookie, so antiforgery adds nothing. Map the API for machine clients:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRunwickManagement(m => m
    .AuthenticationSchemes(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .MapGrants(p => p.HasClaim("scope", "runwick.ops") ? ManagementRoles.Operator : []));

app.MapRunwickManagement("/runwick/api").ForMachineClients();
```

`ForMachineClients()` refuses cookie and Basic schemes. If any configured scheme is one of those, it throws at startup. Runwick ships no bearer handler; use your own.

## Basic authentication

For small setups, `AddRunwickBasic` adds a Basic scheme. You must supply the password check; there are no default credentials.

```csharp
builder.Services.AddAuthentication()
    .AddRunwickBasic(o => o.Verifier = (user, password, ct) =>
        ValueTask.FromResult(user == "ops" && CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals(
            Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(password),
            Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(builder.Configuration["Ops:Password"]!))));

builder.Services.AddRunwickManagement(m => m
    .AuthenticationSchemes(RunwickBasicDefaults.Scheme)   // "Basic"
    .MapGrants(p => ManagementRoles.Operator));
```

- Requests over plain HTTP are refused.
- After 10 failures a minute for one source address and user name, further tries are refused without checking.
- Basic counts as a browser scheme, so `POST` requests still need the antiforgery token.

## Revisions and command IDs

Every control carries the revision the caller last saw, for example "cancel job 42 at generation 1, revision 7". If the target changed in between, the answer is a `409` conflict (`stale_revision` or `stale_generation`), not a surprise.

Every control also carries a `commandId`. If a reply is lost, send the same request with the same command ID: the store returns the original result with `replayed: true`, with no second change and no second audit row.

## Limits

Limits are per process and per signed-in caller. Change them with `Configure`:

| `ManagementOptions` | Default |
|---|---|
| `ReadsPerMinute` | 120 |
| `MutationsPerMinute` | 30 |
| `RevealsPerMinute` | 10 |
| `MaxActiveRequests` | 16 |
| `MaxWaitingRequests` / `MaxWait` | 32 / 1 s |

Over a per-caller limit the answer is `429` with `Retry-After`. When the process is full it is `503 busy`. With several replicas, each replica counts on its own.

List cursors are protected with ASP.NET Core Data Protection. Replicas that share a key ring accept each other's cursors. Set `CursorKey` (32 bytes or more) if they do not.

## Audit

Every successful change writes an audit row in the same transaction as the change: who, what, when, the command ID and the reason you passed. Revealing a payload or an error is audited too, and the data is returned only after the audit row is committed. Read the trail with `Audit.Read`, in the dashboard's Audit page or with `runwick audit list`.

By default the actor is the user's `NameIdentifier` claim (or `Name`), their name, and the scheme used. Override it with `.Actor(principal => new ManagementActor(subject, display, scheme))`.

Denied requests are not audited. Failed sign-ins are logged (event 1401) with a coarse hash of the source, never the address or user name.

## A standalone management host

The API does not need workers. A small internal web app can serve only the API and the dashboard:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRunwick(r => r
    .Application("billing")
    .UsePostgres(connectionString)
    .AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining<SendInvoice>());   // needed only for dispatch from the API
// no AddWorker, no AddScheduler

builder.Services.AddAuthentication().AddRunwickBasic(o => o.Verifier = VerifyAsync);
builder.Services.AddRunwickManagement(m => m
    .AuthenticationSchemes(RunwickBasicDefaults.Scheme)
    .MapGrants(p => ManagementRoles.Operator));
builder.Services.AddRunwickDashboard("default", _ => { });

var app = builder.Build();
app.MapRunwickManagement("/runwick/api");
app.MapRunwickDashboard("/runwick");
app.Run();
```

This process runs no worker and writes no worker heartbeat. It is also a good place to collect application-wide metrics; see [Observability](/docs/observability).

---

# Dashboard

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/dashboard

> A web UI for jobs, queues, workers and schedules, served from inside your ASP.NET Core app.

`Runwick.Dashboard` is a web UI that runs inside your own ASP.NET Core app. It reads and acts through the same layer as the [management API](/docs/management-api), so it has the same permissions, limits and audit trail. Its web files are embedded in the package; you do not need Node or npm.

![Job details](/images/dashboard-job.png)

```bash
dotnet add package Runwick.Dashboard
```

## Setting it up

The dashboard needs `AddRunwickManagement`, because it uses its sign-in schemes and grant mapping by default.

