```csharp
builder.Services.AddAuthentication(CookieAuthenticationDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddCookie(o => o.LoginPath = "/login");

builder.Services.AddRunwickManagement(m => m
    .AuthenticationSchemes(CookieAuthenticationDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .MapGrants(GrantsFor));

builder.Services.AddRunwickDashboard("default", d =>
{
    d.Title = "Billing jobs";             // default "Runwick"
    d.SignOutPath = "/account/logout";    // optional: shows a Sign out button
});

var app = builder.Build();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.MapRunwickDashboard("/runwick");
```

`AddRunwickDashboard` takes a mount ID (1 to 32 characters of `a-z`, `0-9` and `-`). You can register several mounts with different IDs and map each at its own path. `MapRunwickDashboard(path, mountId)` uses `"default"` when you leave out the ID.

You do not have to call `MapRunwickManagement` for the dashboard to work. Map it only if you also want the JSON API or the CLI.

### Options

| `DashboardOptions` | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Title` | `"Runwick"` | Page title |
| `SignOutPath` | `null` | Your own sign-out route, as a path on the same site, including any path base. The button posts an empty form to it. `null` hides the button |
| `AuthenticationSchemes(...)` | The management schemes | Schemes this mount accepts |
| `MapGrants(...)` | The management grant map | Grants on this mount |
| `Actor(...)` | The management actor map | The actor written to audit |

Per-mount schemes are useful when the JSON API uses bearer tokens for machine clients and the dashboard uses cookies for people.

## Order with your own Inertia app

The dashboard is built on Inertia.Net. If your app also uses Inertia, map the dashboard **before** your own `UseInertia()`:

```csharp
app.UsePathBase("/ops");
app.UseAuthentication();
app.MapRunwickDashboard("/runwick");   // first
app.UseInertia();                      // your app's Inertia
```

Otherwise your app's Inertia middleware version-checks the dashboard's requests and sends its pages into a reload loop. Runwick cannot detect the wrong order, so this is on you.

<Callout type="warning" title="Do not put your own routes under the dashboard path">

The dashboard owns everything under its path. If one of your endpoints has a route under it, Runwick logs a critical error and stops the application once it has started. Until that check has run, the dashboard answers `503`.

</Callout>

## Permissions

Each page needs the permission behind the data it shows, and each button needs the permission for its action. The navigation lists only the pages the caller may open; other pages answer `403`.

| Page | Needs |
|---|---|
| Overview, Jobs, Runs, Run | `Jobs.Read` |
| Queues, Queue | `Queues.Read` (pause and resume: `Queues.Control`) |
| Workers, Pools, Scaling | `Capacity.Read` (set capacity: `Capacity.Edit`) |
| Schedules, Schedule | `Schedules.Read` |
| Settings | `Settings.Read` |
| Retention | `Settings.Read` (edit: `Retention.Manage`) |
| Audit | `Audit.Read` |

A payload or an error detail is hidden until someone with `Jobs.ReadPayload` or `Jobs.ReadError` clicks reveal, and every reveal writes an audit row. Errors show only their code until revealed.

Hiding a button is a convenience, not security: the server checks every request again.

## What you see

- **Overview:** key figures with small trend lines, recent failures, queues and recent scaling events.
- **Jobs and Runs:** each job type with its numbers, then the individual runs with filters by queue, state, name and time range. Cancel, retry and rerun from the list or the run page.
- **Run:** a job's status history, its attempts and the resources each attempt used.
- **Queues, Workers, Pools, Schedules:** each with a detail page. Pause and resume queues and schedules, trigger a schedule, set a concurrency limit.
- **Retention and Audit:** the cleanup policy with its progress, and the trail of who did what.

Lists show 50 rows a page with a "Next" link. There are no page counts or grand totals. Each list says when it was read ("as of 12:04:31").

## What it is not

<Callout type="info" title="Know these limits">

- **Not live.** Pages poll every few seconds while the tab is visible (5 s at the fastest, and you can pick a slower interval or turn it off). There is no push channel.
- **No queue-depth totals of its own.** Figures on the Overview are tallies of what one read returned, shown as "50+" when there is more.
- **"Cancel requested" is not "stopped".** Cancellation is cooperative; a running handler stops only when it honours its token. See [Cancellation](/docs/cancellation).
- **A revealed payload cannot be taken back** from a browser that has seen it.
- **Permissions are per application and queue,** not per tenant.
- **Rate limits are per process.** Several replicas each allow the full rate.

</Callout>

## Running it on its own

The dashboard does not need a worker in the same process. A small internal app with only `AddRunwick`, `AddRunwickManagement` and `AddRunwickDashboard` is a common shape. See [A standalone management host](/docs/management-api#a-standalone-management-host).

The repository's `samples/Runwick.Dashboard.Host` shows a complete host: cookie sign-in, three users with different grants, a path base, and the dashboard mounted before the host's own Inertia pages.

---

# Command line

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/cli

> The runwick CLI - contexts, job and queue controls, store administration, and stable output for scripts and agents.

`runwick` is a command-line tool with two halves:

- **Management commands** (`jobs`, `queues`, `schedules`, `events`, ...) talk to a [management API](/docs/management-api) over HTTPS, with your permissions, and are audited like any other caller.
- **Store commands** (`migrate`, `store ...`, and `doctor` with a connection) talk straight to the database, as the migration role.

## Install

```bash
dotnet tool install --global Runwick.Cli
runwick version
```

Self-contained single-file binaries also exist for Linux x64 and Windows x64.

<Callout type="warning" title="Match the CLI to your release">

`migrate` applies the migrations built into the CLI. Use the CLI from the same Runwick release as your application. `runwick doctor` tells you when the CLI and the store disagree.

</Callout>

## Contexts and sign-in

A context saves a server URL, a sign-in method, a user name and the **name** of an environment variable that holds the secret:

```bash
runwick context add prod --url https://ops.example.com/runwick/api \
  --auth basic --user ops --secret-env RUNWICK_PROD_SECRET
runwick context use prod
runwick login        # checks the credentials; stores nothing
```

- `--url` is the prefix you passed to `MapRunwickManagement`. It must be `https://`, or `http://` to a loopback address.
- `--auth basic` sends a user and password; mutations fetch an antiforgery token automatically.
- `--auth bearer` sends `Authorization: Bearer`. The server must map that API group with `.ForMachineClients()`.
- Secrets are never written to the config file. The CLI looks for one in this order: `--secret-stdin`, the context's variable, `RUNWICK_SECRET`, then a hidden prompt (only in human mode at a terminal).

The config file is `$RUNWICK_CONFIG`, or `runwick/config.json` in your application-data folder (`~/.config/runwick/config.json` on Linux). Use `--context NAME` or `--url URL` to override the current context for one command. Other commands: `context list`, `context show`, `context remove`.

## Jobs

```bash
runwick jobs list --state failed --queue billing --limit 20
runwick jobs get 0193c3a1-...
runwick jobs tail 0193c3a1-...                 # follow one job until it ends
runwick jobs cancel 0193c3a1-... --expected-generation 1 --expected-revision 7 --reason "duplicate import"
runwick jobs retry  0193c3a1-...
runwick jobs rerun  0193c3a1-...
runwick jobs cancel-many --file stuck.jsonl    # up to 100 lines of {jobId, expectedGeneration, expectedRevision}
runwick jobs reveal-payload 0193c3a1-... --reason "ticket 4411"   # audited
runwick jobs reveal-error <attempt-id>                            # audited
```

`jobs list` and `jobs get` never show payloads. Only the two reveal commands do, and the server writes an audit row for each.

To create a job of a registered type from a JSON payload (needs `Jobs.Dispatch`):

```bash
runwick dispatch email.welcome --payload @payload.json --queue emails --reason "resend after outage"
echo '{"userId":"..."}' | runwick dispatch email.welcome --payload -
```

`--payload` takes `@file` or `-` for standard input. A payload is never accepted inline.

## Queues, schedules and capacity

```bash
runwick queues list
runwick queues pause default --expected-revision 3
runwick queues resume default

runwick schedules list
runwick schedules pause nightly-report
runwick schedules resume nightly-report --policy runOnce   # skipPaused (default), runOnce or catchUp
runwick schedules trigger nightly-report
runwick schedules revalidate nightly-report

runwick workers list --include-expired
runwick capacity list --kind queue
runwick capacity set queue imports 4
```

## Events, audit and settings

```bash
runwick events tail --follow             # job events, polled every 2 s
runwick events tail --after 9182.3       # resume from a cursor
runwick audit list --target-kind job --from 2026-11-01T00:00:00Z
runwick settings
```

## Expected revisions

Every change says which version of the target you were looking at. If someone else changed it in the meantime, you get `stale_revision` (or `stale_generation`) and nothing happens. Two people acting on the same stale view cannot overwrite each other.

In human and JSON mode you may leave out `--expected-revision` and `--expected-generation`. The CLI then reads the target first, uses what it read, and says which revision it used. In `--agent` mode they are required.

Every change also has a command ID (`--command-id`, generated when you leave it out). If the reply is lost, the CLI resends the same request with the same ID up to 3 times in 30 seconds. The server answers a resend with the original result, so nothing happens twice. If no answer arrives, the result is `outcome_unknown` with the command ID; run the same command again with that `--command-id`.

## Store commands

These run as the migration role. The connection string comes from an environment variable (`--connection-env`) or standard input (`--connection-stdin`). It is never accepted as an argument.

```bash
runwick migrate --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_STORE
runwick store status --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_STORE
runwick store admission --mode drain --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_STORE
runwick store activate-capability --name scheduler --application my-app \
  --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_STORE
runwick store reidentify --confirm --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_STORE
```

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `migrate` | Applies this CLI's migrations. Safe to run again |
| `store status` | Store ID and revision, the revision this CLI expects, each application's admission mode, and counts of leases and worker heartbeats |
| `store admission --mode` (`open`, `drain`, `maintenance`) | Drain stops new work and lets running work finish. Maintenance stops everything but status reads. Add `--application` for one application |
| `store activate-capability --name` (`scheduler`, `rate_admission`) | Turns on a capability for an application. It cannot be undone |
| `store reidentify --confirm` | Gives a restored copy a new identity. Offline only |

`--provider` is `postgres` (default for `store` and `doctor`), `sqlite` or `redis`. `migrate` requires it. How these fit together is in [Upgrades](/docs/upgrades).

## doctor

```bash
runwick doctor
runwick doctor --connection-env RUNWICK_STORE
```

Checks that the server is reachable, the credentials work, the API version matches and the clocks agree within 5 seconds. With a connection it also checks the store: its revision against the CLI's, and the store's durability settings. A check it could not run is reported as `unverified`, never as passed.

## Output for scripts and agents

| Flag | Output |
|---|---|
| (none) | Tables and `key: value` lines for people. Errors go to stderr |
| `--output json` | The API's JSON body on stdout. Errors are JSON on stdout too, with a non-zero exit code |
| `--agent` | Exactly one JSON envelope per command on one line: `ok`, `result`, `error` (with `code`, `retryable` and `hint`), `commandId`, the revisions it saw, and suggested `nextActions` |

`runwick --agent describe` prints every command with its arguments, options, required permission, error codes and exit codes. See [AI agents](/docs/ai-agents) for how to use it.

Exit codes:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | OK |
| 1 | Rejected (conflict, invalid state, not found) |
| 2 | Usage error |
| 3 | Outcome unknown; resend with the same command ID |
| 4 | Unavailable; retry |
| 5 | Not signed in or not allowed |

The CLI never prints secrets, cookies, tokens or connection strings, even with `--verbose`.

---

# Observability

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/observability

> Traces, metrics and logs from Runwick, how to export them with OpenTelemetry, and how to read the numbers.

Runwick uses the standard .NET tools and exports nothing unless you ask:

- **Traces:** one `ActivitySource` named `Runwick`.
- **Metrics:** one `Meter` named `Runwick`, with fixed names, units and attributes.
- **Logs:** `ILogger`, with fixed event IDs.

Payloads, credentials, connection strings and exception messages stay out by default. Job IDs may appear in spans and logs, never in metrics.

## Turning it on with OpenTelemetry

```bash
dotnet add package Runwick.OpenTelemetry
dotnet add package OpenTelemetry.Extensions.Hosting
dotnet add package OpenTelemetry.Exporter.OpenTelemetryProtocol
```

```csharp
using OpenTelemetry.Metrics;
using OpenTelemetry.Trace;

builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry()
    .WithTracing(t => t.AddRunwickInstrumentation().AddOtlpExporter())
    .WithMetrics(m => m.AddRunwickInstrumentation().AddOtlpExporter());
```

`Runwick.OpenTelemetry` adds no exporter; use the one you already have. On the metrics side it keeps only Runwick's own attributes and sets a cardinality limit per instrument.

Without OpenTelemetry, any listener works: subscribe to the `Runwick` source and meter by name (the constant is `RunwickTelemetry.SourceName`).

## Options

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRunwick(r => r
    .Application("my-app")
    .UsePostgres(connectionString)
    .Telemetry(t =>
    {
        t.CollectApplicationMetrics = true;    // this process samples queue depth for the whole application
        t.ApplicationSamplePeriod = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(15);
    }));
```

| `RunwickTelemetryOptions` | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `RecordExceptionDetails` | `false` | Put a cleaned, size-limited exception message on spans and on log event 1011 |
| `MaxSeriesPerInstrument` | 1,000 | Attribute combinations per instrument before measurements go to an overflow series (100 to 10,000) |
| `CollectApplicationMetrics` | `false` | Make this process the application-wide collector |
| `ApplicationSamplePeriod` | 15 s | How often the collector samples (5 s to 5 min) |
| `CollectorName` | `"default"` | Value of the `runwick.collector` attribute |

If you raise `MaxSeriesPerInstrument`, pass the same number to `AddRunwickInstrumentation(o => ...)` so the SDK limit matches.

## Traces

| Span | When |
|---|---|
| `send {queue}` | A dispatch, from prepare to confirmed reply |
| `stage {queue}` | Staging a job inside your own transaction |
| `process {queue}` | One attempt, from claim to stored result. Each attempt starts a new trace, linked to the dispatch |
| `runwick.begin`, `runwick.execute`, `runwick.attempt.cleanup`, `settle {queue}` | Steps inside `process`. Your handler's spans are children of `runwick.execute` |
| `runwick.recover` | Recovery of one expired lease |
| `runwick.schedule.materialize` | The scheduler creating jobs |
| `runwick.management.command` | A management change |
| `runwick.retention.batch` | One cleanup batch |

Lease renewals are not spans; they repeat too often. They show up in metrics.

## Metrics

Durations are in seconds unless noted.

| Metric | Type | What it counts |
|---|---|---|
| `runwick.dispatch.operations` | Counter | Dispatches by result, kind and queue |
| `runwick.dispatch.duration` | Histogram | Dispatch time |
| `runwick.execution.authorized` | Counter | Executions that started, by queue, job name and pool |
| `runwick.execution.duration` | Histogram | Handler time, by queue, job name and outcome |
| `runwick.execution.start_delay` | Histogram | Time from due to start, by queue |
| `runwick.admission.deferred` | Counter | Starts held back (for example by a rate limit), by reason |
| `runwick.attempt.cleanup.duration` | Histogram | Time to dispose the job's DI scope |
| `runwick.settlement.duration` | Histogram | Time to store a result, by settlement result |
| `runwick.storage.operation.duration` | Histogram | Store calls, by operation, result and I/O class |
| `runwick.lease.renewals` | Counter | Lease renewals by result |
| `runwick.lease.margin` | Histogram | Lease time left at renewal, by pool |
| `runwick.lease.authority_lost` | Counter | Attempts that lost their lease, by reason |
| `runwick.recoveries` | Counter | Expired leases recovered |
| `runwick.scaling.decisions` | Counter | Automatic concurrency changes, by pool, direction and reason |
| `runwick.schedule.materialization.delay` | Histogram | How late scheduled jobs were created |
| `runwick.schedule.occurrences` | Counter | Schedule occurrences by disposition |
| `runwick.management.requests` | Counter | Management requests by operation and result |
| `runwick.management.duration` | Histogram | Management request time |
| `runwick.retention.rows` | Counter | Rows deleted by cleanup, by record class |
| `runwick.retention.batches` | Counter | Cleanup batches by class and result |
| `runwick.retention.batch.duration` | Histogram | Cleanup batch time |
| `runwick.telemetry.dropped` | Counter | Log records dropped by Runwick's own limits |
| `runwick.telemetry.overflow` | Counter | Measurements sent to the overflow series |
| `runwick.worker.tickets` | Gauge | Tickets by pool and phase |
| `runwick.worker.target` | Gauge | Target ticket count by pool |
| `runwick.worker.oldest_unsettled.age` | Gauge | Oldest result not yet confirmed by the store, by pool |
| `runwick.worker.admission` | Gauge | Whether a pool is claiming work |
| `runwick.retention.caught_up.age` | Gauge | Time since cleanup last caught up, by class |
| `runwick.queue.due` | Gauge, collector only | Jobs waiting and due, by queue |
| `runwick.queue.oldest_due.age` | Gauge, collector only | Age of the oldest due job, by queue |
| `runwick.schedule.needs_review` | Gauge, collector only | Schedules that need review |
| `runwick.schedule.oldest_overdue.age` | Gauge, collector only | Most overdue schedule |
| `runwick.collector.snapshot.age` | Gauge, collector only | Age of the collector's last sample |

In Prometheus the names become `runwick_queue_due`, `runwick_execution_duration_seconds_bucket` and so on.

## Logs

Categories are `Runwick.Worker`, `Runwick.Dispatch`, `Runwick.Scheduler`, `Runwick.Outbox`, `Runwick.Management`, `Runwick.Retention`, `Runwick.Store` and `Runwick.Telemetry`. Every message has a fixed event ID, for example:

| ID | Event |
|---|---|
| 1003 | A running attempt lost its lease |
| 1004 | A result could not be confirmed |
| 1011 | A handler failed |
| 1101 | A dispatch outcome is unknown |
| 1202 | A schedule needs review |
| 1401 | A management sign-in failed |
| 1501 | A cleanup batch failed |
| 1701 | A role cannot reach the store |
| 1703 | The store schema does not match this binary |

Warnings are limited to 10 a minute per event ID per process. The rest are counted and summarised once a minute (event 1603).

## Reading the numbers honestly

- **Local and application-wide numbers are different.** Worker gauges describe one process and can be summed across processes. Queue depth and the oldest due job come only from processes with `CollectApplicationMetrics = true`. Usually that is one process, for example the [standalone management host](/docs/management-api#a-standalone-management-host).
- **Never sum collector series.** Runwick does not elect a collector. If two processes collect, both report the same queue. Use `max by (runwick_queue)`; the shipped dashboard and alerts do.
- **Missing is not zero.** When a collector's sample is older than three periods, its queue gauges disappear instead of reporting 0, and `runwick.collector.snapshot.age` keeps growing.
- **"Due" is not "runnable".** A due job may still wait for a concurrency slot, a rate limit, a paused queue or a worker that can run it.
- **A handler that succeeded is not a stored success.** If the result could not be confirmed, the span says `runwick.outcome = succeeded` with `runwick.settlement.result = unresolved`. A replayed command is not counted twice.
- **Counts can be lost** when a process crashes. Use them for operations, not for billing or audit.

## Grafana dashboard and Prometheus alerts

`Runwick.OpenTelemetry` ships two files in its package `content` folder (they are also in the repository's `ops` folder):

- `content/grafana/runwick-overview.json`: a Grafana dashboard with dispatch, execution, leases, pools, queues, schedules, management, retention and telemetry-health panels.
- `content/prometheus/runwick-alerts.yml`: alert rules.

| Alert | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `RunwickLeaseMarginLow` | The 5th percentile lease margin of a pool stays below 25 s |
| `RunwickAuthorityLost` | Any attempt lost its lease in the last 10 minutes |
| `RunwickSettlementOld` | A result has been unconfirmed for over 60 s |
| `RunwickDueAgeRising` | A queue's oldest due job has waited over 10 minutes |
| `RunwickFailuresRepeated` | More than 10% of a job type's executions do not succeed |
| `RunwickScheduleLag` | A schedule is over 2 minutes late or needs review |
| `RunwickRetentionFailing` | Cleanup fails repeatedly or has not caught up for 24 hours |
| `RunwickCollectorStale` | No fresh collector sample, or no collector at all |
| `RunwickStoreIncompatible` | Reads `runwick_host_readiness_incompatible`, a gauge **your host must export** from its health checks. Runwick does not emit it |

<Callout type="warning" title="Thresholds are starting points">

The thresholds are not tuned for your workload. Adjust them, especially the due-age and failure-rate rules.

</Callout>

The telemetry follows the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions version pinned in `RunwickTelemetry.SemanticConventionsVersion`, and no other.

---

# Health checks

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/health-checks

> Liveness and per-role readiness checks for ASP.NET Core, and how to map them for your orchestrator.

`Runwick.AspNetCore` plugs Runwick's health into the standard ASP.NET Core health checks. No extra package is needed beyond that.

## Adding the checks

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRunwick(r => { /* ... */ });
builder.Services.AddRunwickManagement(m => { /* ... */ });   // if this host serves management

builder.Services.AddHealthChecks().AddRunwick();
```

Call `AddRunwick()` on the health-check builder **after** `AddRunwick` (and after `AddRunwickManagement`, if you use it). It looks at what the host has registered and adds:

| Check | Tag | Added when |
|---|---|---|
| `runwick-live` | `live` | Always |
| `runwick-producer` | `ready` | Always |
| `runwick-worker` | `ready` | The host calls `AddWorker` |
| `runwick-scheduler` | `ready` | The host calls `AddScheduler` |
| `runwick-management` | `ready` | The host calls `AddRunwickManagement` |

## Mapping the endpoints

Use the tags to split liveness from readiness:

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics.HealthChecks;

app.MapHealthChecks("/health/live", new HealthCheckOptions
{
    Predicate = check => check.Tags.Contains("live"),
});

app.MapHealthChecks("/health/ready", new HealthCheckOptions
{
    Predicate = check => check.Tags.Contains("ready"),
});
```

Then point your orchestrator at them. For Kubernetes:

```yaml
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
```

## What each check means

| Check | Healthy | Degraded | Unhealthy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Live | The worker's internal timer keeps ticking | | The timer stalled. A store outage alone never makes liveness fail |
| Producer | The startup compatibility check passed and the last store call worked | The last call failed less than 30 s ago | Incompatible schema, or failing for 30 s or more |
| Worker | Claiming and finishing work normally | Partly impaired | Draining, store outage, every pool stopped under pressure, or incompatible store |
| Scheduler | Compatible and recently wrote its progress | A recent write failed | Incompatible, or writes keep failing |
| Management | Configuration valid and the periodic store read works | A read failed less than 30 s ago | Failing for 30 s or more |

A few details worth knowing:

- **Checks never wait on the store.** They return cached state. Background refreshers update it every 10 seconds with a 1 second budget. A health request never claims a job.
- **Stale is not healthy.** If a refresher has not succeeded for three periods, the check reports Degraded with reason `stale`.
- **Draining makes a worker not ready, but still alive.** That is what you want during an [upgrade](/docs/upgrades): the orchestrator stops sending traffic but does not restart the process.
- **An empty queue, a paused queue or a backlog nobody can run does not change readiness.** Readiness is about whether this process can do its job, not about the work.

## Reasons stay private by default

Each result carries a short reason code (`ok`, `stale`, `store_unavailable`, `incompatible`, ...) in its description. The default response writer prints only the overall status, so public endpoints show `Healthy`, `Degraded` or `Unhealthy` and nothing more.

If you want the reasons, write a detailed response and put it behind your own authorization:

```csharp
app.MapHealthChecks("/health/details", new HealthCheckOptions
{
    ResponseWriter = async (ctx, report) =>
    {
        ctx.Response.ContentType = "application/json";
        await ctx.Response.WriteAsJsonAsync(report.Entries.ToDictionary(
            e => e.Key,
            e => new { status = e.Value.Status.ToString(), reason = e.Value.Description }));
    },
}).RequireAuthorization("ops");
```

## Without ASP.NET Core

The same data is available from `IRunwickHealth` in dependency injection: `Liveness()` returns one `RunwickRoleHealth`, `Readiness()` returns one per enabled role, each with `Role`, `Status`, `Reason` and `ObservedAt`. A worker service without a web server can expose it however your platform expects, for example by touching a file.

<Callout type="tip" title="The incompatible-store alert">

The shipped Prometheus rule `RunwickStoreIncompatible` reads a gauge that your host exports, set to 1 while any `runwick-*` readiness check reports reason `incompatible`. See [Observability](/docs/observability#grafana-dashboard-and-prometheus-alerts).

</Callout>

---

# Retention

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/retention

> How Runwick deletes old payloads, finished jobs, audit rows and history, and how to tune the cleanup.

Without cleanup, payloads, errors, finished jobs, audit rows and history would grow forever. Every worker process runs a background cleanup loop that removes old records in small, resumable batches. It never removes a record that something still depends on, and it never touches a job that is waiting, running or retrying.

## What gets deleted, and when

There is one retention policy per application. Each kind of record has its own age limit:

| Policy value | Default | What it removes |
|---|---|---|
| Completed detail | 7 days | Payload and error text of jobs that succeeded or were cancelled |
| Failed detail | 30 days | Payload and error text of failed jobs |
| Job history | 90 days | The rest of a finished job (its row, generations, attempts) and its events |
| Audit | 90 days | Management audit rows |
| Scaling events | 7 days | Automatic concurrency history |
| Schedule occurrences | 30 days | Which schedule fires created which jobs |
| Worker presence | 24 hours after expiry | Heartbeat rows of workers that went away |

Jobs go in two steps. First the **detail** expires: payload and error text are deleted, but the job's identity, state and history stay, and the job is marked "detail expired". Revealing its payload then answers `410 detail_expired`. Later, once job history expires, the whole job goes. After that a lookup by its ID answers `404`, and nothing tells it apart from an ID that never existed.

Some records follow fixed rules that no policy can shorten: command receipts until their replay window ends, uniqueness keys until their window ends, rate-limit grants until they leave the rate window, outbox mappings until 24 hours past their horizon. Concurrency scopes, queue controls and schedules are never deleted.

## Changing the policy

The policy is edited through the [management API](/docs/management-api) or the dashboard's Retention page, with the `Retention.Manage` permission. Every edit is checked against the current revision and audited. There is no CLI command for it.

```bash
# read the current policy and its revision (needs Settings.Read)
curl -b jar https://ops.example.com/runwick/api/v1/retention
```

```json
{
  "commandId": "0193c3b2-7f1e-7c4a-9d1e-5b1f0a2c3d4e",
  "expectedRevision": 0,
  "completedDetailHours": 72,
  "failedDetailHours": 720,
  "jobHistoryHours": 2160,
  "auditHours": 8760,
  "scalingEventsHours": 168,
  "scheduleOccurrencesHours": 720,
  "workerPresenceHours": 24,
  "reason": "shorter payload retention for GDPR"
}
```

Post that body to `{prefix}/v1/retention/policy` with the antiforgery header. Revision `0` means the defaults are still in force.

Rules:

- Every value is whole hours, from 1 to 87,600 (ten years).
- Audit is kept at least 7 days.
- Job history must be at least as long as both detail values.
- `null` means keep forever, except worker presence, which is required.

<Callout type="warning" title="Send every value">

A value you leave out of the body is read as `null`, which means *keep forever*. Read the current policy first and send all seven values back.

</Callout>

## Tuning the cleanup loop

The loop runs in every process that calls `AddWorker`. Producer-only processes, schedulers and the standalone management host do not run it. Several workers cooperate through a progress row per record class, so only one batch of a class runs at a time and cleanup resumes where it stopped after a crash.

```csharp
runwick.AddWorker(w => w
    .Pool("main", p => p.Queues("default"))
    .Retention(r =>
    {
        r.BatchRows = 500;
        r.BatchPause = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200);
    }));
```

| `RetentionOptions` | Default | Allowed |
|---|---|---|
| `Enabled` | `true` | |
| `BatchRows` | 100 | 1 to 1,000 rows per batch |
| `BatchDetailBytes` | 1 MiB | 64 KiB to 16 MiB of payload and error text per batch |
| `BatchTarget` | 500 ms | 50 ms to 2 s of database time a batch aims at |
| `BatchPause` | 1 s | 0 to 60 s between batches of one class |
| `IdlePoll` | 60 s | 1 s to 1 h after a pass that found nothing |

A failed batch backs off from 5 seconds, doubling up to 5 minutes. Values outside the bounds stop the app at startup.

### Cleanup is bounded work

Each process runs one batch at a time. It skips rows that are locked, so it never waits on live work, and it pauses while the worker is draining or under pressure. At the defaults that is roughly 100 rows a second for one busy class in one process. A store that finishes more than about 5 million jobs a day needs bigger batches, shorter pauses or more worker processes.

Cleanup does not promise to keep up with any load. It tells you when it falls behind:

- the dashboard's Retention page shows each class's progress and marks a class "behind" when no pass caught up in the last 24 hours;
- the `runwick.retention.caught_up.age` gauge and the `RunwickRetentionFailing` alert (see [Observability](/docs/observability));
- log events 1501 (batch failed) and 1503 (behind).

Cleanup itself writes one summary audit row per class per day, not one row per deleted record. Those rows do not list which rows were deleted. Cleanup never changes a health check.

## Backups and copies

Deleting a row does not erase it from backups, replicas, exports or log pipelines. If you have a legal reason to remove data, you also need a retention plan for those copies. Runwick has no "delete this job now" request and no legal hold.

Restoring a backup brings old rows back; the cleanup loop removes them again on its next passes. See [Upgrades](/docs/upgrades) for what else a restore changes.

---

# Deployment

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/deployment

> Process shapes, containers, the migration step, shutdown timeouts, capabilities and a checklist for going live.

Runwick has no server of its own. It runs inside your processes, and the store (PostgreSQL, SQLite or Redis) is the only shared part. What a process does is decided by its configuration, not by which program it is.

## Roles

| Role | Turned on by |
|---|---|
| Producer | Always: any process with `AddRunwick` can dispatch |
| Worker | `AddWorker(...)` |
| Scheduler | `AddScheduler()` |
| Management host | `MapRunwickManagement(...)` and/or `MapRunwickDashboard(...)` |

A process can have any combination.

## Common shapes

<Tabs>
<Tab label="One app">

One web app dispatches, runs workers, runs the scheduler and serves the dashboard. Simplest to run, and fine for many apps.

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRunwick(r =>
{
    r.Application("shop").UsePostgres(cs).AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining<Program>();
    r.AddHandlersFromAssemblyContaining<Program>();
    r.AddScheduler();
    r.AddWorker(w => w.Pool("main", p => p.Queues("default").FixedConcurrency(8)));
});
```

The trade-off: a slow job and a web request compete for the same CPU, and every deploy restarts both.

</Tab>
<Tab label="Web producer + worker service">

The web app only dispatches (no `AddWorker`). A separate worker service, built with `Host.CreateApplicationBuilder`, runs the handlers. The two can share a contracts project with `Runwick.Contracts`, so the web app needs no handler code.

```csharp
// web app
builder.Services.AddRunwick(r => r.Application("shop").UsePostgres(cs)
    .AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining<SendReceipt>());

// worker service
var builder = Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddRunwick(r =>
{
    r.Application("shop").UsePostgres(cs).AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining<SendReceipt>();
    r.AddHandlersFromAssemblyContaining<SendReceiptHandler>();
    r.AddScheduler();
    r.AddWorker(w => w.Pool("main", p => p.Queues("default").FixedConcurrency(16)));
});
builder.Build().Run();
```

You can scale and deploy the two separately.

</Tab>
<Tab label="Many replicas">

Several identical instances, each dispatching and working. Every replica claims from the same store; leases make sure one job has one owner at a time.

Keep in mind: concurrency limits declared on jobs and queues hold across replicas, because they are kept in the store. But rate limits on the management API, the producer's local limits and the automatic concurrency controller work **per process**. Ten replicas allow ten times the management API rate.

</Tab>
</Tabs>

SQLite supports all of these only when every process is on the same machine. See [Choosing a store](/docs/choosing-a-store).

## Migrations are a separate step

Runwick does not migrate the store when your app starts. Run migrations as a deploy step, with credentials that may create schemas:

```bash
runwick migrate --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_MIGRATE_CS
```

or from code, for example in a one-off job:

```csharp
await RunwickPostgresMigrations.MigrateAsync(migrationConnectionString);
```

The running app can then use a role that only reads and writes data. `migrate` is safe to run again: a second run applies nothing.

A binary works with exactly one store revision. A process that meets a store at another revision refuses to run. So on an upgrade the migration step is part of a short stop of new work, not something you can roll out replica by replica. [Upgrades](/docs/upgrades) has the procedure.

## Containers and shutdown

The worker needs up to 25 seconds to stop cleanly (drain, then cancel, then write results). Give it room at every layer:

| Layer | Default | Set it to |
|---|---|---|
| Runwick `ShutdownBudget` | 25 s | Leave it, or change the slices in [Workers](/docs/workers#shutdown) |
| .NET `HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout` | 30 s | Above Runwick's budget |
| Container grace period (Kubernetes `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`) | 30 s | Above the host's timeout |

```csharp
builder.Services.Configure<HostOptions>(o => o.ShutdownTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(35));
```

```yaml
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
```

If a process is killed early, no data is lost, but its running jobs wait for their leases to expire (60 seconds by default) before another worker takes them. Handlers should honour their `CancellationToken` so the cancel step finishes in time.

Map [health checks](/docs/health-checks): liveness on the `live` tag, readiness on `ready`. A draining worker is not ready but still alive, so the orchestrator stops routing to it without restarting it.

## Capabilities

Schedules and rate limits need a capability turned on once per application, by an operator:

| Feature | Capability | Error without it |
|---|---|---|
| `AddScheduler`, `AddSchedule` | `scheduler` | Startup fails with `scheduler_not_active` |
| `RollingWindow(...)` rate limits | `rate_admission` | Dispatching a rate-limited job is refused with `rate_admission_not_active`; nothing is written |

The order is: start the application once so it registers itself, activate, restart.

```bash
runwick store activate-capability --name scheduler --application shop \
  --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_MIGRATE_CS
```

<Callout type="danger" title="Activation cannot be undone">

Once raised, a capability stays. A binary that does not know it can no longer create work for that application. Activate only when every process that uses the store runs a release that supports it.

</Callout>

## Checklist

<Steps>
<Step title="Pick the store and check its settings">

PostgreSQL 16 to 18 connected directly to the primary; SQLite on a local disk; Redis 8.2 or newer, one primary, with `appendfsync always` and `noeviction`. Runwick refuses unsafe settings at startup.

</Step>
<Step title="Run migrations as their own step">

`runwick migrate` with the migration role, before the app starts. Use the CLI from the same release.

</Step>
<Step title="Activate capabilities you need">

`scheduler` and `rate_admission`, once per application, after its first start.

</Step>
<Step title="Set shutdown timeouts">

Runwick 25 s, host above that, container grace period above the host.

</Step>
<Step title="Map health checks">

`AddHealthChecks().AddRunwick()`, with `live` and `ready` endpoints wired to your orchestrator.

</Step>
<Step title="Secure the management API and dashboard">

Real sign-in, a grant mapping you have reviewed, HTTPS. Share the Data Protection key ring across replicas.

</Step>
<Step title="Export telemetry">

Traces and metrics through OpenTelemetry. Turn on `CollectApplicationMetrics` in one process, import the Grafana dashboard and the alert rules, and tune the thresholds.

</Step>
<Step title="Plan backups and restores">

Back up the store like any database you depend on, and read [Upgrades](/docs/upgrades) before the first upgrade, not during it.

</Step>
</Steps>

---

# Upgrades and restores

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/upgrades

> How to upgrade Runwick safely, why there is no rolling upgrade, and what a restore from backup does and does not bring back.

Read this before your first upgrade. One rule shapes everything else:

<Callout type="warning" title="One binary, one store revision">

A Runwick release works with exactly one store revision. Once the new schema is in place, the previous release cannot run at all: it cannot create work and it cannot finish work. There are no down migrations. The only way back is the backup you took before migrating.

</Callout>

So an upgrade is a short stop of new work: **drain, stop the old processes, migrate, reopen, start the new ones**. Plan for that, not for a rolling deploy.

## Before you start

- Use the CLI from the **new** release for `migrate`, and the **currently deployed** CLI for the `store` commands before migrating. Check with `runwick version`.
- Have the migration-role credentials. The app's runtime role cannot run these commands.
- Know every process that uses the store: workers, producers, schedulers, dashboards, CLI hosts. You must be able to stop each one. Runwick cannot stop them for you, and cannot prove that they stopped.

The examples use PostgreSQL. Use `--provider sqlite` with a database file, or `--provider redis` with a Redis configuration string, the same way. `RUNWICK_STORE` is the name of an environment variable holding the migration-role connection string.

## Upgrade, step by step

<Steps>
<Step title="Back up">

PostgreSQL: `pg_dump -Fc mydb > before-upgrade.dump`. SQLite: stop every process on the file and copy it (with its `-wal` and `-shm` files), or run `sqlite3 runwick.db ".backup before-upgrade.db"`. Redis: copy the AOF or RDB files the way you normally do.

</Step>
<Step title="Look, then drain">

```bash
runwick store status    --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_STORE
runwick store admission --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_STORE --mode drain
```

`store status` shows the store revision, the revision this CLI expects, each application's admission mode, and how many leases and worker heartbeats exist. Drain stops all new work (dispatch, claims, scheduled jobs, retries) and lets running work keep renewing and finish. Add `--application NAME` to drain one application.

If you get `migration_lock_timeout`, a transaction that stages jobs has been open for over 5 seconds. Wait and try again.

</Step>
<Step title="Wait, then stop every old process">

Run `store status` until it shows no owned leases, or decide to abandon what remains (an abandoned lease expires and the new version recovers it). Then stop the old workers, producers, schedulers and dashboards yourself.

Do not read an expired lease or an expired heartbeat as "stopped". A paused or cut-off process looks exactly the same.

</Step>
<Step title="Migrate">

```bash
runwick migrate --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_STORE
```

It prints the store ID, the new revision and what it applied. Running it again applies nothing.

</Step>
<Step title="Reopen">

```bash
runwick store admission --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_STORE --mode open
```

Reopen **before** starting the new processes. A process that starts while its application is drained is refused at startup with `AdmissionClosedException`, because registering its queues counts as new work. Nothing was written; reopen and start it again.

</Step>
<Step title="Start the new release">

Start workers, then producers, then dashboards. Check with `runwick doctor --connection-env RUNWICK_STORE` (the revision check passes when the CLI and the store agree) and `store status`.

</Step>
</Steps>

### If migrate fails

| Code | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `migration_connection_lost` | The session holding the migration lock died | Run again; it resumes where it stopped |
| `migration_lock_timeout`, `migration_lock_unavailable` | Another migrator, or a long transaction | Wait, run again |
| `schema_validation_failed` | Something in the database differs from what this release expects | Do not force it. The store stays at the last good revision and no release can run on it. Read the message, repair or restore, run again |
| `migration_checksum_mismatch` | A released migration was changed | Stop. You are running a different build from the one that migrated this store |
| `migration_unknown` | The store is **newer** than this CLI | You are rolling back by accident. Use the matching CLI, or restore |

### If it goes wrong

- **Before migrate finished:** nothing changed shape. Reopen with `--mode open` and keep running the old release.
- **After migrate:** the old release cannot run. Restore the backup from step 1 and run the old release with the old CLI. Work done after the backup is lost.
- **An old process is still running:** its next call is refused and nothing is written. Stop it anyway.

## Capabilities cannot be undone

`scheduler` and `rate_admission` are turned on with `runwick store activate-capability`. That is a second one-way door, separate from migrations:

- A capability is never lowered. There is no command to turn it off.
- A release that does not know the capability can no longer create work for that application. It can still renew and finish jobs it already holds.
- Each activation writes an audit row and an event.

Activate only after every process on the store runs a release that supports it.

## Schedules after an upgrade

- While an application is drained, the scheduler creates no jobs and its position does not move. After reopening, each schedule's misfire policy decides what happens to the fires it missed: skipped, run once, or caught up.
- If a new release brings a new schedule evaluator or new time-zone data, roll the release out to **every** scheduler host first, and only then change schedule definitions to use it. A host that does not know the new version skips that schedule and says so in its logs.

## Restoring from a backup

A restore is a step back in time, and Runwick cannot tell that it happened. After a restore:

- jobs and results written after the backup are gone;
- a dispatch your callers saw succeed may now be unknown, and resending it creates the job again unless its idempotency key survived;
- schedules move back and their fires run again or are skipped, following each schedule's misfire policy;
- fencing tokens and rate-limit windows can hand out values they already handed out;
- outbox messages delivered after the backup may be delivered again.

Runwick does not undo emails sent or payments taken in the lost window. You reconcile those.

### Replace, or copy?

| Situation | Identity |
|---|---|
| **Replace** a broken store. The original is gone and will never run again | Keep the store ID |
| **Copy** that runs beside the original (staging, inspection, disaster-recovery rehearsal) | Give it a **new** ID before anything connects |

When unsure, give it a new ID. A new ID is harmless. A duplicate ID lets commands meant for one store land in the other.

<Steps>
<Step title="Stop everything that can write">

Workers, producers, schedulers, dashboards, CLI hosts. If the old store is still reachable, put it in maintenance so a straggler is refused: `store admission --mode drain`, then `--mode maintenance`. Maintenance can only be reached from drain.

</Step>
<Step title="Restore it">

PostgreSQL: `createdb restored && pg_restore -d restored --no-owner before-upgrade.dump`. SQLite: copy the file back. Redis: restore the AOF the way you normally do. A backup from an older schema needs the older release and CLI if you want to stay on that release.

```bash
runwick store status --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_RESTORED
```

</Step>
<Step title="Copy only: give it a new identity">

```bash
runwick store admission  --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_RESTORED --mode drain
runwick store admission  --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_RESTORED --mode maintenance
runwick store reidentify --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_RESTORED --confirm
```

`reidentify` refuses unless every application is in maintenance and the store records no live leases or heartbeats. Right after a restore it may refuse because the backup carried heartbeats of processes that were running; wait until they expire. After it succeeds, anything bound to the old ID is refused with `store_identity_mismatch` and nothing is written.

</Step>
<Step title="Reopen and start">

`store admission --mode open`, then start the processes.

</Step>
<Step title="Reconcile">

Go through effects outside the database, lost acknowledgements, schedules, fences and outbox deliveries, as listed above. Decide per job type whether to run again or suppress.

</Step>
</Steps>

## What Runwick does not promise

- No mixed-version operation, no rolling upgrade across schema revisions, no zero-downtime migration. Drain pauses new work, not running work.
- No downgrade. Rolling back means restoring, and restoring loses what came after the backup.
- No proof that an old process has stopped, from leases, heartbeats or time.
- No automatic detection of a copy. You must re-identify it yourself.
- Admission and identity changes write no audit row. Capability activations do.

---

# Delivery guarantees

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/delivery-guarantees

> What Runwick promises about running your jobs, how to make repeated runs harmless, and the list of things it does not claim.

Runwick is at-least-once. A confirmed job is not lost, but its handler can run more than once. Exactly-once is available in one case: effects inside the same database as the job store, through [transactional completion](/docs/transactions). For everything else, use idempotency keys.

## At-least-once

A handler can run again when:

- the worker crashes after the work but before it records the result;
- the worker loses its lease while the handler is still running (for example after a long pause), and another worker takes the job;
- the reply from the store is lost, and the attempt cannot be settled in time.

In each case Runwick runs the job again rather than risk losing it. So write handlers that are safe to repeat.

### When a dispatch is confirmed

`DispatchAsync` returns a `DispatchReceipt` only after the store has confirmed the write. The receipt's `ConfirmedAcknowledgementProfile` says what "confirmed" means for that store:

| Store | Confirmed means |
|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | the transaction committed |
| SQLite | the commit is on disk, with WAL and `synchronous=FULL` |
| Redis | the write is in the append-only file and synced, under `appendfsync always` |

If `DispatchAsync` throws an error whose `Disposition` is `KnownNotApplied`, nothing was written. If it throws `DispatchOutcomeUnknownException` (codes `outcome_unknown`, `cancelled_after_send` or `expired_unknown`), the write may or may not have happened.

### Resolving an unknown outcome

Do not simply dispatch again: that may create a second job. The exception carries the operation ID and the prepared request:

```csharp
try
{
    await dispatcher.DispatchAsync(new ChargeCard(orderId), cancellationToken: ct);
}
catch (DispatchOutcomeUnknownException ex)
{
    // Ask the store what happened to this exact operation...
    var resolution = await prepared.ResolveAsync(ex.OperationId, ct);   // prepared: IPreparedJobDispatcher
    if (resolution.Status == DispatchResolutionStatus.Confirmed)
    {
        // the job exists: resolution.Receipt
    }
    // ...or send the same prepared request again. A replay returns the original result.
    else if (ex.Prepared is { } same)
    {
        await prepared.DispatchAsync(same, ct);
    }
}
```

A prepared dispatch keeps its operation ID, so sending it again replays the same command and never creates a second job. It is valid until its deadline (5 minutes by default). [Dispatching](/docs/dispatching) covers `IPreparedJobDispatcher` in detail.

## Make repeats harmless: idempotency keys

When a handler talks to something outside Runwick's database (an email service, a payment API, another database), pass a key that is the same on every run and let the other side ignore duplicates. A good key is stable and comes from the job, for example the job ID from [`IJobContext.JobId`](/docs/job-context) or a business ID in the payload. Many APIs accept an `Idempotency-Key` header for exactly this.

```csharp
public sealed class ChargeCardHandler(IJobContext context, IPaymentClient payments) : IJobHandler<ChargeCard>
{
    public Task HandleAsync(ChargeCard job, CancellationToken ct) =>
        payments.ChargeAsync(job.OrderId, job.Amount, idempotencyKey: $"charge:{context.JobId}", ct);
}
```

The job ID stays the same across retries of one job. Do not use the attempt ID: it changes on every run.

## Uniqueness is not idempotency

People say "idempotent" for three different problems. Runwick solves two of them.

| You want to avoid | Use |
|---|---|
| Two copies of a job queued at once | `UniqueWhileActive` (an active key) |
| A client retry creating a second job | `UniqueWithinWindow` (a window key) |
| Two jobs running at the same time for one resource | A concurrency limit, for example `PerResource(..., capacity: 1)` |
| A repeated run having a visible effect twice | Idempotency keys in your handler, or transactional completion |

Dispatch uniqueness prevents a duplicate **insert**. It never promises that a handler runs once: retries and recovery can still run the one job more than once. See [Uniqueness](/docs/uniqueness) and [Rate limits and concurrency](/docs/rate-limits-and-concurrency).

## The one exactly-once case

If the handler's effect is a change in the same PostgreSQL database or SQLite file as Runwick's tables, the change and the job's completion can commit together:

```csharp
await using var tx = await connection.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);
// ... your changes on tx ...
await completion.CompleteInTransactionAsync(tx, ct);   // IPostgresJobCompletion or ISqliteJobCompletion
await tx.CommitAsync(ct);
```

Either both are saved or neither is. This covers effects inside that one database only. Redis has no transactional completion. [Transactions](/docs/transactions) has the rules.

## The outbox

To create a job in a store other than your business database, the [outbox](/docs/outbox) commits a message with your data and a relay delivers it. Delivery is at-least-once, with de-duplication on the receiving side for a limited window (7 days by default). It is not exactly-once dispatch and it does not keep order.

## What Runwick does not claim

<Callout type="warning" title="Read this before you rely on Runwick">

- **No exactly-once in general.** A handler may run more than once.
- **Cancellation is cooperative.** It cancels a `CancellationToken`. Your code must observe it. See [Cancellation](/docs/cancellation).
- **A lost lease does not prove the old handler stopped.** Two copies can briefly overlap. Concurrency limits count valid leases, not code that is physically still running. Fencing tokens ([`IJobContext.Fences`](/docs/job-context)) help only if the resource you write to rejects lower values.
- **"Began" does not prove your code ran.** A crash right after an attempt began is recorded as abandoned.
- **Timeouts measure the handler pipeline**, not what happened in the outside world. There is no default timeout.
- **A restored database is a break in history.** Receipts, uniqueness windows and fences from before the restore are not guaranteed to behave as one continuous record.
- **A schedule creates at most one job per occurrence**, and that job is at-least-once like any other. Pausing a schedule does not pause jobs it already created.
- **Counts and metrics can be lost on a crash.** They are not for billing or audit.
- **No high availability claim** for any store. Failover and restored backups are outside what is tested.
- **No platform claims beyond what is tested**: Linux x64 and Windows x64 on .NET 10. No claim for Native AOT or trimming.

</Callout>

---

# Configuration

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/configuration

> Every default in one place, for jobs, workers, producers, stores, retention, the scheduler, the outbox relay and the fixed limits.

All configuration goes through `AddRunwick(runwick => ...)` and the store, outbox and management extensions. Times are as written. Runwick checks every value at startup and refuses a configuration it cannot run safely. It never quietly adjusts a value for you.

## Per job

Set per job with an attribute or the fluent builder, or for all jobs with `runwick.JobDefaults(...)`. Later layers win: library default, then `JobDefaults`, then attribute, then fluent.

| Setting | Default | Attribute / fluent |
|---|---|---|
| Queue | `default` | `[Queue("emails")]` / `.ToQueue("emails")` |
| Priority | `medium` (`low`, `medium`, `high`) | `[Priority("high")]` / `.WithPriority("high")` |
| Maximum executions (counts real starts, so 3 means two automatic retries) | 3 | `[MaxExecutions(5)]` / `.WithMaxExecutions(5)` |
| Execution timeout | none | `.WithExecutionTimeout(...)` / `.WithoutExecutionTimeout()` |
| Retry delay (exponential, half random) | 5 s first, never more than 60 s | `.WithRetryDelay(initial, max)` |
| Re-queue after a worker took a job but never started it | up to 5 times | `.WithMaxUnstartedAbandonments(n)` |
| Delay between those re-queues | 1 s growing to 30 s | `.WithUnstartedRecoveryDelay(initial, max)` |
| Uniqueness, rate limits, concurrency limits | off until you declare them | `.UniqueWhileActive(...)`, `.RollingWindow(...)`, `.MaxConcurrent(...)` and others |

With the defaults, the first retry waits between 2.5 and 5 seconds, the second between 5 and 10. See [Retries and timeouts](/docs/retries-and-timeouts).

```csharp
runwick.JobDefaults(d => d.WithMaxExecutions(5).WithRetryDelay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10), TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2)));
runwick.AddJob<BuildReport>()
    .ToQueue("reports")
    .WithPriority("low")
    .WithExecutionTimeout(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2));
```

## Worker: `WorkerOptions`

Set with `runwick.AddWorker(w => w.Configure(o => ...))`. Most apps never touch these. They are tied together; see [Startup validation](#startup-validation).

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `LeaseDuration` | 60 s | How long a claim on a job lasts before it must be renewed |
| `LeaseSafetyMargin` | 10 s | The worker treats the lease as expired this much early |
| `RenewalInterval` / `RenewalJitter` | 15 s / 3 s | Renew every 12 to 18 s |
| `LeaseWatchdogInterval` | 1 s | How often the safety watchdog checks leases (at most 1 s) |
| `SchedulerAllowance` | 2 s | Allowance for timer lag |
| `ControlRequestTimeout` | 5 s | Longest wait for one claim, renew or finish call |
| `ControlRetryInitialBackoff` / `ControlRetryMaxBackoff` | 100 ms / 1 s | Backoff between retries of those calls |
| `MinimumInvocationMargin` | 15 s | Lease time that must be left to start a handler |
| `ClaimResolutionBudget` / `BeginResolutionBudget` | 15 s / 15 s | How long to resolve an uncertain claim or start |
| `CompletionResolutionBudget` | 30 s | How long to resolve an uncertain finish |
| `CancellationGrace` | 10 s | Time a cancelled handler gets to exit |
| `CleanupBudget` | 10 s | Time for the attempt's scope to dispose |
| `OwnershipCommandLifetime` | 30 s | Deadline of each claim, renew or finish command |
| `RecoveryScanInterval` / `RecoveryScanJitter` | 5 s / 1 s | Scan for jobs of crashed workers every 4 to 6 s |
| `ShutdownBudget` | 25 s | Total time for Runwick's shutdown |
| `ShutdownDrain` / `ShutdownCancellation` / `ShutdownFinalization` | 15 s / 5 s / 5 s | The three shutdown stages; their sum must fit in `ShutdownBudget` |
| `RecordResourceUsage` | `true` | Store CPU time, allocations and working set per attempt |

Keep the host's shutdown timeout (`HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout`, 30 s by default in .NET) above `ShutdownBudget`. Runwick does not change it for you.

### Pools

| Setting | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pool size | fixed 4 | `.FixedConcurrency(n)` with n at least 1, or `.AutoConcurrency(min, max)`; not both |
| Queue weight | 1 | `.Queue(name, weight)`, 1 to 1,000 |
| Lane selection | `Weighted` | `.LaneSelection(...)`: `Weighted`, `StrictWithAging` or `Strict` |
| Lane weights high : medium : low | 6 : 3 : 1 | `.LaneWeights(h, m, l)`; a waiting lane ages after 60 s |
| Most jobs one worker holds at once | 16 | `w.MaxOutstandingAttempts(n)`; the sum of pool maximums must fit |

## Producer: `ProducerOptions`

Set with `runwick.Producer(o => ...)`.

| Option | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `MaxConcurrentCalls` | 8 | Dispatch calls in flight at once; at least 1. On PostgreSQL, raising it adds connections. |
| `MaxWaitingOperations` | 64 | Callers waiting for a slot; more fail with `local_capacity_exceeded` without sending anything |
| `AdmissionWait` | 1 s | Longest wait for a slot |
| `CommandLifetime` | 5 min | How long a prepared dispatch stays valid; also the maximum |

## Stores

| Option | Default | Allowed |
|---|---|---|
| `PostgresOptions.Schema` | `runwick` | only `runwick` |
| `SqliteOptions.WriterBusyTimeout` | 2 s | 100 ms to 30 s |
| `SqliteOptions.ReaderThreads` | 2 | 1 to 8 |
| `RedisOptions.ProfileRecheckInterval` | 30 s | 5 s to 5 min |

See [PostgreSQL](/docs/postgresql), [SQLite](/docs/sqlite) and [Redis](/docs/redis).

## Retention

Cleanup runs in worker processes. Its budgets are set with `w.Retention(r => ...)`:

| `RetentionOptions` | Default | Allowed |
|---|---|---|
| `Enabled` | `true` | |
| `BatchRows` | 100 | 1 to 1,000 |
| `BatchDetailBytes` | 1 MiB | 64 KiB to 16 MiB |
| `BatchTarget` | 500 ms | 50 ms to 2 s |
| `BatchPause` | 1 s | 0 to 60 s |
| `IdlePoll` | 60 s | 1 s to 1 h |

How long records are kept is a stored policy per application, edited through the management API. The defaults:

| Record | Kept for |
|---|---|
| Detail of succeeded jobs | 7 days |
| Detail of failed jobs | 30 days |
| Job history | 90 days |
| Audit | 90 days |
| Scaling events | 7 days |
| Schedule occurrences | 30 days |
| Worker presence | 24 hours |

Cleanup is bounded work, not a promise to keep up with any load. Deleting rows does not erase backups or copies. See [Retention](/docs/retention).

## Scheduler: `SchedulerOptions`

Set with `runwick.AddScheduler(o => ...)`. The scheduler needs the `scheduler` capability raised once per application, or startup fails with `scheduler_not_active`.

| Option | Default |
|---|---|
| `PollInterval` | 1 s while work is due |
| `IdlePollInterval` | 5 s when idle (15 s on PostgreSQL while its listener is healthy) |
| `JobsPerSecond` / `Burst` | 100 / 32 per scheduler process |

Per schedule: misfire policy `RunOnce` with 60 s grace (up to 24 h); catch-up at most 1,000 jobs per episode and 7 days back. See [Schedules](/docs/schedules).

## Outbox relay: `OutboxRelayOptions`

| Option | Default | Allowed |
|---|---|---|
| `Enabled` | `true` | |
| `MaxInFlight` | 4 | 1 to 64 |
| `LeaseDuration` / `RenewalInterval` | 60 s / 15 s | lease at least 5 s and at least 3 renewals |
| `ProviderCallTimeout` | 5 s | shorter than `RenewalInterval` |
| `IdlePoll` | 1 s | positive |
| `RetryInitial` / `RetryMax` | 1 s / 60 s | |
| `TransportLifetime` | 30 s | at most 30 s |
| Acceptance horizon (per message, `OutboxStageOptions`) | 7 days | up to 30 days |

See [Outbox](/docs/outbox).

## Telemetry: `RunwickTelemetryOptions`

Set with `runwick.Telemetry(o => ...)`.

| Option | Default | Allowed |
|---|---|---|
| `RecordExceptionDetails` | `false` | Puts a cleaned, bounded exception message on spans and logs |
| `MaxSeriesPerInstrument` | 1,000 | 100 to 10,000 |
| `CollectApplicationMetrics` | `false` | Makes this process the application-wide metrics collector |
| `ApplicationSamplePeriod` | 15 s | 5 s to 5 min |
| `CollectorName` | `default` | |

## Management and dashboard

Management needs authentication schemes and a grant mapping, or it does not start. There is no anonymous mode. The dashboard title defaults to `Runwick`. See [Management API](/docs/management-api) and [Dashboard](/docs/dashboard).

## Fixed limits

These cannot be configured.

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Serialized payload | 1 MiB of JSON, 32 levels deep |
| Application, queue and pool names | 1 to 128 characters, `[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*` |
| Job names | 1 to 200 characters, same characters |
| Uniqueness and resource keys | 1 to 512 bytes of UTF-8 |
| Business metadata | 16 KiB and 32 entries |
| Batch dispatch | 100 items or 2 MiB |
| Rate limit | 1 to 100,000 per window; window 1 s to 24 h; at most 8 rate scopes per job |

## Startup validation

When the host starts, Runwick checks the whole configuration and throws `RunwickConfigurationException` listing every problem at once. Each entry has a code, the setting it is about, and the rule it broke. Timing problems have the code `invalid_timing`:

```text
Runwick configuration is invalid:
  [invalid_timing] LeaseDuration: V-04: RenewalIntervalMax + 2·ControlRequestTimeout + ControlRetryMaxBackoff + SchedulerAllowance (31000 ms) must be < LeaseDuration − LeaseSafetyMargin (20000 ms).
```

The worker timings must satisfy these rules. The defaults pass all of them:

| Rule | With defaults |
|---|---|
| Every duration is positive and a whole number of milliseconds (`RenewalJitter` and `RecoveryScanJitter` may be 0) | pass |
| `LeaseSafetyMargin` is less than `LeaseDuration` | `10 s < 60 s` |
| `RenewalInterval − RenewalJitter` is above zero | 12 s > 0 |
| `(RenewalInterval + RenewalJitter) + 2 × ControlRequestTimeout + ControlRetryMaxBackoff + SchedulerAllowance` is less than `LeaseDuration − LeaseSafetyMargin` | `31 s < 50 s` |
| `MinimumInvocationMargin` is at least `2 × ControlRequestTimeout + ControlRetryMaxBackoff + SchedulerAllowance` | 15 s ≥ 13 s |
| `LeaseWatchdogInterval` is at most 1 s | 1 s |
| `ControlRetryInitialBackoff` is at most `ControlRetryMaxBackoff` | 100 ms ≤ 1 s |
| `ControlRequestTimeout` is less than `OwnershipCommandLifetime` | `5 s < 30 s` |
| `ShutdownDrain + ShutdownCancellation + ShutdownFinalization` is at most `ShutdownBudget` | 25 s ≤ 25 s |
| Each resolution budget is at least `ControlRequestTimeout` | 15, 15, 30 s ≥ 5 s |
| `RecoveryScanJitter` is less than `RecoveryScanInterval` | `1 s < 5 s` |

<Callout type="tip" title="Scale timings together">

Setting `LeaseDuration` to 30 s on its own fails: 31 s of renewal path does not fit in 20 s of usable lease. Raising `ControlRequestTimeout` to 10 s fails too, because the start margin then needs 23 s. If you change one timing, scale the related ones with it, for example a 120 s lease with a 20 s safety margin and a 30 s renewal interval.

</Callout>

Other startup errors you may see: `invalid_pool` (for example a pool that subscribes a queue no job or `Queue(...)` call registers), `pool_without_queue`, `pool_budget_exceeded` (pool maximums add up to more than the worker's limit), `invalid_policy` for store options, and `missing_store` when no store is configured. [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting) lists the common ones.

---

# Testing

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/testing

> Test handlers as plain classes, fake IJobDispatcher in code that dispatches, and run end-to-end tests against a real SQLite file.

Runwick's public surface is small and made of interfaces, so most tests need no special library: a handler is a plain class, and dispatching goes through `IJobDispatcher`. For the full path (dispatch, claim, run, finish), run a real worker against a temporary SQLite file.

<Callout type="info" title="About Runwick.Testing">

The `Runwick.Testing` package is reserved for test helpers (a recording dispatcher and a direct handler invoker), but in this release it does not contain any public types yet. The patterns on this page use only the main packages.

</Callout>

## Testing a handler

A handler is a class with a `HandleAsync` method. Construct it with its dependencies and call it:

```csharp
public sealed class SendWelcomeEmailHandler(IEmailSender email) : IJobHandler<SendWelcomeEmail>
{
    public Task HandleAsync(SendWelcomeEmail job, CancellationToken cancellationToken) =>
        email.SendAsync(job.UserId, "welcome", cancellationToken);
}

public class SendWelcomeEmailHandlerTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Sends_the_welcome_template()
    {
        var email = new FakeEmailSender();
        var handler = new SendWelcomeEmailHandler(email);

        await handler.HandleAsync(new SendWelcomeEmail(UserId: Guid.NewGuid()), CancellationToken.None);

        Assert.Equal("welcome", Assert.Single(email.Sent).Template);
    }
}
```

Test the things Runwick relies on too:

- **Repeats are harmless.** Call `HandleAsync` twice with the same job and check that the outside effect happened once, or that the same idempotency key was used both times. Runwick can and will run a handler more than once; see [Delivery guarantees](/docs/delivery-guarantees).
- **Cancellation is observed.** Pass a cancelled token and check that the handler stops with an `OperationCanceledException` instead of finishing the work.
- **Permanent failures are permanent.** If the handler throws `PermanentJobFailureException` for bad input, assert that it does.

### Handlers that use `IJobContext`

`IJobContext` is an interface, so a test can pass its own implementation. A small fake with settable properties is enough:

```csharp
sealed class FakeJobContext : IJobContext
{
    public string Application { get; init; } = "tests";
    public JobId JobId { get; init; } = new(Guid.NewGuid());
    public AttemptId AttemptId { get; init; } = new(Guid.NewGuid());
    public int Generation { get; init; } = 1;
    public int ExecutionNumber { get; init; } = 1;
    public int MaxExecutions { get; init; } = 3;
    public string JobName { get; init; } = "test.job";
    public string Queue { get; init; } = "default";
    public string Priority { get; init; } = "medium";
    public int OriginalPayloadVersion { get; init; } = 1;
    public int CurrentPayloadVersion { get; init; } = 1;
    public string SerializerProfileId { get; init; } = "test";
    public int SerializerProfileVersion { get; init; } = 1;
    public DateTimeOffset CreatedAt { get; init; } = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow;
    public IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> Metadata { get; init; } = new Dictionary<string, string>();
    public JobTraceContext Trace { get; init; }
    public IReadOnlyList<ResourceFence> Fences { get; init; } = [];
    public JobScheduleInfo? Schedule { get; init; }
    public JobCancellationCause CancellationCauses { get; init; }
    public IDictionary<object, object?> Items { get; } = new Dictionary<object, object?>();
    public object? Payload { get; init; }
    public TJob GetPayload<TJob>() where TJob : class, IQueueJob => (TJob)Payload!;
}
```

Then test, for example, that a handler uses the job ID as its idempotency key, or behaves differently on the last attempt:

```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task Uses_the_job_id_as_the_idempotency_key()
{
    var context = new FakeJobContext();
    var payments = new FakePaymentClient();
    var handler = new ChargeCardHandler(context, payments);

    await handler.HandleAsync(new ChargeCard(OrderId: 42, Amount: 10m), CancellationToken.None);
    await handler.HandleAsync(new ChargeCard(OrderId: 42, Amount: 10m), CancellationToken.None);

    Assert.All(payments.Calls, c => Assert.Equal($"charge:{context.JobId}", c.IdempotencyKey));
}
```

## Testing code that dispatches

`IJobDispatcher` has two methods. A recording fake that returns a receipt is a dozen lines:

```csharp
sealed class RecordingDispatcher : IJobDispatcher
{
    public List<(IQueueJob Job, DispatchOptions? Options)> Dispatched { get; } = [];

    public Task<DispatchReceipt> DispatchAsync<TJob>(TJob job, DispatchOptions? options = null, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
        where TJob : class, IQueueJob
    {
        Dispatched.Add((job, options));
        return Task.FromResult(Receipt());
    }

    public Task<BatchDispatchReceipt> DispatchManyAsync(IReadOnlyList<BatchDispatchItem> items, BatchDispatchOptions? options = null,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
    {
        Dispatched.AddRange(items.Select(i => (i.Job, i.Options)));
        return Task.FromResult(new BatchDispatchReceipt(new DispatchOperationId(Guid.NewGuid()),
            [.. items.Select((_, i) => new BatchItemResult(i, Receipt(), null))], "test"));
    }

    static DispatchReceipt Receipt() => new(new JobId(Guid.NewGuid()), new DispatchOperationId(Guid.NewGuid()),
        DispatchDisposition.Created, DuplicateMatch.None, PolicyDrift: false, ConfirmedAcknowledgementProfile: "test");
}
```

Use it in place of the real dispatcher:

```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task Signup_queues_a_welcome_email()
{
    var jobs = new RecordingDispatcher();
    var service = new SignupService(new FakeUserStore(), jobs);

    var userId = await service.SignUpAsync("ada@example.com", CancellationToken.None);

    var (job, _) = Assert.Single(jobs.Dispatched);
    Assert.Equal(new SendWelcomeEmail(userId), job);
}
```

A fake cannot tell you whether the real store would accept the job: unknown queues, keys that are too long and payloads over 1 MiB are only refused by the real dispatcher. Cover those with an end-to-end test.

To test how your code handles failures, make the fake throw the real exception types, for example `DispatchOutcomeUnknownException` or `LocalCapacityExceededException`.

## End-to-end with a real SQLite file

SQLite needs no server, so a test can create a fresh database file, start a real host with a worker, dispatch a job and wait for the handler. The handler signals a `TaskCompletionSource` from dependency injection:

```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting;
using Runwick;

public class WelcomeEmailEndToEndTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task A_dispatched_job_runs_on_the_worker()
    {
        var path = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), $"runwick-{Guid.NewGuid():N}.db");
        var connection = $"Data Source={path}";
        await RunwickSqliteMigrations.MigrateAsync(connection);

        var ran = new TaskCompletionSource<Guid>(TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously);
        var builder = Host.CreateApplicationBuilder();
        builder.Services.AddSingleton(ran);
        builder.Services.AddRunwick(runwick =>
        {
            runwick.Application("tests").UseSqlite(connection);
            runwick.AddJob<SendWelcomeEmail>();
            runwick.AddHandler<SendWelcomeEmail, SignalingHandler>();
            runwick.AddWorker(w => w.Pool("main", p => p.Queues("default").FixedConcurrency(1)));
        });

        using var host = builder.Build();
        await host.StartAsync();
        try
        {
            var userId = Guid.NewGuid();
            var dispatcher = host.Services.GetRequiredService<IJobDispatcher>();
            await dispatcher.DispatchAsync(new SendWelcomeEmail(userId));

            Assert.Equal(userId, await ran.Task.WaitAsync(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)));
        }
        finally
        {
            await host.StopAsync();
            foreach (var file in new[] { path, path + "-wal", path + "-shm" })
            {
                File.Delete(file);
            }
        }
    }

    sealed class SignalingHandler(TaskCompletionSource<Guid> ran) : IJobHandler<SendWelcomeEmail>
    {
        public Task HandleAsync(SendWelcomeEmail job, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
        {
            ran.TrySetResult(job.UserId);
            return Task.CompletedTask;
        }
    }
}
```

Tips:

- Give every test its own file. Runwick refuses in-memory databases, so a temporary file is the way to isolate tests.
- Keep the temp directory on a local disk. A network share is refused.
- Leave a generous timeout. Workers poll, and a fresh worker needs a moment to start.
- Use the same registration code as production where you can, and swap only the store line.

### When to test against PostgreSQL or Redis

All three stores give the same job behaviour, so SQLite covers most application tests. Test against your production store when the test depends on store-specific behaviour: staging jobs or completing them in your PostgreSQL transaction, connection limits, or Redis server settings. A disposable server per test run (for example with Testcontainers) works well. Remember to run the store's migration first.

---

# Troubleshooting

URL: https://runwick.temtem.dev/docs/troubleshooting

> Common startup refusals, error codes and stuck jobs, each with its cause and the fix.

Runwick prefers refusing to start over running in a setup that could lose jobs. Most problems therefore show up as a clear error at startup, with a stable code. Every Runwick exception has a `Code` and a `Disposition`: `KnownNotApplied` means nothing was written, `OutcomeUnknown` means it may or may not have been.

## Startup refusals

<Accordion>
  <AccordionItem title="Runwick configuration is invalid (configuration_invalid)">

`RunwickConfigurationException` lists every problem at once, one per line, as `[code] subject: message`. Common codes:

- `invalid_timing`: worker timings break one of the startup rules, for example a shorter `LeaseDuration` without shorter renewals. See [Startup validation](/docs/configuration#startup-validation).
- `invalid_pool`: a pool subscribes a queue that no job or `Queue(...)` call registers, subscribes one twice, or has a bad weight or size.
- `pool_without_queue`, `pool_budget_exceeded`: a pool has no queue, or pool maximums add up to more than `MaxOutstandingAttempts` (16 by default).
- `missing_store`: no `UsePostgres`, `UseSqlite` or `UseRedis`, or an empty connection string.
- `invalid_policy`: a store option is out of range, or the SQLite connection string asks for something refused.

Fix the listed settings. Runwick never adjusts a value for you.

  </AccordionItem>
  <AccordionItem title="scheduler_not_active">

The application registers schedules, but the `scheduler` capability has not been raised. Start the application once so it registers, then, with the migration role:

```bash
runwick store activate-capability --name scheduler --application my-app --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_MIGRATE_CONN
```

Use `--provider sqlite` or `--provider redis` for those stores, and `--name rate_admission` if you use rate limits. Restart afterwards. This is done once per application and cannot be undone. See [Schedules](/docs/schedules).

  </AccordionItem>
  <AccordionItem title="The Runwick schema is not installed, or schema_incompatible">

The store has not been migrated, or it was migrated by a different Runwick version than the one running. Workers never migrate on startup. Run the migration with the same Runwick version as the app:

```bash
runwick migrate --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK_MIGRATE_CONN
```

or `RunwickPostgresMigrations.MigrateAsync` / `RunwickSqliteMigrations.MigrateAsync` / `RunwickRedisMigrations.MigrateAsync` from code. See [Upgrades](/docs/upgrades) for the order of steps when the version changes.

  </AccordionItem>
  <AccordionItem title="Startup refused: the application's admission is closed">

The application was drained or put in maintenance (for example during an upgrade), so new processes are refused with `AdmissionClosedException` (`admission_closed`). Reopen it when the upgrade is done:

